b: scmJS documentation scmJS is a StarCraft: Brood War map editor that runs in a browser tab or as a desktop app. It opens, edits and saves StarCraft maps: .scm , .scx and .chk files and reads .rep files. The latest version of the editor is always available at scmjs.dev/editor . See the getting started page for more information. What it does Beyond the terrain, units, locations and triggers every StarCraft editor has, scmJS does the following. Items marked Browse Plugins are one click away under Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins… rather than installed from the start. Classic or Remastered graphics. Pointed at a Remastered installation, the editor draws with Remastered's terrain, units and moving water; View ▸ Remastered Graphics switches back. See Classic or Remastered graphics . Replays. File ▸ Open Replay… opens a .rep on the map it was played on, with the players' orders on a timeline, build orders and the chat. At scmjs.dev the game also plays back and is analysed: fights, economy and tech. See Replays . Test in the game or the browser. Tools ▸ Test Map puts the map in the game's Maps folder; at scmjs.dev, Tools ▸ Test Map in Browser plays it in a browser tab from your own StarCraft files. See Test Map . Several people on one map. Share the open map and anyone with the link edits it with you, live. See Editing a map together . Triggers as code. TrigScript writes triggers in TypeScript, with tests and a simulator; for Remastered it also builds code that runs in the game itself. AI on your own key. With your Anthropic API key, an assistant reads and edits the open map with you, and Tools ▸ AI lays out maps, writes triggers and briefings, and reviews a map. The prompts are public in ai-engine . See The AI . Triggers as a graph. Trigger Map ( Browse Plugins ) shows which triggers set and read each switch, death counter and location, and what is never set, read or run. The ground as a unit walks it. View ▸ Walkability (Ctrl+Shift+W) draws islands, regions, chokes with their widths, and distances between start locations. Damaged and protected maps. Repair checks each map as it opens and fixes what the game would; Section Explorer ( Browse Plugins ) shows the file byte by byte. See Protected and damaged maps . Nothing lost on save. Unknown or malformed sections and unnamed archive files are written back as they were read, unless the game would refuse the map as it stands. See Opening and saving maps . Terrain from a picture. File ▸ Import ▸ Terrain from Image… turns an image into terrain, cliffs and shores included. See Plugins . Stamps. Save a ramp, a bridge or a mineral line once and lay it down on any map. See Cut, copy and paste . Doodads into terrain. Convert Doodad to Terrain turns a doodad into ordinary tiles you can edit. See Doodads . A recording of the build. Timelapse ( Browse Plugins ) records the map change by change and exports a GIF or WebM video. See Plugins . Maps from scmscx.com. File ▸ Find on scmscx.com… searches the community map archive and opens the map you pick. See Opening a map . Work kept. Maps open in tabs, recovery copies of unsaved work, and the version a save replaced kept as a .bak or under File ▸ Previous Versions. See Saving and Recovery copies . English or Korean. Preferences ▸ General switches the language. See Keyboard and preferences . Installing Running the editor in the browser, as a desktop app or in a container, and giving it the game's graphics from your StarCraft folder. scmJS runs in a web browser, as a desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux, or from a container on your own server. Whichever you choose, the editor needs StarCraft's graphics, which are not shipped with it: on first use it asks for your StarCraft folder and reads them from there once. This page covers each way of running the editor and that first question. The user guide starts once the editor is open. In the browser scmjs.dev/editor is the newest numbered release. The desktop app The releases page has the installers. In a container The editor can also run from a container, for a server on your own network or to run it locally: The graphics The editor draws terrain and units with graphics out of StarCraft's own files. From source Building the editor yourself needs Node.js 22.18 or newer and git:

In the browser scmjs.dev/editor is the newest numbered release. There is nothing to install. Your maps stay on your own disk, and nothing about them is sent anywhere unless you use a network feature, such as a copy kept on your scmjs.dev account, a map you share for others to edit with you, or an AI request on your own Anthropic key. The user guide describes each. scmjs.dev/nightly is rebuilt every night from the latest changes, for trying what is in development. It keeps its own settings, plugins and sign-in, but shares the game's graphics with the stable editor and the play page, so you add them once for all three. Chrome and Edge save a map back to the file you opened. In Firefox and Safari every save is a download, and File ▸ Open Recent asks for the file again. The hosted editor, the nightly and the documentation site count visits, and the editor counts which of its features are used: the name of a dialog that opened, the layer an edit was on, the kind of file a map was saved as. They never send a map, its name, a file name or anything you typed, and set no cookies. Preferences ▸ General ▸ Privacy turns the counting off, and the site's privacy page says exactly what is sent. The desktop app and a copy you host yourself count nothing.

The desktop app The releases page has the installers. These links always point at the newest numbered release: System Download Windows, installer scmJS-windows-x64-setup.exe Windows, zip to unpack and run scmJS-windows-x64.zip macOS, Apple silicon scmJS-macos-arm64.dmg macOS, Intel scmJS-macos-x64.dmg Linux, AppImage scmJS-linux-x86_64.AppImage Linux, Debian and Ubuntu scmJS-linux-amd64.deb The app looks for a StarCraft installation on its own, registers .scm , .scx and .chk so a double-click opens a map, and starts the game for Test Map. Windows # The installer and the app are not code-signed, so Windows shows a SmartScreen screen saying the app is unrecognized. Choose More info , then Run anyway . The zip needs no installation: unpack it anywhere and run scmJS.exe . macOS # Open the dmg and drag scmJS into Applications. macOS refuses to open an app that is not code-signed, so clear the quarantine flag once, in Terminal: xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/scmJS.app Linux # Make the AppImage executable and run it: chmod +x scmJS-linux-x86_64.AppImage ./scmJS-linux-x86_64.AppImage Or install the .deb : sudo apt install ./scmJS-linux-amd64.deb Updates # The app checks for a new version when it starts (a preference, on by default) and when you choose Help ▸ Check for Updates…. A new version shows up as a notice with a Download button. Nothing downloads or installs until you ask, and installing asks about unsaved maps first, as closing the window does. Windows, the AppImage and the .deb install the update themselves. macOS cannot replace an app that is not code-signed, so the app offers the release page instead. A preference lets the app follow the nightly builds instead of the numbered releases. After an update, a notice offers the list of what changed; Help ▸ What's New… shows it at any time. The browser editor does the same. Where it keeps its files # The app's data folder holds the graphics it extracted, the window's size and position, and startup.log , a record of the last launch: System Folder Windows %APPDATA%\scm-js macOS ~/Library/Application Support/scm-js Linux ~/.config/scm-js If the app is slow to open, or opens and shows nothing, startup.log says how long each step of the launch took; attach it to a bug report. Deleting the gamedata folder inside makes the app look for StarCraft again at the next start.

In a container The editor can also run from a container, for a server on your own network or to run it locally: docker run --rm -p 8080:80 ghcr.io/scm-js/scm-js:latest then open http://localhost:8080 . The image is the same editor as the numbered release it is tagged with. It carries no game data, so it asks for your StarCraft folder like the hosted editor. To serve graphics you have already extracted instead, see The container image . Each release also has scmJS-web.zip , the same editor as plain files. Unpack it at the root of any static web server.

The graphics The editor draws terrain and units with graphics out of StarCraft's own files. Blizzard's data is not redistributable and none of it ships with the editor, so on first use the Game Data dialog asks where to get it: The recommended route is your own StarCraft installation, classic (1.16) or Remastered. If you have neither, Blizzard's free map editor download is enough to edit maps and watch replays. What each route gives you: Route Editing Remastered graphics Test Map and playing Replays Your StarCraft: Remastered folder Yes Yes Yes Yes Your classic StarCraft (1.16) folder Yes No, but can be added Yes Yes Blizzard's map editor download Yes No No Yes Test Map and playing means Tools ▸ Test Map, which hands the map to the installed game, and Tools ▸ Test Map in Browser at scmjs.dev, which plays it on the site's play page from your own StarCraft files. Neither works from the map editor download. Replays means File ▸ Open Replay… and watching the game play back. If the editor was opened from a link (a shared map to join, or a copy of a map), that link is handled first, and the question about the graphics follows. Use your StarCraft installation # This is the card marked Recommended at the top of the dialog. In the browser , choose Choose the StarCraft folder… and pick the folder the game is installed in, usually C:\Program Files (x86)\StarCraft . The browser asks whether to upload the folder. Nothing leaves your computer: the editor only reads the files. In the desktop app , there is nothing to do if the game is where its installer put it: the app finds it at start. Otherwise choose Search this computer , or Choose the StarCraft folder… to point at it yourself. Classic or Remastered is told from the folder. A Remastered folder turns on View ▸ Remastered Graphics , which you can untick at any time for the classic look; the guide's Classic or Remastered graphics shows the difference. The editor copies what it needs and keeps it, so this happens once. In the browser the copy also keeps the files the site's play page runs the game from, so the game is set up once for both. The tick box Keep the files for real-time lighting on the play page adds what the play page needs to light units as Remastered does, about 200 MB more. Rough sizes of the copy: Copy Browser Desktop app From a classic (1.16) installation or the download about 140 MB about 30 MB From a Remastered installation about 650 MB about 365 MB From Remastered, with the lighting files about 850 MB — Reading a Remastered installation takes under a minute. No StarCraft installed? # The lower part of the dialog has two ways in without an installation: Download from Blizzard — 83 MB. Blizzard offers its standalone StarCraft map editor as a free download, and the package carries the files the graphics come from. No account, nothing to find on your own disk. The editor fetches only the parts it needs. Choose StarDat.mpq and BrooDat.mpq… (browser only). Pick the two archives yourself, from the map editor download or from a classic installation's folder. A copy made from the map editor download is enough to edit maps and watch replays. Testing a map or playing needs StarCraft installed. Once you have it, open Help ▸ Game Data… , choose Remove copy , and choose the StarCraft folder when the dialog asks again; for Remastered, Add StarCraft: Remastered… also works, as below. Remastered graphics # Choosing a Remastered folder in the first place is all it takes: the editor reads the Remastered graphics with the rest and turns them on. If you installed from a classic copy or the map editor download first and get Remastered later, open Help ▸ Game Data… and choose Add StarCraft: Remastered… under Data sets . It is installed beside the copy you have, and the Data sets list switches between the two. Remastered added tiles, and so doodads, to most tilesets. A map that uses them needs the Remastered files to be drawn; from a classic copy those tiles have no picture. Changing it later # Help ▸ Game Data… brings the dialog back. It shows where the graphics come from now, and lets you: remove the copy ( Remove copy ), after which the dialog offers the routes above again; install a data set , a mod's files beside the game's, and switch between them (see Data sets ); add StarCraft: Remastered beside a classic copy, as above. At scmjs.dev, scmjs.dev/editor/data lists every copy the browser holds, with where it came from and how large it is. Without any graphics the editor still runs: terrain is drawn in flat colours and units as coloured markers, and everything else works.

From source Building the editor yourself needs Node.js 22.18 or newer and git: git clone https://github.com/scm-js/scm-js cd scm-js npm install npm run dev # http://localhost:5173 A source build gets its graphics from npm run extract (see Extracting for a source build ) or from Help ▸ Game Data… like any other copy. The rest, including building the desktop app and the container image, is in development.md .

User guide How to use the editor: a first map, then each layer and dialog — terrain, units, triggers, settings, testing and saving — replays, plugins, and editing a map together. This guide is for map makers. It starts with getting the editor running, walks through a first map, and then goes through each layer and dialog in turn. TrigScript, triggers written as code, has a guide of its own ; the technical side — file formats, game data, writing plugins, building from source — has documents of its own, listed in the README . Beta. This editor needs to be extensively tested. Keep backups of maps you care about, and check anything important in-game before you rely on it. Getting started There are three ways to run scmJS, each covered in docs/installing.md: The editor window The window has nine parts, numbered in the picture below. Classic or Remastered graphics The editor can draw a map with the classic graphics or with StarCraft: Remastered's. Your first map This section walks through a small melee map from start to finish. Terrain Terrain is painted with four brushes, each a tab in the palette: Doodads Doodads are the trees, rocks, ruins, ramps and bridges of a map: pieces of terrain that come with their own tiles and, sometimes, a sprite drawn over them. Units The Units layer places everything the game has a unit for: the three races' units and buildings, heroes, critters, resources, start locations, beacons and powerups. Sprites There are two kinds of sprite. Locations Locations are the rectangles that triggers refer to, as in "bring a unit to *Beacon*" or "create a unit at *Spawn*". Fog of war The fog of war decides which tiles a player starts the game unable to see. Cut, copy and paste To copy part of a map, drag on it with the Cut / Copy / Paste layer active (C) to mark a rectangle, then Ctrl+C or Ctrl+X. Triggers Triggers turn a map into a scenario: *when* these conditions hold, *for* these players, *do* these actions. TrigScript TrigScript writes triggers as code: TypeScript files kept inside the map. Scenario settings The Scenario menu holds the map's own tables. Checking, testing and saving Before a map is played, it can be checked for common mistakes, tried in the game, and saved in the form you want to release. Replays The editor opens StarCraft replays (.rep files) and shows, on the map the game was played on, what the players did: where buildings went down and when, where units were sent, each player'… Plugins Plugins add tools to the editor, and several of the tools in this guide are plugins. Your scmjs.dev account scmjs.dev is the project's own service. Editing a map together Several people can work on one map at the same time, each in their own editor. The AI Tools ▸ AI holds an assistant that reads and edits the open map with you, and tools that lay out maps, write triggers, names and briefings, review a map and rewrite its strings. Keyboard and preferences Press F1 for a list of every shortcut. When something goes wrong If the editor does something strange, the debug console shows what happened, Copy Bug Report puts it on the clipboard, and Report an Issue sends it to the project. What it does not do This section lists what the editor does not do, and the limits worth knowing before you rely on a feature.

Getting started There are three ways to run scmJS, each covered in docs/installing.md : In the browser at scmjs.dev/editor . Nothing to install, and your maps stay on your own disk. As a desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux, from the releases page. It finds a StarCraft installation on its own and opens a map on a double-click. In a container , for a server on your own network: docker run --rm -p 8080:80 ghcr.io/scm-js/scm-js:latest , then open http://localhost:8080 . The game's graphics # StarCraft's graphics do not ship with the editor. On first use it asks where to get them, and the recommended answer is your StarCraft folder : the classic game (1.16) or StarCraft: Remastered. Choose Choose the StarCraft folder… and pick the folder the game is installed in, usually C:\Program Files (x86)\StarCraft . The browser asks whether to upload the folder; nothing leaves your computer, the files are only read. The desktop app looks for an installation on its own, and has a Search this computer button as well. Picking a Remastered folder also turns on Remastered graphics . Without StarCraft installed, the dialog offers Blizzard's free StarCraft map editor download (83 MB), which carries the graphics. You can also pick StarDat.mpq and BrooDat.mpq from a classic installation by hand. What each source allows: Where the files come from Edit maps Watch replays Test or play on scmjs.dev Your StarCraft folder, classic or Remastered Yes Yes Yes StarDat.mpq and BrooDat.mpq from a 1.16 installation Yes Yes Yes Blizzard's map editor download Yes Yes No The files are read once and a copy is kept for next time. The graphics has the steps in full. Without any graphics the editor still runs, with terrain in flat colours and units as coloured markers. Help ▸ Game Data… opens the same dialog later. It shows where the current copy came from and can remove it. Under Data sets it installs a mod's files beside the game's and switches between them, and offers Add StarCraft: Remastered… when you have a classic copy and no Remastered one. A tick keeps the extra files the play page needs for real-time lighting (about 200 MB more). Data sets explains how mods are installed. Opening a map # Ctrl+O (File ▸ Open…) opens a .scm , .scx or .chk file, and so does dropping one on the window. File ▸ Open Recent lists what you have had open before. In Chrome, Edge and the desktop app it reopens the file straight from disk. File ▸ Find on scmscx.com… searches the community map archive and opens the map you pick. A link like https://scmjs.dev/editor/scmscx/35b32Dsq , with the id from the map's address on scmscx.com, opens the editor with that map picked. File ▸ Open from scmjs.dev… lists the maps kept on your scmjs.dev account, with every revision you saved (see Your scmjs.dev account ). File ▸ Open Replay… opens a replay over the map it was played on (see Replays ). A map opens in its own tab, beside the ones already open (see The editor window ). The blank map the editor starts on is the exception: the first map you open takes its place. A map that is damaged, or that a map protector has altered, is checked and repaired as it opens. See Damaged and protected maps .

The editor window The window has nine parts, numbered in the picture below. Menu bar. Every command is here, with its shortcut beside it. The dot at the right end glows while the map has unsaved changes. Toolbar. New / open / save, undo and redo, cut / copy / paste, the active layer and brush size, the grid, locations and fog-of-war toggles, symmetry, find, zoom, and buttons for Player Settings, the Trigger Editor and Test Map. Layer rail. The seven layers, top to bottom: Terrain, Doodads, Units, Sprites, Locations, Fog of War, Cut / Copy / Paste. The keys T D U S L F C switch between them. Palette. What the active layer places: terrain types and brushes, doodads, unit types, sprites, the location list, the fog players, the clipboard options. Map. Drag to paint or place, click to select, double-click for properties. Right-click opens a context menu, or stops whatever you are placing. Minimap. Click or drag on it to move the view. Layers panel. The eye hides a layer's objects from the view; the padlock locks a layer so its tools stop changing the map. Plugin overlays (Walkability, say) are listed under it. Properties. What is selected, or what is under the cursor: for a tile its id, group, elevation, walkability and buildability; for a unit its owner, position and vitals; for a location its bounds and elevation flags. Status bar. The tile and pixel under the cursor, the tile id, map size, tileset, layer and zoom, and a line saying what the last action did or why it was refused. At the right end, your scmjs.dev account (or Sign in to scmjs.dev ), and the AI cell when the AI is on; each is a click to open. Several maps # Open a second map and a row of tabs appears under the toolbar, one per open map, with a glowing dot on any that has unsaved changes. Click a tab to switch, or use the Window menu (Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+Shift+Tab in the desktop app). The × on a tab, a middle click, or File ▸ Close Map closes that map, asking about unsaved changes first. Each map keeps its own undo history, selection and view, so switching back lands where you left off. With one map open the row is hidden. To work on one map at a time, untick Open each map in its own tab in Preferences ▸ General; Open and New then replace the open map. Moving around # Scroll with the mouse wheel (Shift for sideways), the arrow keys (Shift for half a screen), a middle-button drag or the scrollbars, or click on the minimap. A drag that reaches the edge of the window scrolls the view with it, so a stroke, a marquee or a unit being moved can carry on past the screen. It speeds up the further past the edge you push. Zoom with Ctrl++ and Ctrl+−, or the toolbar's magnifiers. Ctrl+0 is 100%, and Ctrl+Shift+0 fits the whole map in the window. Preferences ▸ View can make the wheel zoom instead of scroll. The grid is Ctrl+G. View ▸ Grid Settings… sets its spacing, colour and style. The panels can be hidden from View ▸ Panels, and their widths dragged. Undo # Every layer has its own selection and its own palette. Undo is Ctrl+Z and redo Ctrl+Y. The history is two hundred steps deep and shared across all the layers, so a terrain stroke and the units it stranded come back together. A dialog — player settings, triggers, strings — is its own OK / Apply / Cancel transaction, and each OK or Apply that changed something is one more undo step ("Edit triggers", "Edit settings"), in the same history as the strokes around it.

Classic or Remastered graphics The editor can draw a map with the classic graphics or with StarCraft: Remastered's. View ▸ Remastered Graphics switches between them at any time, for the terrain, the units and the sprites together. The switch changes only how the map is drawn. It does not touch the map, and the brushes behave the same with it on or off. Remastered's pictures have twice the detail, which shows most when you zoom in: at 200% they are drawn pixel for pixel, where the classic ones are each pixel doubled. The Remastered graphics come from a Remastered installation: If you chose your Remastered folder when the editor first asked for the game's files, they are installed and already on. If you installed from a classic copy or Blizzard's download, open Help ▸ Game Data… and choose Add StarCraft: Remastered… under Data sets , then pick the folder Remastered is installed in. The editor keeps a copy of what it needs (a few hundred MB), so this happens once. Installing has the steps in full. Remastered's files also add several hundred doodads to seven of the eight tilesets, and with them installed those doodads are in the Doodads palette, whichever look you draw with. A map that uses one depends on Remastered: it shows blank tiles in an editor with a 1.16 copy, and uses tiles the 1.16 game does not have. Maps that keep to the older doodads are unaffected. Tools ▸ Check Map… says when a map uses any of these tiles, how many, and where the first one is. With View ▸ Animate Water on, water ripples and lava shimmers as they do in Remastered; Desert's tar stays still, as it does in the game. Preferences ▸ View ▸ Graphics sets how strongly and how fast, and whether the editor starts with the Remastered graphics on. A few things differ from the game: units are drawn without its lighting, the minimap keeps the classic colours, and an exported map image has still water. game-data.md explains how the graphics are drawn.

Your first map This section walks through a small melee map from start to finish. Everything here is covered in more depth in the sections that follow. 1. Make the map # Ctrl+N opens New Scenario. Pick a tileset — each is shown as its own ground — a size, and how many players. The terrain list under the size is what the whole map is filled with, and the preview shows the result at its real scale. Place automatically (off by default) lays down one start location per player in a ring; tick it for this map. Give the map a name and a description — both are what players see in the game lobby — and press Create. 2. Shape the ground # Stay on the Terrain layer and the Isometric tab. Pick High Dirt (Badlands; every tileset has a high ground of its own), set the brush to 3×3, and drag across the map. The cliffs around the high ground are laid for you, and where a stroke meets a terrain the new one cannot touch, the terrain in between is put in. Painting Water works the same way and gives you a shore. The brush size keys are [ and ] . Alt+click picks the terrain under the cursor. Ctrl+Z takes back the whole stroke. Ramps are not terrain: they are on the Doodads layer. Type ramp in its search box to list them, click one, and click on a cliff edge; the ghost is red until the footprint sits on ground it fits. 3. Place the bases # Switch to the Units layer ( U ). The start locations are already there. In the palette, Special holds Start Location and Resources holds the mineral fields and the Vespene Geyser, or type a name in the search box. Click a type to arm it, then click on the map to place; Esc or a right-click stops placing. A mineral field holds 1500 minerals and a geyser 5000 gas when placed; double-click one to change the amount, or select a whole line and set them all at once. Eight fields and one geyser is the usual main. Snap to grid keeps buildings and resources on the tile grid where the game expects them. The two ticks above it are the game's own placement rules; a red ghost means the game would drop the unit when it loaded the map, and the status bar says why. For a symmetric map, turn on symmetry with M or the toolbar and pick the mode beside it: what you paint and place is mirrored, and each copy of a start location or base goes to the next player. The Melee Wizard plugin (Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins…) lays out whole bases with the mineral line at the distance the game mines fastest from. 4. Check the players # Scenario ▸ Player Settings… is where each slot's controller, race and colour live. A melee map needs Human and User Selectable on every slot that has a start location; that is what a new map is set to already. Force Settings… groups them into teams for the lobby. Note. A Use Map Settings map is different: give each player a fixed race. The game treats a player left on User Selectable as a melee player, hands them a base and workers, and removes every unit you placed for them. It also removes the units of a human slot nobody takes in the lobby, so put decorations such as beacons on Player 12, the neutral one. 5. Check the map # Tools ▸ Check Map… lists what the game would object to: a start location with no player, units it would leave out, a section it would refuse, and so on. Double-click a line to go to it. View ▸ Walkability (Ctrl+Shift+W) draws the ground as a unit sees it: which areas connect, where the chokes are and how wide, and which pockets cannot be reached at all. It updates as you edit. 6. Save and play # Ctrl+S saves. A new map opens the Save dialog the first time, where the name and the file format are chosen; .scx is a Brood War map. From then on Ctrl+S writes the file in place (Chrome, Edge, the desktop app) or downloads it (Firefox, Safari) — the notice at the bottom right says which. To try the map, press Ctrl+F5 (Tools ▸ Test Map). The game cannot be handed a map from the outside, so the editor writes the map into a scmJS folder under the game's Maps folder, where Single Player ▸ Custom Game lists it; the desktop app then starts the game as well. In the editor at scmjs.dev, Tools ▸ Test Map in Browser plays the map in a browser tab instead. See Test Map . That is a playable melee map. Triggers, briefings, custom unit settings and everything a Use Map Settings map needs are in the sections below.

Terrain Terrain is painted with four brushes, each a tab in the palette: Brush Paints Isometric Terrain types, laying the cliffs and edges around them. The one to use for almost everything. Rect Flat ground of one terrain type, with StarEdit's random variation. No cliffs, no edges. Tile Any single tile by number: cliff pieces, doodad tiles, anything the tileset has. Blend One tile next to a tile you picked, chosen from those whose facing edge continues it. Drag to paint. [ and ] resize the brush from 1×1 to 7×7, Alt+click picks the terrain or tile under the cursor, and right-click offers Pick and Fill Area. The Properties panel breaks the tile under the cursor into group, slot, elevation, walkability and buildability. The isometric brush # The isometric brush is StarEdit's diamond brush. It sets the diamond under the cursor to a terrain and works outward from there: a neighbour that cannot border the new terrain becomes the terrain in between, and cliff faces stack as tall as the tileset draws them. A single click of high ground gives a small mesa; a wider brush gives flat high ground inside a cliff ring. The brush works from the map's isometric record, a part of the file that only editors read. Protected maps often have it stripped; the Repair plugin rebuilds it as such a map opens, exactly where the ground was laid with the isometric brush and as a best guess elsewhere. The Isometric tab warns when the record and the ground disagree, and when part of the map is ground the brush cannot join up with, such as hand-placed tiles or another editor's work. Rect, Tile and Blend # Rect lays flat ground and nothing else, for filling an area you will shape afterwards, or for ground under a doodad. Tile is for the pieces the isometric brush will not give you: a single cliff tile, a doodad's tile, a corner the cliff sets do not have. Blend is for joins the cliff sets never had — dirt into a doodad's base, one edge set into another, a hand-laid shoreline. Click a tile to make it the anchor, and the palette lists for each side the tiles whose opposite edge continues it, best seam first. These three leave the isometric record alone. Overlays and tools # Two overlays on the View menu show what the ground means to the game: View ▸ Walkability (Ctrl+Shift+W) draws the ground as a unit walks it: islands, the areas the map divides into, the chokes between them with their widths, and the distances between start locations. In the editor at scmjs.dev its panel (Tools ▸ Walkability…) can also have the game itself walk the map: the regions the game plans routes over, real units walked between the start locations, a group of twelve units timed through every choke, and how fast each start location mines with 8, 16 and 24 workers. File ▸ Import ▸ Terrain from Image… turns a picture into terrain with the isometric brush, over the whole map or a rectangle. Walkability and Terrain from Image are plugins, on from the start; see Plugins . Tools ▸ Replace Terrain… turns every tile of one terrain type (or one exact tile) into another, over the whole map or the area marked on the Cut / Copy / Paste layer. Tools ▸ Fill Terrain lays the whole map anew. Both are one undo step. Symmetry mirrors what you do across the map's axes or about its centre. M or the toolbar button turns it on and off, and the list beside the button picks the mode: left ↔ right, top ↔ bottom, four-way, a half turn, quarter turns, or either diagonal. The last three need a square map. While a mode is on, the axes show on the map and the ghost shows where the copies will land. The terrain brushes (all but Blend), the fills and the fog brush also paint on the mirror images. Placing a unit, sprite, doodad or location places one at each image as well. Each copy goes to its own player: P1's start location gives P2's under the two-way modes, and P2's, P3's and P4's under the four-way ones. Neutral units and resources stay neutral. A doodad that would have to turn is skipped. Selecting something also selects whatever stands at its images. Dragging then moves them all as mirror images, resizing a location resizes its copies, and Delete removes them all. A map made symmetric by hand works the same way. Each change is one undo step. Tools ▸ Symmetry… describes each mode and has the option to keep copies for the same player instead. The Terrain palette's Remove stranded units tick deletes the ground units a stroke has just left where they cannot walk, which the game would remove at the start, as part of the same undo step. Buildings stay where they are: the game makes them on any ground.

Doodads Doodads are the trees, rocks, ruins, ramps and bridges of a map: pieces of terrain that come with their own tiles and, sometimes, a sprite drawn over them. The palette is built from the current tileset's own groups, with StarEdit's categories and placement rules. Picking a doodad arms placement, and the ghost turns red where the footprint leaves the map, covers another doodad or sits on the wrong terrain. Place anywhere drops that rule; Snap to grid keeps the footprint on StarEdit's two-tile isometric grid, for a move as well as a placement. Right-click or Esc stops placing. Doodads have no names in the game data, so the search box matches what the data does say: the category: bridge , temple , coastal ; the id: #12 ; the footprint: 6×6 ; the sprite or unit an overlay draws: hdrock , Xel'Naga Temple ; ramp , for anything whose tiles are ramp tiles (StarEdit files ramps under cliffs and walls). A placed doodad stays whole — its tiles, its record and any canopy or door overlay — and removing one restores the ground underneath. When you want the tiles without the doodad — a ramp to touch up piece by piece, a cliff edge to paint into — right-click it and choose Convert Doodad to Terrain (the Properties panel has the same button). The tiles stay, the doodad goes, and an overlay stays on as an ordinary sprite. From then on the Terrain layer treats the cells as ground. Place as terrain in the palette does the same at placement, for ramps and cliff pieces you mean to work over by hand.

Units The Units layer places everything the game has a unit for: the three races' units and buildings, heroes, critters, resources, start locations, beacons and powerups. The palette groups them by race, and the search box takes a name or an id. Picking a unit type arms placement, and each click on empty ground places one for the player selected at the top of the palette. Esc or right-click stops placing and drops you into select mode, where a click selects, a drag on empty ground marks a box, and a drag on a unit moves it. Del deletes the selection. Snap to grid puts buildings, resources, start locations and beacons on the tile grid by their placement box, the way StarEdit stores them, and every other unit on the nearest tile centre. Turn it off for pixel placement. It applies to a move as well as a placement, so dragging a unit that sits off the grid brings it back onto it. The placement checks are on by default and refuse a spot with a red ghost and a reason in the status bar. They are the rules the game applies when it loads a map, silently dropping the units that do not fit: no overlapping collision boxes for ground units and buildings; buildable tiles under a building's whole placement box; walkable ground under a unit. The unit in the way gets outlined. Untick the checks to stack units on purpose, and expect the game to keep only the first. Double-click a unit for every field its record holds: owner, position, hit points, shields, energy, resources and hangar count with their "used" ticks, the special properties (cloaked, burrowed, lifted off, hallucinated, invincible), and the related-unit link an add-on or a Nydus Canal uses. The game links two units only when each names the other, so setting the related unit sets the other unit back to this one. With several units selected, only the fields you touch are written to all of them, so a mineral line can be set to one amount in one go. An add-on placed in its spot beside its owner's building is linked to it, as StarEdit does, and so is a building placed where a free add-on of its owner stands. Nydus Canals are linked in pairs as they are placed: each one to its owner's last canal without an exit. A Refinery, Extractor or Assimilator starts with 5000 gas, as a geyser does; without an amount in its record it would have none in the game. Mineral fields and geysers are always placed for Player 12, whatever owner the palette has, as StarEdit places them: a melee game keeps no one else's. Tools ▸ Auto-place Start Locations… puts one start location per player on a ring or in the corners, each moved to the nearest ground the placement checks accept, and selects them so you can drag them where you want. For a melee map, the Melee Wizard plugin (Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins…) lays out symmetric start locations with mineral lines and geysers at the distance the game mines fastest from; see Plugins .

Sprites There are two kinds of sprite. Pure sprites are a graphic drawn where it stands with no unit behind it: tree canopies, markers, glows. Unit sprites are records the game turns into a unit when the map loads, which is how StarEdit does Installation doors and traps. The palette has a tab for each. Pure Sprites lists all 517 entries grouped as Units, Effects and Doodads, the last named after the graphics file since the game has no names for them. Placement is free: click anywhere, no rules to refuse a spot. The Disabled tick is the sprite flag that starts a door or trap closed or switched off. Sprite Properties also shows the 0x4000 bit StarEdit writes on some doodad overlays; the game does not read it, and a sprite faces the way its own animation sets. Doodad overlays are ordinary sprites and can be selected here too. The Properties panel says which doodad one belongs to, and warns that moving it alone leaves the doodad's tiles behind.

Locations Locations are the rectangles that triggers refer to, as in "bring a unit to Beacon " or "create a unit at Spawn ". A melee map needs none. Drag on empty ground to create one, drag the eight handles to resize, drag inside to move, and use the arrow keys to nudge the selected ones (with nothing selected they scroll the view). Snap is off, 8 or 16 pixels, one tile, or 64 pixels; a move snaps the box's corner rather than the pointer, so a box picked up off the grid lands on it. The palette lists every location in use, and Scenario ▸ Locations… is the same list as a sortable table. Double-click one for its name and exact bounds, and for the elevation ticks: a location applies only on the ticked elevations, which is how you keep a trigger from firing on the cliff above it. An amber stripe on a location's row marks one that excludes something. A location can be stored inverted, its right edge left of its left edge or its bottom above its top; some maps do this on purpose, and the bounds in Location Properties can set it. The game finds no units inside such a location, so Bring and the other conditions and actions that look for units there see nothing, while a unit created there still appears at its centre. The map draws an inverted location with a dashed edge, and dragging one of its handles makes it an ordinary location again. A map has a fixed number of location slots — 64 in StarCraft 1.00 maps, 255 in hybrid and Brood War ones. A new location takes the lowest free slot, deleting one empties it, and triggers keep pointing at the slot they named. The 64th slot, numbered 63 in the editor, which counts slots from 0, is Anywhere , the location every trigger can pick, and the game and other editors depend on it covering exactly the map. It is pinned at the top of the list with a lock, never drawn, never picked by a click, and cannot be moved, renamed or deleted. If a map's Anywhere has gone missing or no longer matches the map, the editor offers to put it back. A map built with euddraft (eudplib's build) has no readable locations in the file. Its loader is stored in the location table, scrambled, and the game puts the real locations back when the map starts. Drawn, those slots would cover the whole map, so the editor hides locations when it opens such a map and says so in a notice. Its Show button or the Locations eye brings them back. The next map with real locations shows them again, unless you have turned them on or off yourself in between.

Fog of war The fog of war decides which tiles a player starts the game unable to see. Every player has their own. A new map starts every tile fogged for every player, and that is what the editor draws until the first stroke. Only Use Map Settings games read the fog a map sets: a melee game starts every player fully fogged whatever the map says. Select any of the eight players at the top of the palette and every stroke and fill edits all of them at once; View picks whose fog the map and minimap show. Fog and Clear are the brush modes, Shift-drag paints the opposite, and Alt+click picks up which players have fog on a tile. Fog All, Clear All, Invert and Copy Fog act on the whole map for the selected players. Fogged tiles darken over everything, units and locations included, in the tint the game itself uses for that tileset.

Cut, copy and paste To copy part of a map, drag on it with the Cut / Copy / Paste layer active ( C ) to mark a rectangle, then Ctrl+C or Ctrl+X. On the object layers the same keys act on the selection instead, and the clip is the selection's bounding box carrying just those objects, so a base can be copied from either side. Include says both what a copy takes and what a paste lays down: terrain, doodads, units, sprites, locations, fog. Terrain carries the ground under the doodads too, so a paste without doodads shows plain ground rather than half a tree. Doodads are pasted with their overlays, units get fresh ids with add-on and Nydus links kept when both ends came along, and locations take free slots, which is the one thing a paste can run out of. Ctrl+V arms the pointer with a ghost of the clip. A click stamps it and stays armed for the next; Esc or right-click stops. Merge adds to what is there; Replace clears the units, sprites and doodads under the clip first, though never locations. Terrain from a different tileset is refused, since tile numbers mean something else there, while the objects still paste. The clip survives File ▸ Open, which is how a base moves between maps. A piece worth keeping past this map — a ramp, a bridge, a cliff corner — can be saved as a stamp (Edit ▸ Save as Stamp…, or the right-click menu on the marked area) and laid down on any later map from Tools ▸ Stamp Library…; see Plugins .

Triggers Triggers turn a map into a scenario: when these conditions hold, for these players, do these actions. A Use Map Settings map is built from them. A melee game ignores the map's triggers and applies its own rules, so a melee map needs none. (Blizzard's melee maps carry the three standard ones — defeat, victory, starting resources — for anyone who plays them as Use Map Settings.) Several editors work on the same list of triggers, and you can switch between them freely: The Trigger Editor (Ctrl+T): StarEdit's form. The Text Trigger Editor : the triggers as text in SCMDraft 2's syntax. It is a plugin, installed but off. TrigScript : triggers written as code. See TrigScript . Magenta (Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins…): every trigger as a sentence, with a catalogue of StarCraft: Remastered EUD conditions and actions. Mission briefings have an editor of their own. The trigger reference has a page for every condition and action. To see how a map's triggers fit together, the Trigger Map plugin (Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins…) draws them as a graph: which triggers set a switch, a death counter or a location and which ones read it, with a list of switches nothing sets, counters nothing reads and triggers that never run. The Trigger Editor # Ctrl+T, or Triggers ▸ Trigger Editor…. A player filter on the left, the trigger list in the middle, and for the selected trigger its players, up to 16 conditions and up to 64 actions. The Players tab offers the owners the game hands triggers to: Players 1–8, All Players and the four forces. A trigger ticked for nothing else never runs, so the other groups (Player 9–12, Current Player, Foes, Allies and the rest, which are arguments rather than owners) only show when a trigger already has one ticked, to be cleared. Every condition and action the game has is there, except that Mission Briefing is offered only in briefings, since in a trigger it is never true. Each argument gets a widget of its kind — a player pick, a unit type list, a location list, a number, a text box with the colour codes — and any value the lists do not include can still be typed as a raw number, which is how EUD values and unusual unit ids get in. An item can be disabled without deleting it; a disabled one is kept in the file and skipped by the game. Preserve trigger is the flag that keeps a trigger firing more than once. A new Create Unit , Create Unit with Properties or Set Deaths starts on Terran Marine rather than Any unit : the game creates nothing for a unit class, and Set Deaths on Any unit writes nothing. A Create Unit amount of 0 makes one unit, where elsewhere 0 means all of them. The unit list of the two Create Unit actions holds only what the game will create, the units of StarEdit's palette; larvae, eggs, traps, doors and the like are left out, because the game refuses them. The Text Trigger Editor # The same triggers as text, in SCMDraft 2's TrigEdit syntax, so text from SCMDraft pastes in and text from here pastes back out. Compile checks it and reports the first line that does not parse. It is the TrigEdit plugin, installed but starting off : tick it on in Plugins ▸ Manage Plugins…, and Triggers ▸ Text Trigger Editor… and its Ctrl+Shift+T appear. A leading ; disables a line, and a Flags: block carries the trigger flags SCMDraft has no syntax for. The Briefing switch at the top edits the mission briefing in the same syntax. Mission briefings # Triggers ▸ Mission Briefing Editor… (also Scenario ▸ Mission Briefing…) is the same form over the briefing actions: text, portraits, transmissions and the pauses between them, one briefing per player. The layout matches the briefings on Blizzard's own multiplayer maps. Unit properties slots # Triggers ▸ Unit Properties Slots… is the table behind the Create Unit with Properties action: 64 slots, each the hit points, shields and energy (as percentages), resources, hangar count and special states a trigger applies to the units it creates. The action's argument lists the slots by what they set and opens this editor on one. EUD # For EUD work, the player pick next to a Deaths condition or Set Deaths action has an EPD box: type a memory address and it becomes the player value that reaches it through the deaths table, and a raw value shows which address it reaches. Check Map points out the raw values so they are not mistaken for errors. For named reads and writes of the game (a unit's hit points, a player's minerals), use a TrigScript program or Magenta. Both make maps that play on StarCraft: Remastered only. Importing, exporting and checking triggers # File ▸ Import and File ▸ Export (also Triggers ▸ Import Triggers… and Export Triggers…) carry triggers as .trg files, SCMDraft's format, or as text. An import can be added to the map's triggers or replace them. A .trg holds string numbers rather than text, so it fits only a copy of the same map; text works between maps. Triggers ▸ Validate Triggers is Check Map limited to the triggers.

TrigScript TrigScript writes triggers as code: TypeScript files kept inside the map. It is a plugin, on from the start, and Triggers ▸ TrigScript… opens it once a map is open. Each trigger() call the script makes becomes an ordinary trigger, the same kind the Trigger Editor shows, and plays on any version of the game. Code inside program(() => { … }) runs in the game itself, with variables, arrays, functions and loops, and a map with a program in it needs StarCraft: Remastered . TrigScript has a guide of its own : Quick start : a first script, from opening the window to the triggers it makes. Writing triggers : trigger() and the helpers for writing many at once. Programs : code that runs in the game. Its language and its library of modules have guides of their own: TrigScript language and TrigScript library . Coming from eudplib : where each eudplib and epScript idea went, for map makers who build EUD maps with euddraft. Testing and Simulate : trying the script in the simulator, and tests that run after every change. The workspace : the script window, its files, and the script in a panel beside the map. Reference : every function, and what is not supported.

Scenario settings The Scenario menu holds the map's own tables. Each dialog is its own OK / Apply / Cancel transaction, and what an OK or Apply wrote is one undo step: Ctrl+Z after closing the dialog takes the whole of it back, and Ctrl+Y puts it on again. Map Properties, Players, Forces, Colours # Map Properties (Alt+Enter) is the name and description the lobby shows, the tileset, the size and the revision, with buttons to the rest. Changing the tileset lays the terrain again with a terrain you pick — tile numbers mean something else in every tileset — and drops the doodads, while units, sprites, locations, fog and triggers stay. You can also keep the tile numbers, to see what they draw in the new tileset. Resize / Crop Map… grows or trims the map about a corner or the centre. Both clear the undo history. Player Settings is each slot's controller (Human, Computer, Rescuable, Neutral…), race, colour and force. Force Settings groups the players into up to four teams and sets, per team, allied victory, shared vision, allies and random start locations. Player Colors picks each slot's palette colour and, for Remastered, a custom RGB, random, or the player's own choice; the map repaints as you change them. What the game shows depends on the map's revision: Brood War and Remastered 1.21+ : the game reads the palette colours. Only the first twelve work as a palette colour: for the rest StarCraft 1.16.1 shows a wrong colour and Remastered the player's usual one, and Tools ▸ Check Map says so. StarCraft 1.00, Hybrid and Remastered without Brood War : StarCraft 1.16.1 shows every player in their slot's usual colour, whatever the map says. Remastered takes the colours from its own colour table, which the editor writes whenever a colour is not the slot's own. In Remastered, a custom RGB gives the player any colour, those ten included. Random and the player's own choice both show as Random in the lobby, the player's choice as a list the player can change, and a player left on Random gets a different colour each game. Units, upgrades and technology # Unit Settings , Upgrade Settings and Technology Settings edit the cost and availability tables: a unit's hit points, armour, build time, cost and weapon damage, a custom name, and which players may build it; an upgrade's cost and levels; a technology's cost, and whether each player starts with it or may research it. A row on use default shows the game's own numbers greyed out, and starts from them when you untick it. Strings # Every piece of text a map carries — its name, the force names, location names, every trigger message — is a numbered string, and the String Editor lists them all with where each is used. Edits keep their number, so triggers and locations keep pointing where they did; Delete unused clears out what nothing refers to. The row of buttons inserts the game's colour codes, each drawn in the colour it produces, and the preview under the box shows the string the way the game draws it. The same codes work in every field whose text the game draws: the map name and description, force names, custom unit names, and the text of a trigger or briefing action. Each of those fields shows the string as the game draws it until you click into it, and has a palette button at its right-hand end. The previews follow Remastered's rule, where a colour set on one line carries onto the next. StarCraft 1.16.1 reset the colour at every line break, so an older map's text can show in colours its author did not choose. The 1.16.1 colours tick (also in Preferences ▸ View) switches every preview to the old rule, and the Repair plugin offers to write the resets the old game supplied. Two codes do something you might not expect, in both games: <01> goes back to the colour before the last change rather than to the default, and once the text is grey ( <05> ) the game ignores every later colour code in the string. The previews follow both. File ▸ Export ▸ Strings (.txt)… writes every string to a numbered text file, and File ▸ Import ▸ Strings (.txt)… reads such a file back, replacing the strings by number — a way to translate or proofread a map's text outside the editor. Text that looks garbled. If a map's text opens as nonsense, often Korean or Japanese text in an older map, the editor guessed its encoding wrong. A map file does not say what encoding its text is in, so the editor guesses from the bytes when the map opens. Open Scenario ▸ Map Revision… , choose the right encoding ( Korean , say), and every string is fixed at once. The same choice decides how the text is written on save, so a map made for 1.16.1 on a Korean Windows stays readable there. A new map is UTF-8, which Remastered reads, and a map moved to Remastered's string table becomes UTF-8 too. Western text saved as Windows-1252 can go wrong in Remastered, which reads some of it as Korean: "Ärger Don’t" shows as "훣ger Don뭪" (see the string table ). Text saved as UTF-8 always shows as written. A character the chosen encoding cannot hold is saved as ? ; Check Map and the Save dialog say so beforehand. Sounds and switches # The Sound Editor lists the map's sounds with the .wav files in the archive: import, play, remove, and adopt files the archive carries but the list does not. Import takes any file the browser can decode (MP3, FLAC, AAC, Ogg, WAV in any encoding) and writes it as a WAV in the format picked next to the button. The default, 22050 Hz 16-bit mono, is what the game's own sounds are; the smaller presets are for maps near the size limit. A Play WAV action then names the file. Some maps made for Remastered carry Ogg sounds instead; Remastered plays them in a map of any revision, while StarCraft 1.16.1 stays silent, and Check Map points them out. A trigger can also play one of the game's own sounds, a unit's voice or an interface click, without the file being in the map. In the Trigger Editor, Browse… beside a WAV argument lists the map's sounds and the game's together. Search by file name, by unit, or

Checking, testing and saving Before a map is played, it can be checked for common mistakes, tried in the game, and saved in the form you want to release. Check Map # Tools ▸ Check Map… looks for what the game would refuse or silently drop. A map with no triggers is judged as a melee map and one with triggers as a scenario, since that is how each is played. The file: missing sections, and any section whose length the game does not accept, with what the player would see ( Invalid Scenario in the map list, Error loading scenario file as a game starts, in every game type or only in Use Map Settings, a briefing that does not play); a revision the game does not know; a map side longer than 256; a Brood War tileset on a revision without Brood War, and an Installation map with no triggers, which the game plays only as Use Map Settings. A verification table ( VCOD ) that fails the game's check for the map's players is reported, and Save puts StarEdit's table, which always passes, in its place. Players and start locations: a player without a start location, which eliminates them at once in melee and only moves the opening view in a scenario; several start locations for one player (the game uses the last); start locations for Players 9–12; player colours on a StarCraft 1.00 or Hybrid map, which StarCraft 1.16.1 does not show, and colours past the twelve the game takes from the palette. Units the game leaves out: in a scenario, the placed units of a player whose race is User Selectable (the game removes them and hands out melee start units instead) and of a slot that is not in the game; in melee, everything but start locations and Player 12's resources and critters; ground units standing where they cannot walk; resource amounts past 65,535, which the game keeps as 16 bits; more than 1700 units, or units off the map. Text: a string table past STR's 64 KB of offsets (Save refuses it), or a Remastered string table in a revision that does not read it; a map name or force name longer than the lobby shows (Remastered counts the name's bytes as UTF-8, where a Korean syllable takes three), and a description longer than StarCraft 1.16.1 shows; UTF-8 text a 1.16.1 player sees garbled; Windows-1252 text Remastered shows as Korean; a custom unit name on a type that uses the default settings (the game ignores it). Triggers: a missing or moved Anywhere location; locations that are unused or not set at all (a location action without one does nothing); strings that do not exist; unit and player values the game does not have; condition and action types it does not have, which crash StarCraft 1.16.1 (Remastered takes such a condition as false and skips such an action); Create Unit, Set Resources and Set Score for Players 9–12, which do nothing; Create Unit of a unit class or of a type StarEdit's palette leaves out, which makes nothing; a trigger ticked twice for one player, which runs twice; a trigger with flag 0x02, which defeats every other player each time its actions run; Mission Briefing in a trigger, and a briefing that does not start with it; AI scripts a trigger owned only by people, rescuable or neutral slots cannot run; Play WAV actions with no file in the map, and Ogg sounds, which only Remastered plays; switches tested for Set but never set. Terrain: tiles with bit 15 set, which the game files as a creep flag, though in play such a tile shows no creep and takes no Zerg building; tiles from groups the tileset does not have; tiles only Remastered's tilesets have; a missing or outdated isometric record. A map with triggers gets three more checks: a human player with no way to win or lose: no Victory, and no Defeat or win for another player (in a scenario nobody wins or loses unless a trigger says so); no Set Mission Objectives; with hyper triggers present, a Wait or a person's Transmission in another trigger of the same player, which fights them for the player's one wait slot (see Waits in the trigger reference). Double-click an issue to go to it. The same check runs inside the Save dialog. Test Map # Tools ▸ Test Map (Ctrl+F5) hands the map to the game. The game cannot open a map from the outside, so the editor writes it into a scmJS folder under the game's Maps folder, where Single Player ▸ Custom Game lists it. The desktop app finds the installation (or takes a folder you pick) and starts the game as well. Chrome and Edge write the map into a folder you pick once. Start the game yourself and open the map under Single Player ▸ Custom Game. Firefox and Safari download the map; move it into the game's Maps folder. Tools ▸ Test Map Settings… opens the dialog to change the folder and whether the game starts. Test Map in Browser. In the editor at scmjs.dev, Tools ▸ Test Map in Browser opens the map on the site's play page, scmjs.dev/play, which runs the game in a browser tab. The map goes straight from the editor's tab to that one, and testing again sends the new version to the same tab. The game runs from your own StarCraft files: the first time, the play page asks for the folder StarCraft is installed in. Blizzard's map editor download is not enough for it. How the map is played is set under Edit ▸ Preferences ▸ Plugins ▸ scm-sim : Game type. From the map (the default) plays with the map's own settings when it has computer players or units placed beyond the start locations, and as a melee game otherwise. Use Map Settings and Melee always play that way. Choose on the play page opens the map on the play page's setup screen, which lists the map's forces and slots as the game's own lobby does, and nothing starts until you press Start Game. Your race , your slot for Use Map Settings (the first open one, or a player you name), and for melee the number of computers and their race. Where the map fixes a slot's race or has fewer places, the map's settings win. Note. Test Map in Browser comes with the scm-sim plugin and appears only in the editor at scmjs.dev, not in the desktop app or an editor hosted elsewhere. Savin

Replays The editor opens StarCraft replays ( .rep files) and shows, on the map the game was played on, what the players did: where buildings went down and when, where units were sent, each player's build order and actions per minute, and the chat, on a timeline you can scrub or play. Map makers use it to see which paths and chokes players use, where and when they expand, and whether one start location plays differently from another. Replays come with the Aftermath plugin, which is installed and on from the start. To open one: File ▸ Open Replay… picks one or more replays; File ▸ Open… takes a replay as well as a map; dropping replays anywhere on the editor opens them. Replays from every version of the game are read. View ▸ Aftermath opens Aftermath's panel with no replay in front, to drop replays on. A replay's tab # Each replay opens the map it was played on in a tab of its own. A replay opens view-only: its tab has an eye where the unsaved-changes dot would be, and the status bar says View only . You can scroll, zoom, switch layers and select things, but nothing can be changed or saved: the palette, Layers and Properties panels are hidden (the View menu has the layer switches); the tools do nothing, and every menu item and dialog that would change the map is greyed; the toolbar leaves out Save, Undo and Redo, Cut and Paste, the brush, Symmetry, Players and Triggers, and has an Edit a Copy button in place of Save. Save Copy As… still works. Edit a Copy (the button, or File ▸ Edit a Copy) opens an ordinary copy of the map in a new tab, which asks where to save the first time you save it. Switching tabs switches replays, each keeping its own place on the timeline, and closing the tab closes the replay. The timeline and the panel # While a replay's tab is in front, a timeline runs under the map: Play and Pause, the time and the speed, a graph of the game, and marks for the fights, the chat and players leaving. Space plays and pauses, ← and → go ten seconds back or on (a minute with Shift), and Home and End go to the start and the end. The column on the right has the game's details, the players, and tabs for the build order, the chat and the rest. On the map, each player's buildings and orders are drawn in their colour as the timeline moves. The Aftermath README describes every part. The Replay view # In the editor at scmjs.dev, a replay's tab opens on the Replay : the game itself replaying in the map's place, from the game's files you installed. Blizzard's map editor download is enough for this. A switch in the top-left corner goes between the Replay and the Map , the overhead view with Aftermath's marks and heat maps. The timeline drives whichever is shown. While the Replay is shown, the editor keeps what still makes sense there: zoom works on it: View ▸ Zoom In and Zoom Out, Zoom to Fit, and the toolbar's magnifiers; the grid, the locations and other plugins' overlays are drawn over it, and View ▸ Grid, Locations and Location Names turn them on and off; View ▸ Fog of War shows the game's own fog, through the eyes picked in the Vision menu under the replay: everyone, or one player; the status bar's tile and position follow the pointer, and the minimap shows where the game looks; press or drag on it to move the game's camera; pointing at a unit shows what the game's console would: its name, owner, hit points and what it is doing. What only applies to the map behind it — the layers, selecting, the clipboard, Find, the brush and the map's own toggles such as Units or Elevation — is left off the toolbar and greyed in the menus. Analysis # In the editor at scmjs.dev, every replay you open is also analysed: the game is played through in the background to see what really happened rather than what was ordered. Once it is done, Aftermath shows the units where they stood, what each player really built and lost, the fights and the key moments, and a camera ( Spectate ) that follows the action. View ▸ Replay Analysis opens a larger window with each player's economy and tech over the game. Open several replays of one map and Map stats takes them together: how each start location did, which bases were taken and when, where the fights happened, and the ground no unit ever entered. Note. In the desktop app and an editor hosted elsewhere, Aftermath works from the players' orders alone: there is no Replay view and no analysis.

Plugins Plugins add tools to the editor, and several of the tools in this guide are plugins. Most come installed and on; a few more are a click away in Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins… . Plugin Starts Where What it does Aftermath On File ▸ Open Replay… Opens replays over their map; see Replays Paint On Tools ▸ Paint… (Ctrl+Shift+P) Lines, shapes, spray and text, from the palette's pick Repair On Tools ▸ Repair Map… Repairs damaged and protected maps as they open scm-sim On Tools ▸ Test Map in Browser Plays the map on scmjs.dev/play scmjs.dev On Account menu Your scmjs.dev account scmscx.com On File ▸ Find on scmscx.com… Searches the scmscx.com map archive Stamp Library On Tools ▸ Stamp Library… (Ctrl+Shift+L) Pieces of map kept across maps Terrain from Image On File ▸ Import ▸ Terrain from Image… Turns a picture into terrain TrigScript On Triggers ▸ TrigScript… Triggers as code; see TrigScript Walkability On View ▸ Walkability (Ctrl+Shift+W) The ground as a unit walks it TrigEdit Off Triggers ▸ Text Trigger Editor… (Ctrl+Shift+T) Triggers as SCMDraft text Magenta Browse Triggers ▸ Magenta… Triggers as sentences, with Remastered EUD Melee Wizard Browse Tools ▸ Melee Wizard… (Ctrl+Shift+M) Start locations and mineral lines Section Explorer Browse Tools ▸ Section Explorer… (Ctrl+Shift+H) The map file, section by section and byte by byte Timelapse Browse View ▸ Timelapse… Records the map as you build it Trigger Map Browse Triggers ▸ Trigger Map… The triggers as a graph On plugins are installed and running; Off is installed but needs ticking on in Plugins ▸ Manage Plugins…; Browse is installed from Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins…. A few that need more than a line: Paint lays down whatever the active layer's palette has picked, so it paints units, doodads, sprites, terrain or fog depending on the layer. Stamp Library keeps named pieces — a ramp, a bridge, a cliff corner, a mineral line — in the browser's storage. Click one and it hangs under the pointer, drawn with the map's graphics; click to lay it down. Stamps can be searched, tagged, exported and shared as a line of text. Melee Wizard lays out symmetric start locations, and mineral lines and geysers at the distance the game mines fastest from, with presets for main, natural and third, a symmetry check and a resource summary. Timelapse records one frame per change and plays the recording back with a box around each change. Export it as a GIF or a WebM video. Opening the same file again carries on the same recording. scm-sim is the game engine behind the play page. Besides Test Map in Browser, it is what Aftermath and Walkability use to have the game play a replay or walk a map. It works only in the editor at scmjs.dev. Each plugin's own README, linked in the table, has the details. Adding and managing plugins # Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins… lists the plugins the project publishes; press Install on one and it shows where the code comes from before adding it. The plugins listed there are reviewed before they are listed. Plugins ▸ Manage Plugins… lists what is installed, turns each on or off, and takes the address of any other plugin: a GitHub repository, a link to its plugin.json , or http://localhost:3000/ while you write one. A plugin that has settings keeps them on its own page under Edit ▸ Preferences ▸ Plugins. There is no sandbox: a plugin has the same access as the editor itself, so only add plugins you trust. The Add screen shows the manifest, the repository and the addresses the plugin will fetch from. Browse Plugins also lists two plugins for people writing their own: Hello World , an example with nothing in it but a Tools menu item, and the API Playground , a code editor for trying the plugin API on the open map. Installing plugins, what they are allowed to do, and writing one are covered in docs/plugins.md .

Your scmjs.dev account scmjs.dev is the project's own service. An account there does two things for the editor: it keeps maps for you, with a history of revisions and links that give anyone a copy; it lets you share the map you have open so others can edit it with you at the same time ( Editing a map together ). None of it is required. The editor works completely without an account, and it sends nothing to scmjs.dev until you use one of these features; there is no request at startup unless you are already signed in. All of it lives in the scmjs.dev plugin, which is installed and on from the start. If you would rather not see the Account menu at all, turn the plugin off in Plugins ▸ Manage Plugins…. Signing in # Account ▸ Sign in to scmjs.dev… , or the Sign in to scmjs.dev cell at the right end of the status bar, starts the sign-in. Sign in with Discord: the provider's own page opens in a small window, you approve it there, and the window closes itself. The editor never sees a password, only a display name and an id from the provider. Signed in, the same cell (or Account ▸ Account… ) opens the Account dialog, which shows: your name and the sign-in you used; a Status list of what the account can use: map storage, shared editing, and the AI features (on your own key; see The AI ); how much of your map storage is in use; the maps you are sharing (see Your shared maps ). Its buttons open your account page on scmjs.dev (to link another sign-in, or delete the account and everything with it), open My Maps, and sign out. Under Settings , a tick hides the status-bar cell. scmjs.dev keeps the id and display name from your sign-in and the maps you store there. The account page deletes all of it. Keeping maps on scmjs.dev # Account ▸ My Maps… — also File ▸ Open from scmjs.dev… — lists the maps on your account, newest change first, each with a picture, its tileset, size and player count, and how many revisions it has. The box above the list searches the names, tilesets, file names and notes. The map you last opened or saved from here is picked when the list arrives, and its revisions appear on the right: the number, the note you wrote, the file name, the size and when it was saved. Up and Down move through the list, and Enter opens the map. Open puts the picked revision in the editor, asking first if the map you have open has unsaved changes. Download saves the file to disk as it was uploaded. The note can be added or edited later, and the map renamed. A revision can be deleted, except the last one — delete the map to remove it. Account ▸ Save to scmjs.dev… — also under File, beside Save Copy As — saves the open map to the account, as a new map or as the next revision of one you pick; the map it was opened from or last saved to is picked for you. Write a note saying what changed, and tick whether to include a one-pixel-per-tile picture for the list. The file is what File ▸ Save would write, with the save options you last confirmed, so what comes back is playable. It is a copy: Ctrl+S goes on writing to the file on your disk, and nothing on the account changes until you save there again. Revisions are numbered in order and a number is never reused. Saving a file whose bytes are already on the account costs no storage — only the new note is kept. Storage is 250 MB per account, shown as a bar in both dialogs. Giving someone a copy # A link can hand a map to anyone: whoever opens it gets a copy of the map in their own editor, without signing in. The copy is theirs — it opens as a new file, File ▸ Save asks where to keep it, and nothing they change reaches your map. To edit a map together instead, see Editing a map together . Account ▸ Copy Link to This Map… saves the open map to your account — as the next revision of the map it came from, or as a new map — and gives you the link, already on the clipboard. The link opens the version you just saved, so a link you have posted somewhere does not change under the people who follow it; tick Let the link follow my later saves for one that opens whatever you save to that map next. Pasted into Discord, Slack, a forum or most other places that show previews, a link to the web editor shows a card with the map's name, who shared it, its tileset, size and players, and its picture. A link that has been removed shows a card saying it no longer works. Embed… beside a link in My Maps gives you that card as a picture to put somewhere yourself, with the link around it: a forum post or signature (BBCode), a GitHub README or a Discourse forum (Markdown), or a website (HTML). Pick the large picture (1200 × 630) or the small one (600 × 315) for a signature, and copy the code. The picture's own address opens nothing: only the link you wrap it in does. When the link is removed, the picture says the map is no longer shared. The picture of the map on the card is drawn by your editor when it saves the map to scmjs.dev, so a map saved without the game's graphics installed shows its size instead. In My Maps , the Links part of a map lists its links, how many times each was opened, and Remove for each; a removed link stops working at once and the map stays. Link to #3 makes a link to the revision you are looking at, Link to the newest one that follows your saves. Deleting a revision removes the links to it, and deleting a map removes all of its links. A map can have ten links. Opening a link starts the editor with an Open a Copy dialog showing the map's name, picture, size and who shared it; Open a copy opens it. Account ▸ Open a Map Link… takes a link pasted in, which is the way in the desktop app.

h: When two people change the same thing
b: Editing a map together Several people can work on one map at the same time, each in their own editor. One of them shares the map they have open and sends the others a link; whoever opens it gets the map in their editor, and from then on every change anyone makes shows up for everyone: terrain, doodads, units, sprites, locations, fog, the settings dialogs, triggers, strings and sounds. Each person also sees the others' pointers on the map with their names, a dashed box in their colour around what each of them has on screen, and which dialog they are in. Sharing goes through scmjs.dev: the person who shares needs a signed-in account , and the people joining need only the link. Sharing a map # Account ▸ Share this Map… asks for a name for the map (its own name to start with) and how long to keep it open , and copies it to scmjs.dev when you press Start sharing . The dialog then shows the link: Copy puts it on the clipboard for you to send. A cell appears in the status bar — Shared · 3 people — and clicking it opens the dialog again. Pasted into Discord, Slack or a forum, the link shows a card with the map's name, who shared it and, for a map kept open, its picture. Keep it open decides what happens when people leave: Until everyone leaves (the choice to start with) shares the map only while people are in it. Nothing is stored: sharing ends when you stop it, half an hour after the last person leaves, or when the server restarts. For a day , for a week or for a month saves the map to My Maps and keeps it open at its link, so people can come and go as they like, on different days if they want. Each time everyone has left, the map is saved as a new revision with a note naming who changed it ( Edited together: Kim, Sam ), and the next person to open the link carries on from there. The time counts from the last edit, so a map people are working on stays open, and one nobody has touched for that long ends. The dialog shows the date: ends 3 Oct unless someone edits it . Until I end it keeps it open with no time limit. It still ends after a year with no edits. When a map kept open ends, only the sharing ends: the map and its revisions stay in My Maps. If the map in front came from My Maps, sharing it adds a revision to that map rather than making a second one. The dialog lists who is in, in the colour their pointer is drawn in, and what each of them has open. The link is the key: anyone who has it can join and edit, so send it only to people you want in the map. Only you, as the person who shared it, see the link and the controls: Remove sends one person out of the map. They keep what they had. New link makes the old link stop working without sending anyone out, for when the link went further than you meant. Stop sharing ( End sharing on a map kept open) ends it for everyone. On a map kept open, Leave takes only you out and leaves it open for the others; you can change how long it stays open here too. Up to eight people can be in one map, and an account can share five maps at a time, counting both kinds. A map shared from the desktop app gets a link to the web editor, since that is what anyone can open. Your shared maps # The Shared maps part of Account ▸ Account… lists every map you are sharing: who is in it now, the last edit and who made it, and when it ends. Each has Join , Copy link , New link , how long to keep it open, and End sharing . When you are already sharing five, Share this Map… shows the same list so you can end one first.
