A map kept open also has Embed… in that list and in the Share dialog. Its picture can open a copy of the map (the default; a link to the newest revision is made for it) or the shared map itself. The second lets anyone who sees the picture join and edit, and the dialog says so; New link is the way back if it went further than you meant. In My Maps a map kept open says so ( Shared · 2 editing , or when it ends), and Join opens it with whoever is there; Open still gives you a revision on its own. While you are in one of your maps kept open, a revision of it has Put #N into the shared map , which replaces the map for everyone with that revision: the way back if someone spoiled it. Everyone's undo history starts again, as after a resize, and the map as it was is not kept unless you saved it first. Joining # Open the link in a browser and the editor starts with the Join dialog up. In the desktop app, or in an editor that is already open, paste the link into Account ▸ Join a Shared Map… . The dialog says which map the link leads to, who shared it and how many people are in it; type the name the others will see you by and press Join . The map opens in a new tab beside whatever you had open (or in place of the empty map the editor starts with). Closing that tab leaves the shared map. You can be in one shared map at a time. Joining another leaves the first, which stays open as an ordinary map. Talking to each other # While a shared map is in front, a Chat button sits in the bottom-right corner of the map, next to the tileset and zoom. It opens a small window over the map with what everyone has written and a line to type in; Enter sends. What you type there goes to everyone in the map and nowhere else, and typing in it does not trigger the editor's shortcut keys. When the chat is closed, a new message shows as a notice and as a count on the button. Anyone who joins later sees what was said before them. The chat is kept only while people are in the map: it is gone when sharing ends, or when everyone has left a map kept open, and it is not saved with the map. When two people change the same thing # Your stroke is never cut in two. While you hold the mouse button on the map, other people's changes wait and arrive when you let go. The same happens while a dialog that edits the map is open (Player Settings, the Trigger Editor, Unit Properties and the like); the others see that you are in it, next to your pointer and in the Share dialog. The later change wins. If two people paint t

The AI Tools ▸ AI holds an assistant that reads and edits the open map with you, and tools that lay out maps, write triggers, names and briefings, review a map and rewrite its strings. They come with the scmjs.dev plugin and run on your own Anthropic API key. Adding your key # Make an API key at console.anthropic.com . Open Edit ▸ Preferences ▸ Plugins ▸ scmjs.dev (or Add your key… in the Account dialog), paste the key under Your Anthropic key and press Check and use . The key is checked with Anthropic first, which costs nothing. When it passes, the Tools ▸ AI menu, the assistant and the AI buttons in the editor's dialogs appear. No scmjs.dev account is needed for this. Anthropic bills each request to your Anthropic account. The key stays in your browser: scmjs.dev passes it on with each AI request and keeps no copy. Forget the key on the same page removes it, and the AI features with it. A few things are the same for every feature: What is sent. Only what the feature needs: what you typed and the map's facts (size, tileset, players, what is where), and for some features a picture of the map, the strings or the triggers. The map file itself is never sent. Undo. Every change the AI makes is one undo step, labelled "AI: …", including what it writes to the name and description, strings, triggers, players and unit settings. Cost. Every AI dialog shows its progress while you wait, and what the request cost when it finishes. Where your key goes # Each AI request goes from your browser to the scmjs.dev server with your key attached. The server passes it to Anthropic and sends the answer back. It keeps nothing of the request: not what you typed, not the answer, not your key or your address. To hold everyone to 30 requests a minute, 1,000 a day and 4 at once, it counts requests per address, in memory only: the counts are never written to disk. What Anthropic keeps is set by Anthropic's own terms for the API. What the model is told, and what the editor does with its answer, is public in scm-js/ai-engine . Each AI feature is one file there. The server's sign-in, accounts and limits are not public. If a feature gives you a bad result, open an issue on ai-engine with what you asked, what came back, and the map if you can share it. The assistant # Assistant (Ctrl+Shift+A, or the AI cell in the status bar) opens a conversation about the open map. Ask a question or say what to change, and the assistant reads the map and edits it with the editor's own tools while you watch. What it reads: everything — units and their properties, doodads, sprites, locations, strings, switches, sounds, triggers and the trigger script, unit, upgrade and technology settings, fog, terrain, Check Map results, your selection, and a screenshot of any area. What it changes: nearly everything the editor can, from terrain and units to triggers, players and forces, settings and the map's size. It draws terrain as shapes — a plateau with a ramp that fits, a lane that stays walkable, a river with a bridge — and can tell you whether units can walk from one place to another. Each turn is folded into one block under your message. While it runs, the block shows the latest steps ( ▸ a read, ✎ a change), and the map outlines what is about to change and follows the work, zooming out but never in. Scroll or zoom yourself and the view stays where you put it for the rest of the turn. When the turn ends, the block shows the steps, the time and the cost, with an Undo button that reverses the whole turn. Escape stops a turn. To start a message, use the suggestion chips above the input, or right-click the map and choose Ask AI about this spot / the selection / this area… . Tick Picture to send a screenshot of the visible area. Player Settings has a Set up with AI… button that sets up players and forces from one sentence. After 24 rounds of tool calls the assistant stops and offers to continue. Make Scenario # Make Scenario… builds a whole scenario from a sentence, such as "a madness map" or "a two-lane tower defense". Set the size, tileset and number of players and press Design . The design. The model writes a design document first: the premise, the players and forces, each trigger system and its settings, the layout and its locations, the objectives and the briefing. Edit it directly, or describe what should change and press Design again . A location name can include {p} , as in "Spawn {p}", to build that system once per player. The build. Build works through the design one step at a time, each step a row that passes or fails on its own: the terrain and locations, players and forces, each system, the objectives and briefing, the name, and a Check Map at the end. Common layouts (corner camps, lanes, arenas, a bound's course, a town) are laid out by the editor itself; others are drawn from the model's shapes. Common systems — spawns, income, waves, lives, shops, leaderboards and the like — are built by the editor and shown in green; anything else is written in TrigScript and shown in gold. When it finishes, Review it… or Open the assistant to keep going. Generate Map and Redo Area # Generate Map… lays out a melee map from a description: the number of players, the kind of terrain, where the bases go and the symmetry. It shows a plan first — a rough grid of terrain, the bases with their resources, ramps, a name and the designer's notes. Apply paints it with the isometric brush onto a new map, or onto the open map if it is the same size. Refine sends the plan back with your changes ("more room around the naturals") and a picture of the result. Treat the result as a starting point, and check the ramps against the cliffs before you play. Redo Area… does the same for part of an existing map. Mark an area (or right-click it and choose Redo this area with AI… ) and describe what should be there; the new ground joins the old at the edges. Triggers, names and strings # Write Triggers… turns a description into TrigScript and applies it, keeping the script with

Keyboard and preferences Press F1 for a list of every shortcut. These are the ones the editor starts with; any of the commands can be given other keys on Preferences ▸ Hotkeys: Keys T D U S L F C switch layer [ ] brush size M symmetry on / off Alt+click pick what is under the cursor Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo / redo Del / Esc delete selection / stop placing Ctrl+O, Ctrl+S, Ctrl+N open, save, new Ctrl+Shift+S save as Ctrl+T Trigger Editor Ctrl+Shift+T Text Trigger Editor (when TrigEdit is on) Ctrl+Shift+A AI assistant (with your Anthropic key) Ctrl+F find Ctrl+A select all on the layer Ctrl+G grid Ctrl+0, Ctrl+Shift+0 100%, zoom to fit Alt+Enter map properties Ctrl+F5 test map Ctrl+, preferences Ctrl+Tab, Ctrl+Shift+Tab next / previous open map (desktop app) Ctrl+W close map (desktop app) Preferences (Ctrl+,) are kept in the browser. Nothing is written until OK or Apply, and Reset to defaults puts every page back. The pages down the left: General Language : English or Korean. The default follows the browser's, and a change applies at once. A map's own text is never translated. Startup : the splash screen; whether to reopen the last map (the desktop app does it straight away; a browser that has to ask before reading the file again offers it in a notice); how many recent files to keep. In the desktop app, whether to check for updates at startup, and whether to include nightly builds. Maps : whether each map opens in its own tab, and whether to ask before closing or replacing a map with unsaved changes. New scenario : the tileset, size and revision a new map starts with. Saving : what the Save dialog starts from (how the file was opened, Everything or Smallest ), the compression for a map with no file yet, and whether a save keeps the file it replaces (a .bak , or a previous version in a browser). Recovery : whether to keep recovery copies of unsaved maps, and how often. Privacy (the editor at scmjs.dev only): whether to count which parts of the editor are used. It is on unless you turn it off. When you use a feature, the editor sends its name and a few words about it, such as which dialog opened or which layer an edit was on. When something goes wrong, it sends where in the editor's code the error happened (the file, line and function) and whether the browser was translating the page, but never the error's message. It never sends the map, its name, a file name or anything you typed, and nothing that identifies you. Turning it off also stops the visit count for this browser, and the site's privacy page has the same switch and the details. The desktop app and copies of the editor hosted elsewhere count nothing. Editing : the grid's spacing, colour and style, and what snaps to it (View ▸ Grid Settings… opens this page); what the palettes start on — the owner of placed units, the brush size, the size of a new location; and how many undo levels each map keeps. View : whether the mouse wheel scrolls (Ctrl+wheel zooms) or zooms, and whether a wheel zoom keeps the tile under the pointer in place; whether water and units animate and how fast; whether the map starts out drawn with Remastered's graphics; which cells the status bar shows; and whether string previews follow Remastered's colour rule or 1.16.1's. Testing : Test Map's folder, and in the desktop app whether the game starts after the map is written. Plugins : what to do when an installed plugin has a newer version (tell you, do nothing, or install it — see docs/plugins.md ), and each plugin's own settings page. Storage : where the game data comes from, and everything the editor keeps in the browser, one row per setting or cache, with a plugin's own data under its name. Each row can be cleared on its own, or Clear all data throws the lot away. Maps are not part of that list and are not touched by it. The recovery copies and the previous versions of saved files have their own lines. Export writes the settings, the plugins' included, to one file, and Import reads such a file into another browser or machine; caches and the recent files stay behind. Hotkeys : every command and its keys. + on a row waits for the next keys you press and adds them (Esc stops waiting); the × on a key removes it. A command can have several keys or none. Keys used by two commands, or by a command and a plugin, are marked. A plugin's keys are tried first; between two commands, the one higher in the list wins. Delete, Esc, the arrows, Tab, Enter, Space and F11 keep their own jobs and cannot be given to a command. A plain key such as T never fires while you type in a text box, and most Ctrl shortcuts leave a text box's own undo, clipboard and select-all alone. The browser keeps Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+W for its own tabs, so Next Map and Close Map start with no keys there; give them others if you want them. The placement options, the panels and the recent files are remembered too. What's new # Help ▸ What's New… lists what changed in each release, newest first, with the release you are running open and the older ones folded below it. The part written for plugin authors is folded as well. The notes come with the editor, so the list works offline and always matches the version in front of you; a nightly build shows the notes of the last release. The version line in Help ▸ About scmJS… opens the same list. The first time you start a release with new notes, a notice says the editor has been updated and offers the list. It appears once per release. The notes are written in English. In the desktop app, Help ▸ Check for Updates… looks for a newer version.

h: When part of the editor fails
b: When something goes wrong If the editor does something strange, the debug console shows what happened, Copy Bug Report puts it on the clipboard, and Report an Issue sends it to the project. Damaged and protected maps # The Repair plugin checks every map as it opens, the way the game reads it. Protected maps in particular often have parts missing, damaged or repeated. Safe repairs are made at once : the ones that only write what the game already does, or put back what the editor needs, such as the isometric record a protector stripped. They do not mark the map as changed, and the next save writes them. Judgement calls are left to you , such as a player slot with a race the game does not have. A cell in the status bar ( Repaired 3 · 1 to review ) opens a list that says what the game does about each one and what the repair would change. Undo in that list puts the file back as it opened. Tools ▸ Repair Map… runs the check again, and Edit ▸ Preferences ▸ Plugins ▸ Repair can make it ask before repairing anything, or not check at all. To look at the file section by section and byte by byte, install Section Explorer from Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins…. Protected and damaged maps has the details. The debug console # View ▸ Debug Console opens a strip along the bottom of the window with the log in it: maps opened and saved, plugins started and stopped, where the game data came from, and every error the page threw. The log is kept whether the strip is open or not, so opening it after something odd happened still shows what happened. The last couple of thousand lines are kept; Clear empties it, for starting clean before reproducing something. Warnings and Errors narrow the list to what went wrong; the box beside them filters on any text. Verbose adds a line for every edit and every call a plugin makes into the editor. It answers "which plugin did that?", it is noisy by design, and it turns itself off when you next load the editor. When part of the editor fails # If a panel, the palette, the map view or the menu bar hits an error it cannot draw past, that part alone is replaced by a short notice with the error in it. Everything else keeps working, your maps included. Try again draws the part afresh, and Show the log opens the debug console at the line that says what failed. A dialog that fails is closed, and a notice says so with the same Show the log button. What you had changed in it and not yet applied is lost; what you had applied is in the map. If the whole editor fails, a plain page takes its place with the error, the end of the log, and Copy the log and Save the log… for a bug report. Your maps are still open behind it: Try again brings the editor back with them. A recovery copy of each map with unsaved changes is written as that page appears (unless you switched recovery copies off in Preferences), so Reload offers them back too. Copying a bug report # Help ▸ Copy Bug Report puts the log on the clipboard with a short header above it — the version, the browser or desktop app, where the game data came from, the map's size and tileset, and the plugins with their versions — ready to paste into an issue, a forum post or a message. A long session is trimmed to its most recent lines so the paste fits in an issue; when it is, the report says so. The console's own Copy does the same without the trim, and Save… writes the whole log to a file, for when it is too long to paste. Filing an issue # Help ▸ Report an Issue… opens a new issue on GitHub with the report already filled in, under three questions: what you did, what you expected, and what happened. Answer those, check the rest, and submit. You need a GitHub account. The issue holds a shortened log. If the lines that matter were cut, use Copy Bug Report and paste the full report over it. Nothing is sent until you submit the issue yourself. The report names the map file you have open, the plugins you have installed and the version you are running, and nothing else about you.

What it does not do This section lists what the editor does not do, and the limits worth knowing before you rely on a feature. Undo and history # Undo takes back what a dialog's OK or Apply wrote, as one step. What you change inside an open dialog before that is not in the history; Cancel is the way back. The larger editors (triggers, the briefing, strings, sounds, switches, and the unit, upgrade and technology settings) ask before Escape, the close button or a click outside the dialog throws away changes you have not applied. Resizing and changing the tileset clear the undo history. A step that rewrites thousands of triggers (a TrigScript build, say) is kept, but the oldest steps are then dropped sooner than the undo-levels setting says, so the history does not grow without bound. Browsers and the desktop app # In Firefox and Safari, every save is a download, and a recent map reopens through File ▸ Open instead of straight from disk. Chrome, Edge and the desktop app write in place. In a browser, Tools ▸ Test Map writes the map where the game lists it but cannot start the game; in Firefox and Safari it downloads the map. Tools ▸ Test Map in Browser, at scmjs.dev, plays it in a browser tab instead. The Windows zip does not register .scm , .scx and .chk , since nothing is installed. A map dragged onto scmJS.exe still opens. On macOS the app sees a new version but cannot install it until the app is code-signed, so it offers the download page instead. Terrain and objects # The isometric brush needs the map's isometric record. The Repair plugin, on by default, rebuilds one a protected map had stripped. Symmetry does not mirror the Blend brush or pasting. The Tile brush copies the same tile to each image, so an edge tile faces the same way on both sides; use the isometric brush for cliffs and shores. Changing the tileset lays the terrain again and drops the doodads; the units, sprites, locations, fog and triggers stay. Triggers and text # In the Trigger Editor, EUD values are raw numbers: the EPD box turns a memory address into the player value that reaches it, but nothing names what an address holds. For named reads and writes of the game, use a TrigScript program or the Magenta plugin. Both play on Remastered only. Transmission is the one briefing action no Blizzard map uses, so its layout could not be checked against one. TrigScript's programs play on Remastered only; trigger() works on every version. The full list is under TrigScript's reference . A character the map's text encoding cannot hold is saved as ? . Check Map and the Save dialog say so beforehand. The Korean translation was not written by a native speaker. A review is welcome (see docs/development.md ). The scmjs.dev features # Keeping maps on an account and editing a map together run on scmjs.dev and need a connection. Keeping and sharing maps need an account; joining a shared map needs only the link. The AI features need your own Anthropic API key and a connection (see The AI ).

TrigScript Triggers written as TypeScript: a quick start, triggers made by code, programs that run in StarCraft: Remastered, testing, the workspace and the reference. TrigScript lets you write a map's triggers as code. The code is TypeScript, and it is kept inside the map. TrigScript is a plugin that is on from the start: Triggers ▸ TrigScript… opens it as soon as a map is open. A script can make two kinds of things: trigger() program() What it makes Ordinary triggers in the map's list Code that runs inside the game Plays on Every version of StarCraft StarCraft: Remastered only Good for Anything the Trigger Editor can do, without the repetition Counters, timers, per-player state, loops over units, keys and chat Each trigger() call becomes one trigger, the same kind the Trigger Editor shows. The code around the calls runs only while the script is applied, so a loop over the players, a helper that returns the ten triggers a shop needs, or a table of waves all end up as plain triggers. Code inside program(() => { … }) runs in the game instead. It has variables, arrays, text, functions, classes, loops and sleep , so a lives counter or a wave timer is a loop rather than a dozen triggers with hand-numbered death counts. TrigScript builds programs into the map itself when it is saved , in under a second, and a map with a program in it needs StarCraft: Remastered . If the map must play on the classic game, use trigger() only. TrigScript works beside the editor's other trigger tools. The Trigger Editor shows the triggers a script made, and the Text Trigger Editor (the TrigEdit plugin, installed but off until you turn it on) shows them as text. The Trigger Map plugin, from Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins…, draws how triggers depend on each other. See Triggers in the user guide. What each condition and action does in the game is in the trigger reference . The words this page uses are explained under Terms . Quick start This makes a map where Player 1 wins by walking a Marine onto a marked spot. Writing triggers A trigger is one call: Examples of triggers Each of these is a complete main.ts, and each plays on every version of the game. Programs Everything inside program(() => { … }) runs in the game: Examples of programs Each of these is a complete main.ts for a map that needs StarCraft: Remastered. Showcase Maps made with TrigScript, each with its whole script and a recording of it played in StarCraft: Remastered. Coming from eudplib This page is for map makers who already write EUD maps with eudplib, in Python or in epScript, and build them with euddraft. Testing and Simulate TrigScript can run a script without starting the game, in a simulator built into the editor. The workspace This part covers the TrigScript window, the panel beside the map, and what happens to the script when the map is saved. Reference not() flips a comparison or a switch test, and turns always() into never(). Troubleshooting The TrigScript window stays on "Loading the editor…".

Quick start This makes a map where Player 1 wins by walking a Marine onto a marked spot. Open a map, or make one with File ▸ New (Ctrl+N). In Scenario ▸ Player Settings, give Player 1 a fixed race such as Terran. A player left on User Selectable gets a melee base instead of the units you place; see Your first map . On the Units layer ( U ), pick Player 1 at the top of the palette and place a Terran Marine. On the Locations layer ( L ), drag a box a short walk away from the Marine. Double-click the box and name it Beacon . Open Triggers ▸ TrigScript…. Replace the contents of main.ts with: trigger(P1, [ bring(P1, units.AnyUnit, locations.Beacon, ">=" , 1 ), ], [ displayText( "You found the beacon." ), victory(), ]); As you type locations. , the editor offers the map's locations by name. Save the map (Ctrl+S). Saving applies the script: the trigger goes into the map's trigger list. The status bar at the bottom of the TrigScript window shows how many triggers the script made and where they start in the list, such as 1 trigger at #1 . Press Play (F5) in the TrigScript window, or use Tools ▸ Test Map in the editor. The first time, Test Map needs to know where the game is; see Test Map . In the game, open Single Player ▸ Custom Game, pick the map from the scmJS folder, and choose Use Map Settings as the game type. Walk the Marine to the beacon. To see what the script made, open the Trigger Editor (Ctrl+T). The trigger is there with a script badge. From here, Writing triggers explains the parts of a trigger, and Examples of triggers has complete scripts to start from.

h: Many triggers from a little code
b: Writing triggers A trigger is one call: trigger(AllPlayers, [ bring(CurrentPlayer, units.AnyUnit, locations.Beacon, ">=" , 1 ), ], [ displayText( "You found it!" ), preserve(), ]); trigger(players, conditions, actions, options?) records one trigger: players is one player or a list of them. conditions is a list of conditions, up to 16. actions is a list of actions, up to 64. options are the trigger's flags by name. { preserve: true } is the same as the preserve() action; disabled , ignoreGameEnd and the others are listed in the Reference . The order of the trigger() calls is the order of the triggers in the map. Conditions and actions # Every condition and action the game has is a function named after StarEdit's name for it, in camel case: bring , deaths , command , accumulate , elapsedTime , createUnit , displayText , setResources , moveUnit , order , runAiScript , victory . The one exception is the Switch condition, which is switchIs , because switch is a reserved word. The arguments come in the order the Trigger Editor shows them. Where the Trigger Editor offers a list, the argument is a short word: a comparison is ">=" , "<=" or "==" ; a modifier is "set" , "add" or "subtract" ; a resource is "ore" , "gas" or "oreAndGas" ; an order is "move" , "patrol" or "attack" ; a unit count is a number or "All" . The full list is in the Reference . StarEdit's own labels, such as "At least" , work too. Hover over any function in the editor to see its arguments. not(condition) is the opposite of a condition, where one condition can say it: not(bring(…, ">=", 1)) is "at most 0". Names from the map # Units, locations and switches are named the way the map names them: Each display name becomes an identifier: Terran Marine is units.TerranMarine , and Terran Siege Tank (Tank Mode) is units.TerranSiegeTankTankMode . The display name works as well: units["Terran Marine"] . locations. lists the map's locations, and switches. its switches, by number and by any name the map gives them. P1 … P12 , CurrentPlayer and AllPlayers are constants. The other player groups are under players : players.Force1 , players.Foes , players.Allies . A plain number works wherever a name does. That is how an EUD player or an unusual unit id gets in. The editor checks the names as you type. A location passed where a unit belongs is an error, and so is a name the map no longer has. Many triggers from a little code # The script runs when it is applied, and everything TypeScript offers is available at that moment. A loop makes the same trigger for several players, a function returns a list of actions, a table holds the numbers, and a template string builds the text: function reinforce(p: Player) { return trigger(p, [deaths(p, units.TerranMarine, ">=" , 10 )], [ createUnit(p, units.TerranSiegeTankTankMode, 1 , locations.Spawn), setDeaths(p, units.TerranMarine, "subtract" , 10 ), displayText( "Reinforcements have arrived." ), ], { preserve: true }); } for ( const p of [P1, P2, P3, P4]) reinforce(p); Nested lists are flattened, and false , null and undefined entries are skipped. A helper can return a list of actions, and a condition can be written hardMode && bring(…) . A condition is a value here: the game tests it later, when the map is played. So if (bring(…)) outside a program does not do what it looks like, and the editor says so. The test belongs in a trigger's conditions, or in an if inside a program . Several files # A script can have several files. import { x } from "./name" brings in another file of the map's script; nothing else can be imported. The library is available everywhere without an import, and also as the module "trigscript" for anyone who prefers import { trigger, bring } from "trigscript" . Hyper triggers # hyperTriggers(P8) anywhere in the script adds the usual three preserved triggers of sixty-two waits, so that the game goes through the trigger list every 2 frames instead of every 31 ( Hyper triggers ). Give them to a player whose other triggers never wait, usually a computer slot: each player has one wait slot, and the hyper triggers keep it busy ( Waits ). A map with a program does not need them, since its build already makes the list run every frame: the build leaves hyper triggers out, the script's and the map's own alike, and says so in a notice, as it does for a trigger owned by a player group the game runs no list for (Players 9 to 12, Foes, Allies, Neutral, Non-Allied Victory Players).

Examples of triggers Each of these is a complete main.ts , and each plays on every version of the game. They assume a map with locations named Beacon , Spawn , Base , Hill and Shop . Use your own names; the editor completes them. Starting resources and a welcome. No preserve, so the trigger runs once, and CurrentPlayer means each player in turn. trigger(AllPlayers, [always()], [ setResources(CurrentPlayer, "set" , 500 , "ore" ), setResources(CurrentPlayer, "set" , 100 , "gas" ), displayText( "Hold the hill for five minutes to win." ), ]); Hyper triggers. One line, and the whole trigger list runs every 2 frames. Player 8 is the computer slot here, and nothing else in the script makes that player wait. hyperTriggers(P8); Something for every player. A helper returns the trigger, and a loop calls it. Death counts are the game's own counters. Subtracting ten after the reward lets the trigger fire again at the next ten, which preserve: true allows. function reinforce(p: Player) { return trigger(p, [deaths(p, units.TerranMarine, ">=" , 10 )], [ createUnit(p, units.TerranSiegeTankTankMode, 1 , locations.Spawn), setDeaths(p, units.TerranMarine, "subtract" , 10 ), displayText( "Reinforcements have arrived." ), ], { preserve: true }); } for ( const p of [P1, P2, P3, P4]) reinforce(p); A shop. Bring a civilian to the shop with enough minerals, and four marines appear at the spawn. The civilian is moved out first, so the trigger does not fire again on the next pass. price is an ordinary constant used twice. const price = 150 ; trigger(AllPlayers, [ bring(CurrentPlayer, units.TerranCivilian, locations.Shop, ">=" , 1 ), accumulate(CurrentPlayer, ">=" , price, "ore" ), ], [ moveUnit(CurrentPlayer, units.TerranCivilian, 1 , locations.Shop, locations.Spawn), setResources(CurrentPlayer, "subtract" , price, "ore" ), createUnit(CurrentPlayer, units.TerranMarine, 4 , locations.Spawn), displayText( `Four marines for ${price} minerals.` ), ], { preserve: true }); A map that already has triggers. Open TrigScript, press … and choose Import the Map's Triggers . Every hand-made trigger comes back as a trigger() call, in its order, and applying the script replaces the whole list with what it makes. From there a repeated trigger becomes a loop, a number used in ten places becomes a constant, and the rest stays as it was.

h: What is worked out when the script is applied
b: Programs Everything inside program(() => { … }) runs in the game: program(() => { let wave = 0 ; let alarm = false ; while ( true ) { if (bring(P1, units.AnyUnit, locations.Beacon, ">=" , 1 ) && !alarm) { alarm = true ; displayText( "They are coming." ); } if (alarm) { createUnit(P8, units.ZergZergling, 4 , locations.Spawn); wave += 1 ; } if (wave >= 10 ) defeat(); sleep(seconds( 20 )); } }, { owner: P1 }); A map with a program needs StarCraft: Remastered. The programs are built into the map when it is saved or tested (see Saving and building ). Note. Building a program also changes how the rest of the map runs: the game goes through the trigger list every frame instead of every 31 frames. A preserved trigger that adds a mineral then adds twenty-four a second at Fastest. What is worked out when the script is applied # This is the one rule to keep in mind. Everything the program reads from outside its body is worked out once, when the script is applied , before the game starts: a constant, a helper, a condition, an action. The editor underlines those parts with dots, so you can see the boundary as you type. That is what lets a helper written outside the program supply actions inside it. In the picture, the lines beside the gold bar run once in the editor, and the lines beside the blue bar run in the game, where price is the number 150 and reward(P1) is the action the helper made. It also means a program variable cannot reach a condition, an action or a helper. The location and the player of an action, and the amount a condition compares with, are fixed when the script is applied. To compare with a variable, read the quantity and compare it yourself: minerals(P1) >= price (see Reading the game ). These parts of an action can follow a variable: the amount of setResources , setDeaths , setScore and setCountdownTimer ; the unit count of createUnit , killUnitAt , removeUnitAt and giveUnits ; an action's unit type; a text: displayText and print , the objectives, a leaderboard's label, a transmission and a unit type's name take any text the program made. A sound's path or the next scenario's name is a text written in the script. How a program runs # A program runs every frame, from where it left off. It starts on frame 2, the game's first pass. Its body runs until it reaches a sleep() or its end, all within one frame of the game, and the next frame it carries on from there. A body that ends stops for good. So the loop above is a game loop: it looks at the beacon, sends a wave if the alarm is up, and sleeps twenty seconds. In the picture, a program that sleeps three frames at a time runs on frames 2, 5 and 8, while one that sleeps a frame at a time runs on every frame. Time is sleep . sleep(seconds(15)) gives the frame back and carries on that much later, while other programs and the map's triggers go on. frames(n) and minutes(n) make a duration too. Something that keeps its own time is a task beside the program, or another program ( Waiting and tasks ). The game's own wait() is allowed in a program, but it is a different thing: it holds the rest of its trigger for the time, and it uses the player's one wait slot, so any other Wait of that player stops until the slot is free ( Waits ). Use it for a short pause, such as a text and then a sound, and use sleep to pass time. Two kinds of second. A second of sleep(seconds(n)) is 24 frames, which is one real second at Fastest. A game second is 16 frames at every speed. elapsed() , countdown() and the Elapsed Time and Countdown Timer conditions count game seconds, so at Fastest they run about one and a half times as fast as sleep seconds: after sleep(seconds(14)) , elapsed() reads about 21. Edges. if (rose(bring(…))) is true on the frame the condition becomes true, and not again until it has been false in between. once(…) is true the first time only. random() is a coin toss, and random(n) a whole number from 0 to n − 1. Owners and per-player programs # A program runs for its owner , as that player, while that player is in the game. The owner is Player 1 unless { owner: … } says otherwise. An owner of AllPlayers , a force or a list of players makes a per-player program . The same code runs for each of those players who is in the game, computers included. CurrentPlayer is that player, and every variable is per player, each with its own copy. That is how lives, scores and cooldowns are written once. let total = shared(0) is one value that all of them share. { name: "waves" } names a program. The name appears in the Explorer, and a test finds the program by it. What a program can use # A program is written in nearly all of TypeScript. The TrigScript language guide covers each part in full. In short: Values : numbers, booleans, texts, units, players and records. u8 , u16 and u32 are numbers that are never below zero, and a number holds a fraction once one is stored in it ( Variables and numbers ). Arrays, maps and sets , fixed or growing, with their methods ( map , filter , sort and the rest), patterns and spread ( Arrays , Tables, maps and sets ). Functions and classes , including functions kept in variables, closures, extends and try / catch ( Functions , Classes , Errors ). Time : sleep , async and await , tasks that run beside the program, and Promise.all and race ( Waiting and tasks ). The game : every condition's quantity as a number, loops over units and their fields, events such as on.died , and the game's own tables through stats() ( Reading the game , Units , Events , The game's tables and memory ). The players : keys, clicks, the cursor and typed lines ( Keys, the mouse and chat ). Text and sound : texts with values, lines of JSX, and sounds the script makes ( Text , Sounds and imported files ). Libraries : nine modules that come with TrigScript, such as trigscript/ui for menus and trigscript/cutscene for scenes, and libraries other plugins provide ( TrigScript library ). A few of these together: a wave every thirty seconds, each bigger than the l

Examples of programs Each of these is a complete main.ts for a map that needs StarCraft: Remastered. Like the trigger examples , they assume locations named Beacon , Spawn , Base , Hill and Shop . Waves from a table. The table is ordinary data, and the program walks it: one wave every forty-five seconds, then it waits for the last attacker to die. A for … of over a list known when the script is applied is written out once per entry, so w.unit and w.n are plain values in each copy. The program runs as Player 1, so victory() is Player 1's; a team needs a trigger() for the others. const waves = [ { unit: units.ZergZergling, n: 8 }, { unit: units.ZergHydralisk, n: 6 }, { unit: units.ZergUltralisk, n: 2 }, ]; program(() => { displayText( "The first wave arrives in thirty seconds." ); sleep(seconds( 30 )); for ( const w of waves) { createUnit(P8, w.unit, w.n, locations.Spawn); order(P8, w.unit, locations.Spawn, locations.Base, "attack" ); minimapPing(locations.Spawn); sleep(seconds( 45 )); } while (command(P8, units.AnyUnit, ">=" , 1 )) { sleep(seconds( 2 )); } displayText( "The last wave is broken." ); victory(); }); Lives, per player. One program runs for every player, and lives is a separate counter for each. When the hero dies, the game's death count for it goes to 1. The program resets that count, takes a life, and either brings the hero back or ends the game for that player. The sleep(frames(1)) at the end of the loop makes it look once a frame. program(() => { let lives: u8 = 3 ; while ( true ) { if (deaths(CurrentPlayer, units.JimRaynorMarine, ">=" , 1 )) { setDeaths(CurrentPlayer, units.JimRaynorMarine, "set" , 0 ); lives -= 1 ; if (lives == 0 ) { displayText( "No lives left." ); defeat(); } else { createUnit(CurrentPlayer, units.JimRaynorMarine, 1 , locations.Spawn); displayText( "Your hero returns." ); } } sleep(frames( 1 )); } }, { owner: AllPlayers }); King of the hill. A point a second for holding the hill alone, shown on a leaderboard, and a win at a hundred. points is a program variable, and the amount of setScore follows it. players.Foes means "anyone at war with the current player", so the check is written once for everyone. trigger(AllPlayers, [always()], [leaderboardPoints( "Hill" , "custom" )]); program(() => { let points: u16 = 0 ; while ( true ) { if (bring(CurrentPlayer, units.AnyUnit, locations.Hill, ">=" , 1 ) && !bring(players.Foes, units.AnyUnit, locations.Hill, ">=" , 1 )) { points += 1 ; setScore(CurrentPlayer, "set" , points, "custom" ); if (points >= 100 ) { displayText( "The hill is yours." ); victory(); } } sleep(seconds( 1 )); } }, { owner: AllPlayers }); Random events. Every two minutes, a coin toss decides which of two things happens. program(() => { while ( true ) { sleep(minutes( 2 )); if (random()) { displayText( "Reinforcements pour from the nydus canal." ); createUnit(P8, units.ZergZergling, 12 , locations.Spawn); } else { displayText( "A supply drop: 100 minerals for everyone." ); setResources(AllPlayers, "add" , 100 , "ore" ); } } }); A beacon that opens a gate, once. once() is true only the first time its condition holds, so this runs once however long the unit stands there. Two things happen on their own clocks, so there are two programs. program(() => { while ( true ) { if (once(bring(P1, units.AnyUnit, locations.Beacon, ">=" , 1 ))) { displayText( "The gate opens." ); killUnitAt(P12, units.LeftUpperLevelDoor, "All" , locations.Base); setSwitch(switches.Switch1, "set" ); } sleep(frames( 1 )); } }); program(() => { while ( true ) { if (switchIs(switches.Switch1, "set" )) { createUnit(P8, units.ZergHydralisk, 2 , locations.Spawn); sleep(seconds( 30 )); } else { sleep(seconds( 1 )); } } }); A heal that each Marine gets once every ten seconds. A Map keyed by units keeps a number for each of them. A unit that has died reads as no unit in the loop over the map, which is where its entry is deleted. program(() => { const wait = new Map<Unit, number >(); while ( true ) { for ( const u of unitsAt(locations.Hill, { owner: P1, type : units.TerranMarine })) { if (!wait.has(u)) { u.heal({ percent: 100 }); wait.set(u, 10 ); } } for ( const [u, left] of wait) { if (!u || left <= 1 ) wait.delete(u); else wait.set(u, left - 1 ); } sleep(seconds( 1 )); } });

Showcase Maps made with TrigScript, each with its whole script and a recording of it played in StarCraft: Remastered. Bad Apple!! # Watch it on YouTube . The shadow-art video for "Bad Apple!!" played on the minimap, in time with the song. The fog of war is the screen: a tile lit this frame is white, a tile seen before is grey, so each frame of the game shows one frame of the video, 5,216 of them. The video is a file of the script. Import Video… turned it into bad-apple.video , a tile a pixel at 128 × 96, and when the script is built the fog library works out, for every frame, the units whose sight covers exactly its white parts. In the game each of those units is made and taken away in the same trigger pass, and what it saw stays lit until the next frame, when the library has the game put every tile back in fog. A frame takes about 125 units on average and 356 at the most. The language guide describes files the script imports and the fog library . import { fog } from "trigscript/fog" ; import badApple from "./bad-apple.video" ; const W = 128 , H = 96 ; // The camera waits below the board: the minimap draws the camera's box over // whatever is under it. const PARK = reserveLocation( "bad apple: the camera, below the board" ); // Rows `from` to `to` of the board lit, as a picture: one step of the curtain the // video opens and closes behind. const band = ( from : number , to: number ) => fog.picture( Array . from ({ length: H }, (_, y) => (y >= from && y < to ? "#" : "." ).repeat(W))); const STEP = 4 ; const board = band( 0 , H); // White falls over the board from the top, a second long, then slides off the bottom. const fall = Array . from ({ length: H / STEP }, (_, i) => band( 0 , (i + 1 ) * STEP)); const lift = Array . from ({ length: H / STEP - 1 }, (_, i) => band((i + 1 ) * STEP, H)); const credits = () => { displayText( "\x04Bad Apple!! feat. nomico" ); displayText( "\x05Alstroemeria Records, after a Touhou Project song by ZUN. Shadow art video by Anira." ); }; program( async () => { centerLocation(PARK, 64 * 32 , 116 * 32 ); centerView(PARK); await sleep(frames( 24 )); credits(); displayText( "\x05Played on the minimap with the fog of war, written in TrigScript." ); for ( const p of fall) { fog.light(P1, 0 , 0 , p); await nextFrame(); } let i = 0 ; while (i < 72 ) { fog.light(P1, 0 , 0 , board); await nextFrame(); i++; } for ( const p of lift) { fog.light(P1, 0 , 0 , p); await nextFrame(); } await sleep(frames( 12 )); playWav( "staredit\\wav\\badapple.ogg" , 0 ); await fog.play(P1, badApple); // The song runs a little past the last frame. await sleep(frames( 48 )); for ( const p of fall) { fog.light(P1, 0 , 0 , p); await nextFrame(); } displayText( "\x04Fin." ); credits(); i = 0 ; while (i < 120 ) { fog.light(P1, 0 , 0 , board); await nextFrame(); i++; } for ( const p of lift) { fog.light(P1, 0 , 0 , p); await nextFrame(); } }); The for … of loops are written out once per picture when the script is built, so each step of the curtain is a fixed set of units; the while loops run in the game. The map. 128 × 128 Badlands. The top 96 rows, the picture, are all one tile, 23778, laid with the Tile brush: of the tiles measured, its lit and fogged colours lie furthest apart on the Classic minimap. The 32 rows below have never been seen, so they stay black, and the camera waits there. There are no units, so nothing lights the fog but the script. Player 1 is the human and Player 2 a computer: Remastered will not start a Use Map Settings map without a computer slot. The song is in the map's archive as a stereo Ogg file, staredit\wav\badapple.ogg , which Remastered plays. Import Video… also takes a sound file, as a .sound file of the script that playWav plays (mixed to mono). Playing it. Host a multiplayer game alone, which runs at Fastest, the speed the video was imported for. Switch to Classic graphics (Options ▸ Graphics, or F5): Classic draws the minimap a pixel a tile, sharp, where Remastered graphics blurs it. Turn the music volume down, so the game's own music does not play over the song. "Bad Apple!! feat. nomico" is by Alstroemeria Records, an arrangement of a song from the Touhou Project by ZUN; the shadow-art video is by Anira. Neither comes with the editor or the plugin.

h: The same ideas, side by side
b: Coming from eudplib This page is for map makers who already write EUD maps with eudplib, in Python or in epScript, and build them with euddraft. A TrigScript program does the same kind of work: code that runs inside StarCraft: Remastered, reading and writing the game's memory. Most of what you know carries over, and this page says where each idea went. Which one to use # TrigScript suits you when you want to work in one place: the code is checked against the map's own names as you type, Simulate and tests try it without starting the game, and saving the map builds it, in the browser or the desktop app. Its language is TypeScript, with arrays that grow, classes, closures, try / catch and async , and the same script can make ordinary triggers for the classic game beside the programs. eudplib stays the better fit when a map depends on an euddraft plugin or a community library that TrigScript has nothing like, when you want euddraft's map protection, or when you already have a build you are happy with. TrigScript does not read eudplib or epScript code: moving a map over means writing its code again. The same ideas, side by side # eudplib, epScript TrigScript EUDVariable() , var x = 0; let x = 0; inside a program() ( Variables ) PVariable , getcurpl() / setcurpl() A per-player program, { owner: AllPlayers } : every variable is per player, and CurrentPlayer is that player ( Owners ) onPluginStart() The start of a program's body, before its loop beforeTriggerExec() , afterTriggerExec() A loop in the program: while (true) { …; await nextFrame(); } ( How a program runs ) EUDIf() , EUDWhile() , if , while in epScript if , while , for , switch , with conditions of the game where a boolean goes ( Control flow ) DoActions(…) , an action as a statement An action as a statement: setDeaths(P1, units.TerranMarine, "set", 0); @EUDFunc , function in epScript function , called or written out by the compiler ( Functions ) EUDFuncPtr A function kept in a variable, and closures ( Functions as values ) EUDArray , EUDVArray number[] , fixed or growing, with push , map , filter , sort and the rest ( Arrays ) foreach (cunit : EUDLoopCUnit()) , CUnit for (const u of unitsOf(P1)) , u.hp , u.order(…) ( Units ) f_dwread_epd , SetMemory , MemoryEPD stats() and memory.* for the named fields; memory() and setMemory() for any address ( The game's tables and memory ) StringBuffer , f_sprintf A template literal: displayText(`Wave ${wave}`) ( Text ) The MSQC plugin (keys and the mouse) keyPressed , keyHeld , clicked , mouse , with nothing to configure ( Keys, the mouse and chat ) The chatEvent plugin chatted(player, "-spawn {n} {what:unit}") and on.chat The .eds file and an euddraft run Saving the map One difference shows up everywhere: a unit's fields. eudplib reads them as the game keeps them, so hit points are in 256ths and an owner is a number. TrigScript's fields are in the units the game shows ( u.hp is whole hit points, u.owner a player), and only the fields that have been seen working in Remastered are there. A counter of lives , in epScript as a euddraft plugin, then in TrigScript: var lives = 3 ; function beforeTriggerExec() { if (Deaths(P1, AtLeast, 1 , "Terran Marine" )) { lives -= 1 ; SetDeaths(P1, SetTo, 0 , "Terran Marine" ); if (lives == 0 ) { setcurpl(P1); DisplayText( "Out of lives." ); } } } program(() => { let lives = 3 ; while ( true ) { if (deaths(P1, units.TerranMarine, ">=" , 1 )) { lives -= 1 ; setDeaths(P1, units.TerranMarine, "set" , 0 ); if (lives == 0 ) displayText( "Out of lives." ); } sleep(frames( 1 )); } }); The program runs as Player 1, so displayText is already Player 1's. Its loop is the beforeTriggerExec of the epScript, and the sleep gives the frame back. A loop over units : Player 1's Marines under 20 hit points healed to 40. function beforeTriggerExec() { foreach (cunit : EUDLoopCUnit()) { if (cunit.owner == P1 && cunit.unitType == $U( "Terran Marine" ) && cunit.hp < 20 * 256 ) { cunit.hp = 40 * 256 ; } } } program(() => { while ( true ) { for ( const u of unitsOf(P1, { type : units.TerranMarine })) if (u.hp < 20 ) u.hp = 40 ; sleep(frames( 1 )); } }); The epScript examples here were built with euddraft 0.11 and eudplib 0.81. Speed and size # We built the same test maps both ways, with TrigScript's own build and with eudplib, and ran them on the same machine. The figures are from October 2026, and they are rounded: Building a small test map took under a second in the editor, against about five seconds through euddraft. Running : a benchmark of program statements ran in about half eudplib's time, and a loop over units cost about half as much a unit. Arrays, text with numbers in it and tasks came out several times faster. One thing is slower: throwing an error costs about three times what it does in eudplib. Map size : TrigScript's maps came out larger on most test maps, usually 1.2 to 1.6 times eudplib's: 2.9 MB against 1.8 MB for the units test map. The tasks test map came out smaller, 1.4 MB against 2.1 MB. Neither kind of map plays on StarCraft 1.16.1: that version refuses writes past the end of the deaths table, which such a map makes from its first frame. A script of trigger() calls alone, with no program, plays on every version. What does not carry over # Map protection. euddraft's freeze scrambles a map against copying. TrigScript adds no protection, by decision: a map stays one the editor, and anyone else's, can open. euddraft plugins and Python libraries. TrigScript has its own library of modules , and other scmJS plugins can provide libraries of their own . Neither runs Python. Fields nobody has checked. memory() and setMemory() reach any address, as eudplib does, but the named fields are only the ones seen working in Remastered. Writing a unit's position, for one, ends a Remastered game with "EUD not supported", so it is not offered. The community. eudplib has years of maps, guides and libraries behind it, many of them in Korean. TrigScript's own build is new, from October 20

Testing and Simulate TrigScript can run a script without starting the game, in a simulator built into the editor. Simulate shows what the script does in its first twenty seconds. Tests are checks you write that run after every change. Neither adds anything to the map. The simulator models death counts, switches, preserve, the order of the trigger list, the game's arithmetic and the map's players. It has units: the ones placed on the map, then whatever createUnit makes, giveUnits hands over, moveUnit moves and killUnitAt kills, which bring and command count. It leaves out what it cannot know without the game: nothing walks, nothing fights and nothing is built, so no unit dies unless the script (or a test) kills it. Scores and the countdown read 0, and keys, clicks, the mouse and chat read as nothing. The picture sets the two lists side by side. The simulator keeps the game's time, so the frames it lists are the frames the game would act on: the first pass on frame 2, then one every 31 frames, or every frame in a map with a program. A Wait holds its trigger for its time at Fastest. See How triggers run . Simulate # Simulate (Ctrl+F5 in the TrigScript window) runs the script for 480 frames, twenty seconds of the game at Fastest. It lists, under the code, every action that ran with its frame and its line in the script, and the final value of every program variable. Triggers and programs run side by side, so a death count a program sets is seen by a trigger. A program or a trigger of a force runs for each of its players, and each line says whose it is. Simulate is a check on the logic. A script that waits for the enemy to die waits for ever here; for the fight, write a test that kills the units, or play the map. Tests # A test is ordinary TypeScript that runs in the simulator after every change that compiles. It never runs in the game and adds nothing to the map. If you have used Vitest or Jest, the names are the same: test , describe , beforeEach , test.only , test.skip , test.each and expect , imported from "trigscript" . A test of a trigger: import { test, expect } from "trigscript" ; trigger(P1, [bring(P1, units.TerranCivilian, locations.Shop, ">=" , 1 )], [ moveUnit(P1, units.TerranCivilian, 1 , locations.Shop, locations.Spawn), createUnit(P1, units.TerranMarine, 4 , locations.Spawn), ], { preserve: true }); test( "a civilian at the shop buys four marines" , (sim) => { sim.place(P1, units.TerranCivilian, locations.Shop); sim.seconds( 3 ); expect(sim.count(P1, units.TerranMarine, locations.Spawn)).toBe( 4 ); }); A test of a program, which reads the program's variables by name: import { test, expect } from "trigscript" ; // A Marine on the beacon calls the next wave, each bigger than the last. program(() => { let wave = 0 ; while ( true ) { if (countUnits(P1, units.TerranMarine, locations.Beacon) > 0 ) { wave += 1 ; createUnit(P8, units.ZergZergling, wave * 4 , locations.Spawn); print( `Wave ${wave}` ); killUnitAt(P1, units.TerranMarine, "All" , locations.Beacon); } sleep(frames( 1 )); } }, { name: "waves" }); test( "the second wave is bigger" , (sim) => { sim.place(P1, units.TerranMarine, locations.Beacon); sim.until(() => sim.program( "waves" ).wave === 1 ); sim.place(P1, units.TerranMarine, locations.Beacon); sim.until(() => sim.program( "waves" ).wave === 2 ); expect(sim.count(P8, units.ZergZergling, locations.Spawn)).toBe( 12 ); expect(sim).toHavePrinted( "Wave 2" ); }); Every test gets sim , a world of its own: the map's placed units, locations and players, the script's programs and triggers, and the same random() results every run. Time in a test is the game's: nothing runs on frame 1, the first pass is on frame 2, and sim.frames(3) gives a program two runs. What a test does With Change the world sim.place(player, type, location, count?) , sim.kill(unit) , sim.remove(unit) , sim.give(unit, to) , sim.move(unit, to) Let time pass sim.frames(n) , sim.seconds(n) , sim.until(() => …) Act as a player sim.press("F2") , sim.click() , sim.type("-give 100") , sim.moveMouse(x, y) Read the world sim.count(player, type, location?) , sim.units(filter?) , sim.resources(player) , sim.deaths(player, type) , sim.switch(n) Read a program sim.program("waves").wave See what was shown sim.printed() , expect(sim).toHavePrinted("Wave 2") place gives the new units back, and kill stands in for a fight. until fails the test if its condition is still not true after 2400 frames, so no test hangs. What a player does is found by the program on the next frame. sim.program(…) gives a program's variables by their names in the code: numbers, texts, arrays, and a record as an object. Name the program in its options ( { name: "waves" } ), or give its place in the script, counting from 0: sim.program(0) . For a per-player program, name the player too: sim.program("lives", P2) . A test fails when an expect does not hold, when it throws, and when a program does something that is always a mistake and that the game would pass over in silence, such as reading past the end of an array. A test that means to check for that says expect(sim).toHaveFaulted() . Tests live beside what they test, as above, or in files whose names end in .test.ts , in any folder. A test file can import the script's own functions and test them as plain TypeScript. A test file is never part of the map: main.ts cannot import one, and a trigger() or a program() inside one is an error. In the editor, every test( has a mark in the margin (passed, failed or not run), and a click on the mark runs that test. A failure is shown where it happened, as expected 7, got 6 at the end of the line. The Testing view, from the strip at the far left, lists the tests by folder, file and describe . It runs all of them, one of them or the ones that failed, and can show only the failing ones. The status bar keeps the count. Test Results , under the code, has the chosen test's message, what it printed and what happened frame by frame. A failing test is a warning, not an error:

The workspace This part covers the TrigScript window, the panel beside the map, and what happens to the script when the map is saved. Opening the script # Triggers ▸ TrigScript… opens the map's script in a window laid out like VS Code, with the same keys: Part What is there Explorer (left, Ctrl+B) The script's files as a tree, and under them the programs with their variables Strip at the far left Switches the sidebar between the Explorer and Testing Tabs (over the code) One per open file Icons right of the tabs Play (F5), Simulate (Ctrl+F5), Apply (Ctrl+Shift+B), Pick from map , beside the map or in a window, and … for the rest Panel (under the code, Ctrl+J) Problems , Output , Simulate , Test Results and Settings (Ctrl+,) Status bar Problems, tests, whether the triggers are in the map, the last build Command palette (F1) Every command main.ts is where the script starts. New file and New folder add to it, and a row's pencil and bin rename and remove a file. To move a file or folder, drag it onto a folder, or rename it with a folder before its name. The import s that pointed at it are rewritten to match, and the notice that says so has an Undo . Folders mean nothing to TrigScript itself: tests/ is a habit, not a rule. Edits are saved into the map as you type, since the files are part of the map archive, like a sound. Ctrl+S saves the map from inside the TrigScript window too. The code is checked as you type, against the map's own names: locations. completes to the locations the map has, units. to every unit type (and the map's custom names), switches. to the switches, and players. to the forces. The status bar counts the problems, and a click on the count opens Problems , the list of them. The Settings view holds what the map's author chose about how its programs are built, kept in the map so it builds the same on any computer: the memory for arrays that grow, how deep a function may call itself, and whether a failing test stops the build. Beside the map # The TrigScript window covers the map. To keep the map in reach, open the script beside the map : use the icon right of the tabs, or Triggers ▸ TrigScript beside the map. It is a panel over the map that blocks nothing: drag it by its title, resize it by its corner, and keep placing units while the code sits next to them. Beside the map, the names in the code and the objects on the map know about each other: Ctrl+click on locations.Beacon scrolls the map to the location and flashes it. Hovering over the name says where it is and how big. Pick from map (the target icon, or a right-click in the code): click a location or a unit on the map, and its name ( locations.Beacon , units.TerranMarine ) is typed at the cursor. From the window, it first moves the editor beside the map. When you rename a location or a switch the script mentions, a notice offers to Update references in every file. It follows the name the way the code does (an alias from import { locations as L } counts) and leaves comments, strings and anything merely spelled the same alone. Applying the script # Applying the script runs it and puts the triggers it recorded into the map's trigger list as one block. The block replaces the one from the last apply, or is added at the end the first time. There is no step to remember: saving the map applies the script , and so do Test Map and anything else that writes the map out. A save then builds the programs, as the picture shows and Saving and building explains. Apply (Ctrl+Shift+B) applies the script without saving, so you can look at the triggers in the Trigger Editor first. A click on the status bar's trigger count does the same. Play (F5) applies the script, builds the map as Save would, and hands it to Test Map to start it in the game. Output , in the panel, keeps what each of them reported. The Trigger Editor shows the script's triggers with a script badge and does not let you edit them. Open TrigScript there jumps to the file and line that made a trigger. The Text Trigger Editor fences them in comments. Hand-made triggers around the block are left alone, and a hand-made trigger inserted before the block just moves the block along. If the script has an error when the map is saved, the map is saved anyway, with the triggers from the last script that worked, and a notice names the file and the line. Triggers edited by hand # Editing one of the script's triggers outside the script makes the block stale . The editor says so the next time the script opens: how many triggers are still the script's, and how many were changed. While the block is stale, saving the map does not apply the script, and the notice on Save says so. The notice offers two ways out: Apply replaces the unchanged triggers and keeps the edited ones as hand-made triggers right after the new block, so a wave system tuned in one trigger does not come back twice. Append instead leaves all of them as they are and adds a fresh block after them. Import the Map's Triggers (under … ) goes the other way: it rewrites the map's hand-made triggers as trigger() calls, in their order, so a map made in the Trigger Editor can carry on as a script. Saving and building # A script with programs is built when the map is saved, tested or exported. TrigScript lays the programs out in the file being written, as the game's own triggers after the map's strings, and makes the file a Remastered one. It takes under a second, and nothing else has to be installed. The build also tidies the map as euddraft's build would: a null terrain tile becomes tile 1, and a placed unit's flags are made to agree with its values. The Output panel of the TrigScript window lists what it changed. A notice shows while the build runs, and its Save without it button saves at once, without the programs. A script with something TrigScript does not take yet is not built: Problems says which line and why, as a warning, and the save's notice says so again, with a button to save without the programs. The rest of the map is s

Reference Terms # Term Meaning Frame One step of the game. 24 a second at Fastest. Pass One time the game goes through the trigger list: every 31 frames, every 2 with hyper triggers, every frame in a map with a program. Game second 16 frames, at every game speed. What Elapsed Time and the countdown timer count. Wait slot Each player has one. A Wait takes it, and the player's other Waits wait for it. Apply Run the script and put its triggers into the map's trigger list. Block The run of triggers in the list that the script made. Build Turn the programs into the saved map. Only a script with programs is built. Per-player program A program owned by several players, run for each with its own variables. Triggers # trigger(players, conditions, actions, options?) One trigger. players is a player or a list; up to 16 conditions and 64 actions. { preserve, disabled, ignoreGameEnd, ignoreDisplay, conditionsMet, paused, waitSkipDisabled, flags } The options: each trigger flag by name, and flags for raw bits. preserve() The same as { preserve: true } , as an action. not(condition) The opposite condition. "Exactly n" has none, and is an error. disabled(item) The condition or action kept in the trigger but switched off. hyperTriggers(owner?) The three triggers that make the list run every 2 frames. condition(type, …) , action(type, …) A record by raw type number, for anything the tables do not know. memory(address, comparison, value) , setMemory(address, modifier, value) EUD: a value in the game's memory, through the deaths table. not() flips a comparison or a switch test, and turns always() into never() . Argument words # StarEdit's labels work too. Argument Words Comparison ">=" , "<=" , "==" Modifier "set" , "add" , "subtract" Switch state "set" , "cleared" Switch action "set" , "clear" , "toggle" , "randomize" Resource "ore" , "gas" , "oreAndGas" Score "total" , "units" , "buildings" , "unitsAndBuildings" , "kills" , "razings" , "killsAndRazings" , "custom" Order "move" , "patrol" , "attack" Alliance "enemy" , "ally" , "alliedVictory" Unit state (doodads, invincibility) "enable" , "disable" , "toggle" Count A number, or "All" displayText(text) always displays; displayText(text, false) follows the player's subtitle setting. Names # P1 … P12 , CurrentPlayer , AllPlayers Constants. players. Every player group: Force1 … Force4 (and the force's own name), Foes , Allies , Neutral , NonAlliedVictory , and the twelve players. units. Every unit type by name as an identifier ( TerranMarine ) or a string ( units["Terran Marine"] ), and by the map's custom names. AnyUnit , Men , Buildings , Factories . locations. The map's locations by name; Anywhere and NoLocation . switches. Switch1 … Switch256 , and any name the map sets. aiScripts. The AI scripts by StarEdit name; a four-letter code as a string works too. weapons. , upgrades. , techs. The game's weapons, upgrades and technologies, for stats() . colors. The player colours. A number Accepted wherever a name is: an EUD player, an unlisted unit id. Inside a program # Each row links to where the TrigScript language guide explains it. program(body, options?) Code that runs in the game. Options: owner (a player, AllPlayers , a force or a list) and name . Owners game(fn) A function that runs in the game, for programs to call. It can live in any file and be imported. Functions in other files let n = 0 , let f = false , let s = "" , let u: Unit | null = null , let p = { … } A number, a boolean, a text, a unit, a record. Variables u8 , u16 , u32 , fixed Numbers never below zero, and a number with a fraction. Whole numbers , fractions u32(x) , i32(x) The same 32 bits read the other way, where a u32 meets a plain number. Math.sqrt , Math.hypot , Math.sin , Math.cos , Math.atan2 , … Fixed numbers. Math.min , max , abs , floor and clamp(x, lo, hi) work on whole ones. number[] , string[] , Unit[] , { … }[] , number[][] Arrays. One that is pushed to grows. Arrays forEach , some , every , find , findIndex , reduce , map , filter , sort , reverse Array methods that take a function, on arrays and on units ( unitsOf(P1).filter(…) ). The methods push , pop , shift , unshift , splice , slice , concat , join , toSorted , Array.from , [...xs] Growing, cutting and copying arrays. Record<K, V> , Map<K, V> , Set<K> Tables keyed by an id of the game, by any number, or by units. Tables class , extends , get / set , static , instanceof Classes, in the program or at the top of any file. Classes const f = (x: number) => … , return () => … Functions kept as values, and closures. Functions as values try , catch , finally , throw new Error(…) Errors. One nothing catches is shown in red in the game. Errors shared(value) In a per-player program, one value for all the players. sleep(duration) , await sleep(…) , await nextFrame() , await until(…) Pause the program. frames(n) , seconds(n) , minutes(n) make a duration. Waiting start(f()) , t.cancel() , Promise.all , Promise.race Tasks that run beside the program. Tasks wait(ms) The game's own Wait, which uses the player's wait slot. Prefer sleep . rose(condition) , once(condition) True on the frame the condition becomes true; true the first time only. random() , random(n) A coin toss; a whole number from 0 to n − 1. deaths(p, unit) , bring(p, unit, location) , score(p, kind) , … A comparing condition without its comparison and amount reads the number. Reading the game minerals(p) , gas(p) , resources(p, kind) , countUnits(p, unit, location?) , kills(p, unit) , countdown() , elapsed() Reads by plainer names. race(p) , slot(p) , isHuman(p) , hasLeft(p) , supply(p, of?) The player. unitsAt(location, filter?) , unitsOf(player, filter?) , allUnits(filter?) The units a for…of runs over. Units first(filter?) , nearest(type, location, filter?) , randomUnit(filter?) One unit, or null . u.hp , u.shields , u.energy , u.kills , u.cooldown , u.buildTime , u.stim …, u.invincible Read and written. u.hp = 0 kills. A unit's fields u.maxHp , u.owner , u.type , u.x

Troubleshooting The TrigScript window stays on "Loading the editor…". The first time it opens, it downloads the code editor and TypeScript from jsDelivr, so it needs an internet connection once. After that the browser keeps them. The status bar shows a red problem count. Click it to open Problems , and click a problem to go to its line. While the script has an error, saving still works: the map keeps the triggers from the last script that worked, and a notice names the file and line. The status bar says "Not applied yet" or "Changes not applied". The script's triggers in the map are older than the script. Saving or testing the map applies it, or press Apply (Ctrl+Shift+B). The status bar says "Triggers edited outside the script". Someone edited the script's triggers in the Trigger Editor or the Text Trigger Editor, and saving does not apply the script until that is settled. Click the item and choose Apply or Append instead ; see Triggers edited by hand . A notice says the map renamed something the script names. A location or switch was renamed on the map. Update references changes the script to match. The programs are not built. Look at the status bar of the TrigScript window: built by TrigScript : the programs are built by TrigScript itself on every save. If the game shows nothing, the Output panel has the last build's lines, and Problems may name a line. Build failed or Saved without its programs : the map was saved with the script in it, but its programs do not run in the game. Show the log on the notice, or the Output panel, says why. Fix the error and save again. A map with a program does not start in the game. Programs need StarCraft: Remastered. For the classic game (1.16.1), use only trigger() . Nothing happens in the game. Check that the game type is Use Map Settings : melee games ignore the map's triggers. Check that the trigger's players are in the game, and see the trigger reference for owners the game never runs. The Trigger Map plugin shows which triggers can never run. A typed line does nothing. A single-player game has no chat. Host a multiplayer game, alone if you like. Simulate or a test never sees an enemy die. The simulator does not fight. In a test, kill the units with sim.kill(unit) . A test fails with "still not true after 2400 frames". The condition given to sim.until() never became true. Give until a larger limit as its second argument, or check the script with Simulate.

h: What a program does not have
b: TrigScript language What a program can say: numbers, arrays, maps, functions, classes, errors, tasks, units, events, input, text, sounds and libraries, and where it differs from TypeScript. This is the language of a TrigScript program: what the code inside program(() => { … }) can say, and what it does in the game. Start with the TrigScript guide if you have not written a script yet. It has the quick start, trigger() , the workspace and testing. Come here when a program needs something the guide only mentions, or when you know TypeScript and want to know where a program is different. A script has two halves. Outside program() , the script is TypeScript: it runs when the script is applied, with all of the language and its standard library, and what it records is ordinary triggers. Inside program() , every line has to become something the game can do while the map is played. Most of TypeScript comes through unchanged. These pages say what each part does, and what to write instead of the few parts that are not there. Page What is on it TrigScript beside TypeScript The whole comparison in one table The script and the program What is worked out when the script is applied, and what runs in the game Variables and numbers Numbers, booleans, records, undefined ; u8 , u16 , u32 ; fractions and Math Arrays Fixed and growing arrays; arrays of records, units, texts and arrays; the methods; patterns and spread Tables, maps and sets Lists the script made, tables keyed by an id of the game, Map and Set Control flow Loops within the frame, unrolled loops, labels, switch Functions Inlined and called functions, functions that call themselves, game() , functions as values and closures Classes Fields, methods, extends , and how an instance is kept Errors try , catch , finally , throw and classes of error Waiting and tasks sleep , async and await , tasks, Promise.all and race , generators, edges Owners and per-player programs One program for every player, and shared() Reading the game Every condition's quantity as a number; facts about the players Units Loops over units, picks, a unit's fields and what it can be told Events on.created , on.died , on.killed , on.morphed , on.order The game's tables and memory stats() for costs, weapons, upgrades and colours; memory Keys, the mouse and chat Presses, clicks, the cursor, typed lines; local and sync() Text Texts with values, string variables and their methods, lines of JSX Sounds and imported files Clips made when the script is built; videos, pictures, sounds and MIDI the script imports Libraries The standard library's nine modules, and libraries other plugins provide What a program does not have What is refused, and what to write instead Every example on these pages compiles as it is written. A line that ends with a comment such as // 80 prints that when the example runs. Examples that name locations assume the map has them: Beacon , Spawn , Base , Pen , Gate , Exit and Cursor . TrigScript beside TypeScript The table is about the inside of a program. The script and the program A program sits inside a script, and the two run at different times. Variables and numbers Variables hold numbers, booleans, texts, units and players. Arrays Arrays hold numbers, booleans, texts, units, records, instances of a class, functions or other arrays. Tables, maps and sets A list the script made is a table a program can look things up in. Control flow if/else, while, do, for, switch, break, continue, labels and c ? a : b all work. Functions Arguments pass by value, as in TypeScript. Classes Classes are TypeScript's, declared inside the program or at the top of any of the script's files. Errors try, catch, finally and throw work as in TypeScript. Waiting and tasks A program runs every frame, from where it left off. Owners and per-player programs A program runs for its owner, Player 1 unless { owner: … } says otherwise, as a trigger would: as that player, and only while that player is in the game. Reading the game Every quantity a condition compares is also a value. Units The units on the map are objects. Events **on.* runs a function each time something happens to a unit**, from the frame it is written on. The game's tables and memory stats() reaches the game's own tables: what a unit type costs, what a weapon does, a player's upgrades. Keys, the mouse and chat What the players do is keyPressed, keyHeld, clicked, mouse and chatted. Text displayText and print take a template literal, or texts joined with +, with the program's numbers in it, name(p) and color(p): Sounds and imported files playWav(sound, 0) plays a sound: one of the game's own files by its path, one of the map's sounds by its name (sounds.Name, from the Sound Editor's list), or a clip the script makes when … Libraries TrigScript comes with nine modules written for programs, imported as "trigscript/<name>". What a program does not have Outside program() the script is all of TypeScript, since it simply runs.

TrigScript beside TypeScript The table is about the inside of a program. Same means it is written and behaves as in TypeScript. Where it differs, the table says how. Anything that is missing is refused with a message as you type, never passed over in silence. TypeScript In a program What is different Types: annotations, interface , type , unions of literals, tuples, generics, as , ! , satisfies Same Erased, as in TypeScript. Some also decide things: u8 , u16 and u32 are widths, fixed is a number with a fraction, and Map<UnitType, V> is kept differently from Map<number, V> . let , const , var Same A variable needs a first value ( let n = 0 ). A const whose value the script already knows is worked out when the script is applied and costs the map nothing. number Different A whole number of 32 bits, signed, that wraps at its ends as x | 0 does. It holds a fraction once one is stored into it. No NaN , Infinity or bigint . / of whole numbers is whole division, and dividing by 0 gives 0. boolean Same Assigned with = only: no ||= or &&= . string Mostly length , s[i] and slice count characters, where JavaScript counts UTF-16 units; they differ only past U+FFFF. A made text holds 1 023 bytes. replace and split take a text, not a regular expression. null , undefined Mostly A unit or an instance may be none ( if (u) , u?.kill() ).
