Columns side by side, each as tall as the program says: the walls of a raycaster, a bar chart. fog.play(player, video, x?, y?) Play a video, a frame of it every frame; resolves at its end. fog.show(n) Keep this frame's picture for n frames and wait them out: a picture drawn every other frame at half the cost. fog.SHAPES Each brush's shape, as rows of text. The module adds a program of its own, which clears the board every frame, and it takes one of the map's free locations. Pictures and videos come from files the script imports ( Files the script imports ).

Screen trigscript/screen is a grid of pixels shown on the map as units, so the minimap shows the picture: a game of Snake or Tetris played on the minimap, a score in big digits. import { Screen, sprite } from "trigscript/screen" ; const SHIP = sprite([ ".1." , "111" , "1.1" ]); program( async () => { const screen = new Screen( 4 , 4 , 24 , 16 ); // 24 × 16 pixels, its top left on tile (4, 4) screen.reveal(P1); let x = 10 ; let score = 0 ; while ( true ) { if (keyHeld(P1, "Left" )) x = Math.max(x - 1 , 0 ); if (keyHeld(P1, "Right" )) x = Math.min(x + 1 , 21 ); screen.clear(); screen.rect( 0 , 15 , 24 , 1 , 5 ); // the ground, in colour 5 screen.blit(SHIP, x, 12 ); screen. number (score, 1 , 1 , 2 ); // digits 3 × 5 pixels, in colour 2 screen.present(); score += 1 ; await nextFrame(); } }); A pixel is 0 (empty) or a colour from 1 to 7. Drawing changes the grid, and present() shows it: each pixel is a unit on the map, two tiles across, owned by the player whose colour it is. Only the pixels that changed since the last present() are made or taken away, so a still picture costs nothing to show. Draw through the methods; a pixel written into the grid directly is not seen. What the map needs. The players who own the pixels are, for colours 1 to 7, Players 3, 4, 5, 1, 6, 7 and 8. Give each the colour the screen should show (cyan, yellow, purple, green, red, blue, orange), and make none of them a computer, since a computer moves its own units. StarCraft: Remastered will not start a game without a computer, so make Player 2 a computer. It owns no pixel. A pixel is an Overlord unless the screen is made with "solid" . An Overlord flies, so the screen can be over any ground, Space included; the minimap draws each as a dot with a gap round it. A "solid" pixel is a Pylon, which the minimap draws as its whole two-tile footprint, so pixels side by side join into one block; a Pylon needs buildable ground and none of the map's own units in the way. A player sees the pixels only where they have vision, so call screen.reveal(player) once, before the first present() . Name What it does new Screen(x, y, width, height, look?) A screen of width × height pixels (2 048 at most), its top left on tile (x, y). look is "dots" (the default) or "solid" . clear(color?) , set(x, y, color) , get(x, y) Fill it, set one pixel, read one. rect(x, y, width, height, color) , line(x0, y0, x1, y1, color) A filled rectangle; a line, both ends drawn. sprite(rows) , blit(sprite, x, y) A picture from rows of text ( "1" … "7" , anything else see-through), and drawing it. number(n, x, y, color) A whole number's digits, 3 × 5 pixels each. reveal(player) Let a player see the screen. present() Show what was drawn. <ScreenView screen width height /> The same grid in a player's text area, a square a pixel, for a ui.lines view.

Music trigscript/music plays music written as patterns: a note's name per step, held with - , rests with . . Everything is made when the script is built. Each note an instrument plays becomes a sound once, and a song becomes a table of which sound starts on which frame. import { music } from "trigscript/music" ; const lead = music.presets.chip(); const bass = music.presets.bass(); const drums = music.drums(); const song = music.song({ bpm: 120 }, music.track(lead, "C5 - E5 - G5 - - . | A5 - G5 - E5 - - ." ), music.track(bass, "C3 - - - - - - - | F3 - - - - - - -" ), music.track(drums, "kh h sh h kh h sh h | kh h sh h kh kh sh h" ), ); program( async () => { start(music.loop(song)); // the song again and again, beside the program playWav(lead.note( "C6" , 0.1 ), 0 ); // an instrument's note on its own, as a sound effect }); Patterns. A step is a word, a quarter of a beat unless the song says otherwise. A note's name starts a note ( C4 , F#5 , Bb2 ); notes joined by + sound together ( C4+E4+G4 ); - holds what sounds a step longer; . is a rest; | is only for the eye. @ after a step's notes says how loud ( C4@0.5 ). A drum kit's step is its sounds' letters: kh is the kick and the hat together. Instruments. music.synth makes notes from waves, music.fmSynth by FM, and music.strings plucks them; music.sampler plays a recording of one note at every pitch, from a sound file the script imports. music.presets has instruments to start from: supersaw , pad , bass , acid , lead , chip , keys , bell and pluck . music.drums() is a kit made from nothing, a letter a drum: k kick, s snare, c clap, h closed hat, o open hat, t tom, r rim and x crash. music.kit makes one from clips of your own. Longer songs are written in sections. Parts are named once, and each section says what they play in it; a pattern shorter than its section plays again until the section is full. Chords are written by name, with a template that says how their notes are played: import { music } from "trigscript/music" ; const parts = { keys: music.part(music.presets.keys()), bass: music.part(music.presets.bass()), drums: music.part(music.drums()), }; const verse = music.section( 4 , { keys: music.chords( "Am F C G" , "1+2+3 - . 1+2+3 . . 1+2+3 -" , { octave: 4 }), bass: music.chords( "Am F C G" , "1 - . 1 . 1 3 -" , { octave: 2 }), drums: music.beat({ k: [ 0 , 3 , 4 ], s: [ 2 , 6 ], h: [ 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] }, 8 ), }, { name: "verse" }); const song = music.arrange({ bpm: 120 , steps: 2 }, parts, verse, verse.with({ keys: null })); program( async () => { await music.play(song); print( "The song is over." ); }); Music that follows the game. music.stems cuts a song of sections into a sound for each bar of each layer, and music.conduct plays them as a Band says: which section, which layers, and a stinger on the next beat. import { music, Band } from "trigscript/music" ; const parts = { keys: music.part(music.presets.keys()), drums: music.part(music.drums()) }; const calm = music.section( 2 , { keys: music.chords( "Am F" , "1+2+3 - - -" , { octave: 4 }) }, { name: "calm" }); const fight = music.section( 2 , { keys: music.chords( "Am F" , "1+2+3 . 1+2+3 ." , { octave: 4 }), drums: music.beat({ k: [ 0 , 4 ], s: [ 2 , 6 ], h: [ 0 , 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] }, 8 ), }, { name: "fight" }); const cut = music.stems(music.arrange({ bpm: 120 , steps: 2 }, parts, calm, fight), { layers: { drums: [ "drums" ], keys: [ "keys" ] }, }); program( async () => { const band = new Band(); band.loop = true ; // a section plays again until told otherwise start(music.conduct(cut, band)); await until(bring(P8, units.AnyUnit, locations.Base, ">=" , 1 )); band.go(cut.section( "fight" )); // from the next bar }); What the game does with it. A bar lasts a whole number of frames (42 ms each at Fastest), so the tempo is the nearest that fits, and song.bpm says which. A sound starts within 21 ms of its frame. The game plays 32 sounds at once, and a song that would need more is refused. Notes that overlap add up with no limiter, so keep volumes down. music.render(song) mixes a song into one sound when the script is built instead: every note exactly in time and only one sound playing, but nothing can change while it plays. A program plays to its own player; a program of every player plays to each. Name What it is synth(options) , fmSynth(options) , strings(options) , sampler(clip, root?) Instruments. instrument.note(name, seconds) is one note as a sound. presets.supersaw() … presets.pluck() Instruments to start from, each taking the options of what it is made with. drums(options?) , kit(hits) Drum kits: one made from nothing, or a clip a letter. track(instrument, pattern, options?) , song(options, ...tracks) A pattern for an instrument, and tracks played together. Options: pan , volume , fx , reverb ; bpm , steps , beats , swing . part(instrument, options?) , section(bars, parts, options?) , arrange(options, parts, ...sections) A song in sections. section.with({ … }) is a section with some parts changed, null resting one. chord(symbol, octave?) , chords(progression, template, options?) , over(notes, template) Chords by name, and a template that plays them. beat(hits, steps?) A drum bar from the steps each letter plays on. transpose(p, semitones) , stretch(p, by) , repeat(p, n) Patterns changed. midi(notes, parts, options?) A song from a MIDI file the script imports. riser(seconds) , impact() , pump(beat) A rise into a drop, a boom to land on, and a pumping effect. render(song, options?) The song mixed into one sound when the script is built. play(song) , loop(song) Play a song note by note, once or again and again. stems(song, options) , new Band() , conduct(stems, band) Music that follows the game: band.go , queue , mute , unmute , sting , stop .

Libraries from other plugins A plugin can provide a library of its own: TrigScript modules a script imports by the library's name, as it imports the standard library by trigscript/… . import { spawnWave } from "waves/spawn" is the module spawn of the library waves , and import { spawnWave } from "waves" is its index . While the plugin is on, the editor completes the library's names, and hovering one shows the library's own source and comments. import { announce, spawnWave } from "waves" ; program(() => { for ( let wave = 1 ; wave <= 5 ; wave++) { announce( `Wave ${wave}` ); spawnWave(P2, units.ZergZergling, wave, locations.Spawn); sleep(seconds( 20 )); } }); The map keeps its own copy. When the script is applied, which saving does, each library the script imports is copied into the map beside the script's files, and from then on the map builds with that copy. So a map opened where the plugin is not installed still builds, and so does a map shared with someone who has another version of the plugin. A library the script stops importing leaves the map at the next apply. A newer version is offered, not taken. When the installed plugin has a different version of a library from the map's copy, the editor says so and offers Update , which replaces the copy. Keep the map's copy leaves it as it is. A library is TrigScript, like the script's own files, and runs with the same rights: a library in someone else's map is no different from that map's own script. A module joins the build only when something imports it. Making a library for your own maps is a plugin of your own that provides the modules. How is in the TrigScript plugin's README , and Plugins covers writing a plugin.

Plugins Installing plugins, writing your first one, the core concepts, putting things on screen, and a tour of the API. A plugin is a small program the editor loads from a public Git repository or a web address. It can add menu items, hotkeys, dialogs, panels, map tools and overlays, and it can read and change the open map through the same undo model the built-in tools use. This page has eight parts: Using plugins : installing a plugin, what it is allowed to do, and updating or removing it. For map makers. Writing a plugin : the files, loading from your machine, bundling, translating, testing, debugging and publishing. Core concepts : the rules that hold across the whole API. Recipes : complete snippets for common jobs, such as a problems panel, a brush of your own, or triggers generated from a table. Putting things on screen : every place a plugin can show something, and the options each one takes. The API, group by group : what each group is for and the rules a signature does not show. Plugins to read : the project's own plugins, by what each one is a good example of. Every call has its own entry in the API reference , generated from the editor's declarations. This page teaches and gives the rules; it links into the reference for signatures and options. How the editor loads plugins internally is in docs/development.md . Using plugins This part is for map makers: how to install and update plugins, and what you are trusting when you do. Your first plugin This part builds one small plugin from nothing to a published repository. Writing a plugin A plugin is one TypeScript or JavaScript file exporting an activate(api) function, next to a plugin.json, in a public repository. Core concepts The rules on this page hold across the whole API. Recipes Complete snippets for common jobs, each using several parts of the API together. Putting things on screen Everything a plugin shows goes through api.ui, plus the menu, context-menu and hotkey groups. h: Keeping a plugin up to date
Where a plugin keeps its data
b: Using plugins This part is for map makers: how to install and update plugins, and what you are trusting when you do. What is available # These plugins come with the editor and start on: Walkability, Paint, Repair, Terrain from Image, TrigScript, Stamp Library, scmscx.com, scmjs.dev, scm-sim and Aftermath. TrigEdit, the Text Trigger Editor, comes with the editor too but starts off; tick it on in Plugins ▸ Manage Plugins… when you need it. The rest are in Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins… : Melee Wizard, Section Explorer, Magenta, Trigger Map, Timelapse, Hello World and the API Playground among them. The user guide says what each one does and where it appears, and each repository has its own README. The plugins that come with the editor are defaults : they are built in, so a fresh install has them without going to the network. A default can be turned off but not removed. Installing one # From the list. Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins… , then Install on a row. From an address. Plugins ▸ Manage Plugins… , then paste the address. From a link. A link to the editor ending in ?plugin=github:scm-js/<repository> offers that plugin when the editor opens: the same confirmation as Browse Plugins if it is not installed, or a notice with Turn It On if it is installed but off. The documentation's Try it links use this to offer the API Playground. Only the project's own repositories can be named this way. In every case the editor shows where the code comes from and asks before it adds anything. An address can take any of these forms: Address What it points at github:owner/repo A GitHub repository, at its default branch. github:owner/repo@v1.2 A tag, branch or commit of it. github:owner/repo@v1.2/plugins/mine A folder inside a repository, for several plugins in one. https://github.com/owner/repo/tree/v1.2/plugins/mine The same, copied from the browser's address bar. https://…/plugin.json A plugin's manifest anywhere: GitLab, a gist, your own server. https://…/plugin.ts A single plugin file with no manifest. http://localhost:3000/ A folder holding plugin.json on your own machine, while you write a plugin. What you are trusting # There is no sandbox. A plugin has the same access as the editor: it can read and change the open map, read and write the files in the map archive and the editor's browser storage, and make network requests. It is the same trust a browser extension asks for, so only add plugins you trust. Before any code is fetched, the Add screen shows what the plugin says about itself (name, version, author, description and icon from its plugin.json ), links to its repository, and the addresses the code will come from. Nothing has run yet, so this is the moment to look at the repository. The screen has three options: Option Default What it does Enable it now on Start the plugin as soon as it is added. Pin to this version on Store the exact commit the address points at today, so the plugin never changes under you. Load from a copy saved here off Keep a copy of the plugin's files in this browser and load from that until you press Reload. A plugin that needs another one (see Requiring another plugin ) lists it under Also installs . Keeping a plugin up to date # A pinned plugin never changes by itself; a push to its repository reaches nobody who has it installed. To move forward, use the buttons in Plugins ▸ Manage Plugins…: Check for update on a row asks the repository for its newest release. The answer is on the row: Up to date , Could not check , or an Update to … button that shows the new manifest and asks before changing anything. Check all for updates answers every row at once, in a line under the button. It reads the plugin lists first and asks a repository only for a plugin no list carries. Update all appears when two or more rows offer an update. It installs them one after another without the confirmation screen, and each plugin keeps its settings. A version that needs a newer editor is left, and the line under the button says so. Only releases (version tags) count; commits pushed after the newest release are not offered. Browse Plugins also marks v… available on a row when its list carries a newer version than the one you run. Preferences ▸ Plugins ▸ Plugin updates decides whether the editor looks for you. It reads the plugin list at most once every six hours. Choice What happens Tell me (default) A notice names what is newer, with a button to Manage Plugins. Do nothing Nothing is checked until you press a row's button. Install them Newer versions of the plugins you added yourself are installed. Defaults, plugins loading from a saved copy, plugins that are off, and versions that need a newer editor are only named in the notice. Defaults move with the editor: each release carries the versions it was tested with, and a default is never checked until you press its button. Updating one makes it an ordinary plugin fetched from its repository at each start; Revert on the row goes back to the version the editor ships. The other buttons on a row: Reload fetches the plugin again and replaces any saved copy. For a pinned plugin that is the same commit, so it is mostly for plugins you are writing. Turning a plugin off removes everything it added: menu items, hotkeys, dialogs, panels, overlays and listeners. Remove also takes it off the list. Defaults cannot be removed. A plugin that fails to load raises a notice with a button to Manage Plugins, where its row shows the error. Where a plugin keeps its data # In the browser. A plugin's settings appear in Preferences ▸ Storage as one row under its id, with a button to clear them. Clear all data removes them too. In the map. A plugin can keep files inside the map archive, so they travel with the map. TrigScript keeps its scripts this way. The Save dialog lists these files and can leave them out. Sources # Browse Plugins reads registries : JSON files listing plugins and the address each installs from. The project's own is scm-js/registry , and the Sources button adds other

Step 5: load it from your machine
b: Your first plugin This part builds one small plugin from nothing to a published repository. The plugin is Base Check : it counts the mineral fields and geysers near each start location, lists them in a panel, and can set every short mineral field back to the full amount. It is about seventy-five lines, and it uses the parts of the API most plugins use: reading the map, a panel, an edit with undo, events, storage, a menu item and a hotkey. You need nothing installed. The first three steps run in the editor's API Playground; the files come in step 4. Before you start # Open the editor and a melee map, or make a map with File ▸ New and a few start locations and mineral fields, so the plugin has something to count. Install the API Playground from Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins…, and open Tools ▸ API Playground. The playground is a code editor in which api is already defined. Ctrl+Enter runs what you wrote against the open map. On the documentation site, steps 1 and 3 have a Try it link that opens the editor with the code already in the playground. Trying the API first describes the playground in full. Step 1: read the map # Reading needs no setup. api.document.scenario() is the open map, api.query answers questions about it, and api.consts has the numbers the map file uses, so the code does not hard-code that a vespene geyser is unit 188. const { tile, unit } = api.consts; const radius = 12 * tile; // unit positions are in pixels; a tile is 32 of them function census() { const units = api.document.scenario()?.units ?? []; return api.query.startLocations().map((start) => { const near = units.filter((u) => Math.hypot(u.x - start.x, u.y - start.y) <= radius); return { start, minerals: near.filter((u) => api.consts.isResource(u.unitId) && u.unitId !== unit.vespeneGeyser).length, geysers: near.filter((u) => u.unitId === unit.vespeneGeyser).length, }; }); } for ( const row of census()) { api.log(api.names.player(row.start.owner), `${row.minerals} mineral fields, ${row.geysers} geysers` ); } Try it Run it and the playground's output lists one line per start location. Two things to notice: Nothing throws without a map. scenario() answers null and startLocations() an empty list, so the code above prints nothing instead of failing. Players count from 0. start.owner 0 is Player 1, as in the map file. api.names.player turns the slot into the name the editor shows. Step 2: show it in a panel # A panel floats over the map without blocking it. Its mount function receives an empty element to fill, and api.ui.widgets builds lists, buttons and fields that look like the editor's own. The list is rebuilt whenever the units change, and clicking a row takes the view to that start location. Replace the for loop at the end of step 1 with this, keeping census , and run again: api.ui.panel({ title: "Base Check" , width: 280 , mount(body) { const show = () => { const items = census().map((row) => ({ label: api.names.player(row.start.owner), hint: `${row.minerals} minerals · ${row.geysers} gas` , value: row.start, })); body.replaceChildren( items.length > 0 ? api.ui.widgets.list(items, { onPick: (start) => api.view.goTo({ kind: "unit" , index: start.index }) }) : api.ui.widgets.hint( "This map has no start locations." ), ); }; show(); const subscriptions = [api.events.on( "units" , show), api.events.on( "document" , show)]; return () => subscriptions.forEach((s) => s.dispose()); }, }); Place or delete a mineral field while the panel is open and the count follows. The function mount returns is its cleanup: it runs when the panel closes, and here it stops the two listeners. The "document" event covers opening another map or switching tabs. Step 3: change the map # Every change to terrain or objects goes through api.document.edit . It takes the label Edit ▸ Undo will show and a function, and everything the function does becomes one undo entry. Here the edit sets every mineral field holding less than the standard 1500 back to 1500, and flashes the ones it changed. const { unit } = api.consts; const units = api.document.scenario()?.units ?? []; const short = units.flatMap((u, index) => api.consts.isResource(u.unitId) && u.unitId !== unit.vespeneGeyser && u.resourceAmount < unit.defaultMinerals ? [index] : [], ); const result = api.document.edit( "Top up minerals" , (tx) => tx.updateUnits(short, () => ({ resourceAmount: unit.defaultMinerals })), ); if (result.changed) api.view.flash({ units: short }); api.ui.status( `${result.units} mineral fields topped up` ); Try it Press Ctrl+Z in the editor and the amounts go back. You did not mark anything as modified, repaint the map or write the undo record: the transaction does all three. The function you pass must not be async ; Asynchronous calls explains why. Step 4: make it a plugin # A plugin is two files in a folder: plugin.json , which describes it, and plugin.ts , which exports a function the editor calls with api . In the playground, Export as Plugin… saves a zip with both files and the typings and build setup already in place. Or make the folder by hand: plugin.json : { "name" : "Base Check" , "version" : "1.0.0" , "description" : "Counts the resources at each start location and tops up short mineral fields." , "entry" : "plugin.ts" , "icon" : "⛏️" , "api" : 1 } plugin.ts is the three steps put together, with the radius kept as a setting in api.storage , a menu item and a hotkey: import type { PluginApi } from "@scm-js/plugin-api" ; export default function activate(api: PluginApi ) { const { tile, unit } = api.consts; const w = api.ui.widgets; let radius = api.storage.get( "radius" , 12 ); // in tiles let panel: ReturnType< typeof api.ui.panel> | null = null ; const isMineral = (id: number ) => api.consts.isResource(id) && id !== unit.vespeneGeyser; function census() { const units = api.document.scenario()?.units ?? []; return api.query.startLocations().map((start) => { const near = units.filter((u) => Math.hypot(u.x - start.x, u.y - start.y) <= radius * tile); return { start, mi

Writing a plugin A plugin is one TypeScript or JavaScript file exporting an activate(api) function, next to a plugin.json , in a public repository. There is no build step to start with: the editor fetches the source, transpiles it in the browser and calls activate . Your first plugin walks through writing one. This part covers each piece in turn. Trying the API first # The API Playground plugin lets you call the API before setting anything up. Install it from Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins… and open Tools ▸ API Playground. Its panel has a code editor where api is already defined. Write a few lines, press Ctrl+Enter, and they run against the open map. Stop removes everything the run added: menu items, listeners, panels, overlays, map tools and timers. Running again stops the previous run first. Undo Run undoes the run's edits to the map. The list at the top has worked examples, one idea each. Export as Plugin… saves the snippet as a zip holding plugin.json , a plugin.ts with the snippet as the body of activate , and the typings and build setup described below. A whole plugin.ts pasted in runs too: its activate is called, and what it returns is called on Stop . Type api. for completion. Hovering over a name shows its documentation, the same text as the API reference . On the documentation site, an example that runs as it is written has a Try it link. It opens the editor with the example in the playground, and offers to install the playground if you do not have it. Nothing runs until you press Run. Copy Link , at the foot of the panel, makes the same kind of link for your own snippet. Examples without a link are fragments: they need something only your plugin has, such as a server to talk to or a variable defined elsewhere. Note. A snippet runs as the playground, so a command or service id without a dot is prefixed with the playground's id and can replace the playground's own. Use a dotted id of your own ( "my-plugin.open" ) while you try things. Starting a plugin # Start from Hello World , or from a snippet exported from the playground. Hello World's plugin.ts is about ninety lines, mostly comments. The repository also has a Korean catalogue ( ko.ts ) with the test that keeps it complete, and the typings, type-check, build and CI described below. The two files # plugin.json : { "name" : "Hello" , "version" : "1.0.0" , "description" : "Says hello from the Tools menu." , "entry" : "plugin.ts" , "icon" : "icon.svg" , "api" : 1 } Field Meaning name The only required field. id Used for storage keys, command and service names, and log lines. Derived from name when absent. version , description , author , homepage Shown on the Add screen and in Manage Plugins. entry The source file. Defaults to plugin.ts , then plugin.js . api The API version the plugin needs. An older editor refuses to load it. icon See The icon . build A pre-built bundle to load instead of the source. See Building . requires Other plugins this one needs. See Requiring another plugin . plugin.ts : import type { PluginApi } from "@scm-js/plugin-api" ; export default function activate(api: PluginApi ) { api.menu.add( "Tools" , { label: "Say Hello" , enabled: () => api.document.isOpen(), run: () => api.ui.status( `Hello, ${api.document.info()?.name}!` ), }); } Try it activate may be async . It may also return a function, which runs when the plugin is turned off; What you add is removed for you says when you need one. The icon # icon is shown in Manage Plugins and in the title bar of your plugin's dialogs. icon Meaning "icon.svg" , "art/mark.png" An image beside the manifest ( .png .svg .jpg .gif .webp .avif .ico ). "https://…/mark.png" An image anywhere. "data:image/svg+xml,…" An image inline in the manifest. "🗺️" Up to four characters, drawn as text. Anything else, or an image that fails to load, shows the default plugin mark. Draw for a 30 px square (it is also shown at 14 px) with no frame: an icon that is a bordered square looks like a second checkbox next to the row's own. Terrain from Image's icon.svg is an example. Loading it from your machine # Serve the plugin's folder with cross-origin requests allowed: npx serve --cors . Paste http://localhost:3000/ into Plugins ▸ Manage Plugins…, and press Reload on its row after each change. For completion and type-checking in your own code editor, install the typings: npm i -D @scm-js/plugin-api The package is types only: one index.d.ts . The import type line is removed before the file runs, so the package matters only for editing and type-checking. A value imported from it type-checks and is then undefined when the plugin runs; everything you need at run time comes from api . The same files are tagged at scm-js/plugin-api if you prefer a git dependency. The package's major version is the API version, so ^1 in package.json is right. New calls arrive in minor versions, since they break nothing that does not use them. Imports and dependencies # Relative imports work , with or without an extension ( ./convert , ./convert.js meaning convert.ts , or a folder's index.ts ). Package imports need a bundle. import x from "some-package" is refused when the editor loads source, because it has no module resolver. import type from @scm-js/plugin-api is fine, since it is removed first. For a real dependency, including a UI framework, ship a bundle (see Building ). Building # A plugin can ship a bundle and name it in the manifest: "build" : "dist/plugin.js" The editor then imports that one file instead of compiling your source file by file. It is faster for anything bigger than one file, and the only way to use an npm dependency. Keep entry in the manifest too: it is what people read, and what loads when no bundle is published. The project's plugins all build with one esbuild command: "build" : "esbuild plugin.ts --bundle --format=esm --target=es2022 --platform=browser --outfile=dist/plugin.js" , "dev" : "npm run build -- --watch" Commit dist/plugin.js , because the editor loads it straight from the repos

h: Asynchronous calls, and the one synchronous builder
What you add is removed for you
Several maps, and maps to look at only
b: Core concepts The rules on this page hold across the whole API. The rest of the guide refers back to them instead of repeating them. Units, players and ids # Tiles and pixels. Terrain, fog and rectangles count tiles. Units, sprites and locations are placed in map pixels, 32 to a tile ( api.consts.tile ). A rectangle is { x0, y0, x1, y1 } in tiles, with x1 and y1 exclusive. Players count from 0. owner 0 is Player 1, as in the map file. api.names.player(slot) gives the name the editor shows. Ids are the game's. A unit id is its row in units.dat (0 is the Terran Marine), and upgrades and technologies likewise. api.names turns any of them into a name, and api.consts has the ones the map file treats specially, so a plugin does not hard-code them. Asynchronous calls, and the one synchronous builder # Asynchronous calls return promises. There are no completion callbacks. When the user dismisses something (Esc, Cancel, a right-click, the ×), the promise resolves with null or false instead of rejecting, so the normal path needs no try . This covers opening, saving and exporting maps, loading game data, and everything that waits for the user (pickers, confirm , prompt and so on). const rect = await api.ui.pickArea({ prompt: "Pick an area to flatten" }); if (rect) { // null: Esc, a right-click, or no map await api.tileset.load(); // the graphics the fill needs const [, ground] = api.terrain.types(); // the tileset's second flat terrain if (ground) api.document.edit( "Flatten" , (tx) => tx.stampTerrain(rect, ground.id)); else api.ui.status( "The tileset graphics are not installed." ); } Try it The remaining callbacks are real callbacks: event listeners, widget handlers, a dialog's mount , and the pointer and draw hooks of map tools and overlays. A transaction's function must be synchronous. document.edit(label, build) and document.update(label, build) commit the moment build returns. An async function would commit at its first await , and the rest would change the map outside the undo entry. TypeScript refuses one, and the editor catches it at run time too. Wrong, because the edit commits at the await and the placement lands outside it: api.document.edit( "Place" , async (tx) => { await api.data.load(); tx.placeUnit( 0 , 0 , 128 , 128 ); }); Right: await first, then write. await api.data.load(); api.document.edit( "Place" , (tx) => { tx.placeUnit( 0 , 0 , 128 , 128 ); }); Try it For long work, api.ui.progress shows a panel over the map that does not block editing. Check cancelled() in your loop. Its signal is an AbortSignal , so a fetch(url, { signal: job.signal }) stops when the user cancels. The three kinds of write # Every change a plugin makes to the map goes through one of three calls, matching the editor's own three ways of writing: a brush stroke, a dialog's OK, and a raw file edit. Call Covers Undo If your function throws document.edit(label, build) Terrain and objects: tiles, ISOM, units, sprites, doodads, locations, fog. One history entry. Rolled back. document.update(label, build) Tables and settings: triggers, briefing, strings, switch names, name and description, players, forces, unit / upgrade / tech settings, sounds, map revision. One history entry, as with a settings dialog's OK. What was written stays, as one entry. document.sections.* The file's raw bytes, any section. None, and the history is cleared. Nothing is written. In both transactions each operation applies immediately, so a later one sees what an earlier one did. Calling the transaction after the function has returned throws. The transaction marks the map modified, saves the right file sections and repaints; you do none of that yourself. The map you read is read-only. document.scenario() is the editor's own live object, typed read-only all the way down: a line that writes to it does not compile, because a direct write would skip undo, never be saved and never repaint. Copy what you want to change ( { ...scn.units[0], x: 64 } is an ordinary record) and hand it to a transaction. A helper of your own that only reads takes ReadonlyScenario , or readonly UnitRecord[] for one of its lists. What you add is removed for you # Menu items, hotkeys, commands, services, dialogs, panels, overlays, map tools and listeners are all tracked. Turning the plugin off, reloading it or removing it takes them away whether or not you cleaned up. Disposables. Everything add , on , register and provide return is a Disposable . Keep the ones you want to remove early and ignore the rest. Cleanup functions. A dialog's or panel's mount may return a function, which runs when it closes. Use it for listeners that should stop with the panel rather than with the plugin. What the API cannot see. Timers, sockets and workers are yours to stop. Return a function from activate and the editor calls it when the plugin is turned off: import type { PluginApi } from "@scm-js/plugin-api" ; export default function activate(api: PluginApi ) { const timer = setInterval(() => api.log( "still running" ), 60_000 ); return () => clearInterval(timer); } Late writes are refused. Once a plugin is turned off, anything it left behind can no longer change the map: writes do nothing and log a line in the Debug Console. A part you remove as a whole. api.scope() gives a child api whose registrations go together, for a mode the user turns on and off. When no map is open # The editor can have no map open, and a plugin starts before the first map does. Reads answer null , [] or false instead of throwing. The exception is the raw-bytes path, document.sections , whose file() and bytes() throw. Writes change nothing. edit and update return a result with changed: false . Menu items should say so. Give an item enabled: () => api.document.isOpen() and it is greyed out until a map is open. The game's files may be missing too: the editor works without them, so anything that needs the tileset, the unit graphics or the game's tables degrades. A terrain operation writes nothing and says so in its r

b: Recipes Complete snippets for common jobs, each using several parts of the API together. Every one runs in the playground as written; in a plugin, the same lines go inside activate(api) . The API, group by group explains each call they use. A problems panel that follows the map # Check Map's findings in a docked panel, refreshed after every change. Clicking a row goes to the unit, location or trigger, or opens the settings dialog the problem is in. const w = api.ui.widgets; api.ui.panel({ title: "Problems" , dock: "right" , grow: true , mount(body) { const show = () => { const issues = api.query.validate(); body.replaceChildren( issues.length === 0 ? w.hint( "Check Map finds nothing wrong." ) : w.list(issues.map((issue) => ({ label: issue.text, title: `${issue.level}: ${issue.where}` , value: issue.target })), { onPick: (target) => { if (!target) return ; if (target.kind === "dialog" ) api.ui.open(target.id); else api.view.goTo(target); }, }), ); }; show(); const subscriptions = [api.events.on( "commit" , show), api.events.on( "document" , show)]; return () => subscriptions.forEach((s) => s.dispose()); }, }); Try it A heat map of where the units are # An overlay drawn from the map's own data: units counted in blocks of four tiles, and each block tinted by how many it holds. The count is redone when the units change, not on every repaint, because draw runs each time the view moves. const BLOCK = 4 ; // tiles let blocks = new Map< string , number >(); function count() { blocks = new Map(); for ( const u of api.document.scenario()?.units ?? []) { const key = `${Math.floor(u.x / api.consts.tile / BLOCK)},${Math.floor(u.y / api.consts.tile / BLOCK)}` ; blocks.set(key, (blocks.get(key) ?? 0 ) + 1 ); } } count(); const overlay = api.ui.overlay({ name: "Unit density" , draw(ctx, view) { const size = BLOCK * view.tilePx; for ( const [key, units] of blocks) { const [bx, by] = key.split( "," ).map(Number); ctx.fillStyle = `rgba(255, 120, 40, ${Math.min(0.7, units * 0.12)})` ; ctx.fillRect(view.x(bx * BLOCK * api.consts.tile), view.y(by * BLOCK * api.consts.tile), size, size); } }, }); for ( const event of [ "units" , "document" ] as const ) { api.events.on(event, () => { count(); overlay.redraw(); }); } Try it A brush of your own # A map tool that paints the Terrain palette's current terrain while the button is held, and commits the whole drag as one undo entry when it is released. Collecting during the drag and writing once on release is what makes one stroke one Ctrl+Z. await api.tileset.load(); const stroke = new Map< string , { d: { x: number ; y: number }; px: number ; py: number }>(); function add(px: number , py: number ) { const d = api.terrain.diamondAt(px, py); if (api.terrain.isDiamond(d)) stroke.set( `${d.x},${d.y}` , { d, px, py }); tool.redraw(); } const tool = api.ui.mapTool({ name: "Terrain pencil" , hint: "drag to paint, Esc to stop" , onDown(p) { add(p.px, p.py); }, onMove(p) { if (p.down) add(p.px, p.py); }, onUp() { const terrain = api.terrain.active().terrain; // whatever the Terrain palette has picked const diamonds = [...stroke.values()].map((s) => s.d); stroke.clear(); api.document.edit( "Terrain pencil" , (tx) => { for ( const d of diamonds) tx.paintIsom(d, terrain); }); }, draw(ctx, view) { ctx.fillStyle = "#ffd24a" ; for ( const { px, py } of stroke.values()) ctx.fillRect(view.x(px) - 3 , view.y(py) - 3 , 6 , 6 ); }, }); Try it Copies of the selection under the symmetry setting # Place a copy of every selected unit at each of its mirror positions, following whatever Tools ▸ Symmetry is set to, with the Units palette's placement checks. const scn = api.document.scenario(); const selected = api.selection.units(); if (!scn || selected.length === 0 ) { api.ui.status( "Select some units first." ); } else if (api.terrain.symmetry() === "none" ) { api.ui.status( "Turn on Tools ▸ Symmetry first." ); } else { const originals = selected.map((index) => scn.units[index]); const result = api.document.edit( "Mirror units" , (tx) => { for ( const u of originals) { // The first point is the unit's own position; the rest are its images. for ( const p of tx.mirrorPoint(u.x, u.y).slice( 1 )) { if (tx.canPlaceUnit(u.unitId, p.x, p.y)) tx.placeUnit(u.unitId, u.owner, p.x, p.y); } } }); api.ui.status( `${result.units} units placed` ); } Try it Triggers generated from a table # Attack waves written as data and turned into triggers through the text format. The triggers name a location, so the snippet adds it first if the map does not have one. const waves = [ { after: 60 , unit: "Zerg Zergling" , count: 8 }, { after: 180 , unit: "Zerg Hydralisk" , count: 6 }, { after: 300 , unit: "Zerg Ultralisk" , count: 2 }, ]; if (api.triggers.names().locationByName( "Spawn" ) === undefined ) { const t = api.consts.tile; api.document.edit( "Add the Spawn location" , (tx) => { tx.addLocation({ left: 2 * t, top: 2 * t, right: 6 * t, bottom: 6 * t }, "Spawn" ); }); } const source = waves.map((wave) => ` Trigger("Player 8"){ Conditions: Elapsed Time(At least, ${wave.after}); Actions: Create Unit("Player 8", "${wave.unit}", ${wave.count}, "Spawn"); }` ).join( "\n" ); try { let added = 0 ; api.document.update( "Add the waves" , (tx) => { added = tx.triggers.fromText(source); }); api.ui.status( `${added} triggers added` ); } catch (error) { api.ui.status(String(error)); // a parse error names the line } Try it A plugin that regenerates its triggers should also claim them , so the Trigger Editor shows them as generated and the user does not edit them by hand. The write is delayed until typing pauses. const FILE = "my-plugin\\notes.txt" ; function read() { const bytes = api.document.extras.get(FILE); return bytes ? new TextDecoder().decode(bytes) : "" ; } api.ui.panel({ title: "Map notes" , width: 320 , mount(body) { const area = api.ui.el( "textarea" , { rows: 10

h: Showing that work is in progress
b: Putting things on screen Everything a plugin shows goes through api.ui , plus the menu, context-menu and hotkey groups. There is no UI framework: a dialog or panel hands you an empty element, and you fill it with plain DOM, using api.ui.widgets for controls in the editor's own style. Surface Call Use it for Status line, notices, questions status , toast , confirm , alert , prompt A line of feedback, or a simple question. Dialog dialog(spec) A form or workspace that covers the map until closed. Panel panel(spec) Something kept open while the user works: floating, docked right, or in a strip under the map. Status item, map button statusItem(spec) , mapButton(spec) Something that stays visible without a panel. Preferences page preferencesPage(spec) Your plugin's settings. Dialog slot dialogSlot(id, spec) A button or row in a built-in dialog's footer. Map tool mapTool(spec) Taking over the pointer on the map. Overlay overlay(spec) A drawing over the map the user switches on and off. Picks pickArea , pickTile , pickObject , pickFiles Asking the user to choose something. File type fileType(spec) Opening a kind of file the editor does not. Map view mapView(spec) Another way to look at a map, in the map's place. Menus and keys menu.add , contextMenu.add , hotkeys.add Reaching your plugin's commands. Where the main pieces appear: a menu item (1), a floating panel (2), a docked panel (3), a status bar cell (4) and a map button (5). The icon beside each is the plugin's own. Messages and questions # status(text) sets the status bar line, and statusText() reads it back. toast({ kind, title, detail }) shows a notice over the map that goes away by itself. It is how Save reports. confirm , alert and prompt ask simple questions in the editor's style. confirm resolves false and prompt resolves null when the user cancels. open(id, payload) opens one of the editor's own dialogs, such as "preferences" or "validateMap" . ask(id) does the same for a dialog that answers ( "newMap" , "saveAs" , "confirmClose" ) and resolves true when the user went through with it. openDialogs() lists what is open now. // File ▸ New's own dialog, then a word about what came of it. if ( await api.ui.ask( "newMap" )) api.ui.toast({ kind: "ok" , title: "New map" , detail: api.document.info()?.name }); else api.ui.status( "No new map made." ); Try it Building content # api.ui.widgets builds controls that look like the editor's own, as plain DOM elements: Widget What it is button , checkbox A button (with primary and busy ), a labelled checkbox. text , number , select Input fields and a drop-down. segmented A few buttons of which one is on, for a short choice that should stay in view. tabs A row of tabs over a panel each. A tab is filled the first time it is shown and kept after. form A two-column grid of labelled fields. group , row , column , separator A titled box, and layout. hint Small dimmed explanatory text. list A list of rows with a label and hint, picked with a click. spinner , progressBar , skeleton , busy , statusLine , steps , fold Waiting and work in progress; see Showing that work is in progress . api.ui.el(tag, props, ...children) makes any other element. The WidgetsApi reference has each widget's options. Tooltips. api.ui.tooltip(element, content) puts the editor's own tooltip on an element of yours. The content is a line of text, or a function that builds what to show where the pointer is. A function is called again as the pointer moves, so a chart can say what is under it; return null to show nothing at that spot. Leave out the element's title , or the browser's tooltip shows as well. See the example in the reference . Dialogs # A dialog is modal and covers the map. mount(body, handle) fills an empty element; the rest of the spec is optional: Option What it does size "sm" , "md" , "lg" , "xl" or "full" . tall A fixed height instead of the content's own, for a body that scrolls or fills. buttons The footer, left to right. Left out, a single Close; an empty list removes the footer. A button's run may return false to keep the dialog open. flush The body runs edge to edge, for content that draws its own frame. onPaste , onDrop Files and text pasted into the dialog or dropped on it. keepOpenOnEscape Keep the dialog open when Esc was meant for something inside it, such as a code editor's popup. slot Offer a slot of your own for other plugins to add to; see Dialog slots . The handle mount receives can close() , setTitle() and setBusy(label) . To pick something on the map from a dialog, close it, pick, and reopen it with the result, as Terrain from Image does. The dialog covers the map, so a pick cannot run while it is open. const w = api.ui.widgets; const owner = w.select( Array . from ({ length: 8 }, (_, slot) => ({ value: slot, label: api.names.player(slot) }))); const count = w. number ({ value: 4 , min: 1 , max: 12 }); api.ui.dialog({ title: "Place marines" , size: "sm" , mount: (body) => body.append( w.form([{ label: "Player" , field: owner }, { label: "How many" , field: count }]), w.hint( "They are placed in a row from the middle of the view." ), ), buttons: [ { label: "Cancel" }, { label: "Place" , primary: true , run: () => { const view = api.view.visible(); const t = api.consts.tile; const y = ((view.y0 + view.y1) / 2 ) * t; const x = ((view.x0 + view.x1) / 2 ) * t; api.document.edit( "Place marines" , (tx) => { for ( let i = 0 ; i < Number(count.value); i++) tx.placeUnit( 0 , Number(owner.value), x + i * t, y); }); }, }, ], }); Try it Panels # A panel blocks nothing: the user keeps editing while one is open. Its mount works as a dialog's does, and it closes with its × or handle.close() . Option What it does dock "float" (the default) over the map; "right" in the dock under the built-in panels, for anything kept open while working; "bottom" in a strip under the map, as wide as the map, for a timeline or a console. width Floating only, in CSS pixels; 260 by default. height Floating: a fixed height, so the body scr

The API, group by group This part covers what each group is for and the rules that matter when using it. Each section links to its page in the API reference , which has every call's signature, options and further examples; the examples here are the ones the reference does not have. The examples are written as playground snippets, with api already defined. In a plugin the same lines go inside activate(api) . Core concepts has the rules that hold for every group. api.document # Reference The open map as a whole. Reading: isOpen() , info() (name, size, tileset, whether modified or view-only), history() (the undo and redo labels), and scenario() for the whole parsed map, read-only. Writing: edit and update (see The three kinds of write ), and undo() / redo() . Files: open , create , save , saveAs , close , export (the map as a File , the way Save writes it, ready to upload) and renderImage (a PNG). Testing a built map: test(bytes, fileName, { launch }) hands bytes of your own, such as a map your plugin built, to Tools ▸ Test Map. On the desktop the game is started when launch is true (the user's preference when left out). In a browser the file goes into the test folder the user picked; with none picked it answers null and never downloads. Whole-map changes: resize and changeTileset . Both clear the undo history, as the editor's own dialogs do. Several open maps: id() , list() and activate(id) ; see Several maps . Files inside the archive: extras lists, reads and writes files stored next to the scenario ( list , get , set , remove ). Keep yours in a folder of your own ( my-plugin\notes.json ); they are written on the next Save. Reading, and a file of the plugin's own that travels with the map: const info = api.document.info(); if (info) api.log( `${info.name}: ${info.width} × ${info.height}, ${info.tileset}${info.modified ? ", unsaved changes" : ""}` ); const name = "my-plugin\\notes.json" ; const stored = api.document.extras.get(name); const notes = stored ? JSON.parse( new TextDecoder().decode(stored)) : { opened: 0 }; notes.opened++; api.document.extras.set(name, new TextEncoder().encode(JSON.stringify(notes))); api.log( `runs of this snippet on this map: ${notes.opened}` ); Try it A new map beside the open one, and a picture of it: if ( await api.document.create({ width: 96 , height: 96 , tileset: "jungle" , name: "Sketch" , startLocations: 2 , into: "new" })) { const png = await api.document.renderImage({ pixelsPerTile: 4 }); if (png) await api.ui.saveFile(png, "sketch.png" ); } Try it The open map, written as Save would write it, sent to Test Map: const file = await api.document. export (); const outcome = file && ( await api.document.test( new Uint8Array( await file.arrayBuffer()), file.name, { launch: false })); api.ui.status(outcome ? `Written to ${outcome.path}` : "No test folder chosen yet." ); Try it api.document.sections # Reference The map file as a list of sections, as the game reads it and Save writes it, with unsaved edits already included. Section Explorer is built on it, and Repair uses its helpers. Reading. list() gives each section's name, offset, size and what the editor knows about it. bytes(index) is one section's payload, combined(name) what the game uses when a name is repeated, and file() the whole file. Writing. write , rename , insert , remove , move and replaceFile . After each: The file is parsed again from scratch and becomes the open map, so the change reaches every part of the editor, even for sections it does not understand. The undo history and selections are cleared, and the "document" event fires with reason "replace" . The call returns the parser's warnings . Indices shift after an insert or remove, so call list() again. The map is marked modified. The exception is replaceFile(bytes, { asOpened: true }) , which takes the bytes as the file that was opened. Use it for a repair made right after "open" , so the map does not ask to be saved when nothing the user did changed it. Save still writes the bytes. Helpers for repairs. required() (the sections this map's revision must have), defaults(name) (what File ▸ New would write), trailing() (bytes after the last readable section), chkOf(file) (the scenario inside an .scx / .scm ) and rebuild(names?) (re-encode sections from the editor's model, fixing sizes, repeats and broken string offsets). // Sections the map must have and does not, and sections that appear more than once. const sections = api.document.sections.list(); const present = new Set(sections.map((s) => s.name)); api.log( "missing:" , api.document.sections.required().filter((name) => !present.has(name))); api.log( "repeated:" , [... new Set(sections.filter((s) => s.occurrences > 1 ).map((s) => s.name))]); Try it api.document.buildSteps # Reference For a plugin that compiles something into the map, such as a script turned into triggers. A build step runs whenever the map leaves the editor (Save, Test Map and document.export ), so the user keeps one file and keeps editing the unbuilt map. api.document.buildSteps.add({ id: "compile" , label: "My Compiler" , // Only maps that carry the plugin's source file are built. applies: () => api.document.extras.get( "my-plugin\\main.txt" ) !== null , async run({ map, fileName, purpose }) { api.log( `building ${fileName} (${map.length} bytes) for ${purpose}` ); return map; // an .scx in, an .scx out: return your compiled map here }, }); Try it applies() is asked on every save and must be cheap. While it is false, Save is unchanged. run gets the map as Save would write it and returns the built map. Steps from several plugins run one after another, in activation order. purpose is "save" , "test" or "export" . The editor keeps the unbuilt scenario inside the file and shows that one when the map is opened again, so generated triggers never appear in the trigger list. See Opening and saving maps . A step cannot cost the user a save. If run throws, the map is saved unbuilt and a notice shows your error message, so write

Trigger reference Every trigger condition and action: what it does, its arguments, its text form and where it is stored in the map. Every trigger condition and action in StarCraft and Brood War: what it does in the game, the arguments it takes, how it is written as text, and where each argument is stored in the map file. The game's behaviour described here is StarCraft 1.16.1's, found by running test maps. Much of StarCraft: Remastered's trigger code has been read as well, and the parts a map maker would notice were checked by playing test maps. What it does differently is under In StarCraft: Remastered . Each condition and action has a number, a line in the text form, and a table of where its arguments are stored. These come from the same tables the editor reads and writes maps with. The text form is SCMDraft 2's TrigEdit syntax, so an example line can be pasted into SCMDraft or into the editor's Text Trigger Editor. In scmJS, triggers are edited in: the Trigger Editor (Triggers ▸ Trigger Editor…, Ctrl+T), a form like StarEdit's; the Text Trigger Editor (Ctrl+Shift+T), the same triggers in the text form. It comes with the TrigEdit plugin, which is installed but off until you turn it on in Plugins ▸ Manage Plugins…. Triggers ▸ Import Triggers… and Export Triggers… use the same text without it; TrigScript (Triggers ▸ TrigScript…), triggers written as code. Each condition and action is a function named after it, such as setDeaths ; see the TrigScript guide ; the Mission Briefing Editor (Triggers ▸ Mission Briefing Editor…), for briefings . The Trigger Map plugin, from Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins…, draws which triggers set and read each switch, death count and location, and lists triggers that can never run. See Triggers in the user guide. How triggers run A trigger is a list of up to 16 conditions and up to 64 actions, and the players it runs for. Conditions A condition is a test a trigger makes on every pass, unless the trigger is part way through its actions. Actions An action is what a trigger does once its conditions hold. Mission briefing actions A mission briefing is the screen before a single-player mission: portraits, text and speech, one briefing per player. Players and groups The sections from here on are reference tables. Argument values These are the values the enumerated arguments take, and the number each is stored as. The trigger record Triggers are stored in the map's TRIG section, one 2400-byte record per trigger, in the order of the list. EUD An *EUD* trigger uses a player or unit value outside the game's tables to reach other parts of the game's memory. In the source

h: Condition and action numbers the game does not have
b: How triggers run A trigger is a list of up to 16 conditions and up to 64 actions, and the players it runs for. When every condition holds, the game carries out the actions in order. A trigger that should run straight away has Always as its condition; a trigger with no conditions at all runs straight away too. The trigger cycle # The game does not check triggers continuously. It goes through them in passes , one every 31 game frames: 1.3 seconds at Fastest, 2.1 seconds at Normal. The first pass is on the game's second frame, so an Always trigger runs at once. A pass comes after that frame's units have moved, fought and died, so a unit killed in a frame already counts in that frame's pass. In a pass the game takes the players in the game in order, Player 1 to Player 8, and for each goes through that player's triggers top to bottom, in the order of the list. It asks a trigger's conditions in order and stops at the first false one, so the conditions after it are not even asked. If they all hold, it carries out the actions in order. What one trigger does is seen by every trigger after it in the same pass, with one exception for counts of units (see Counting units ). Two things bring the next pass forward to the very next frame, for every player: a Wait running out, and the countdown timer reaching 0. Game speed does not change the 31-frame cycle or game time: a game second is 16 frames at every speed, for Elapsed Time and the countdown alike. It changes only how long a Wait lasts ( Waits ). Hyper triggers # A Wait of 0 runs out on the frame after it starts, and the pass it brings forward comes the frame after that. So the fastest the game goes through the triggers is once every 2 frames . It never manages every frame. Hyper triggers use this: two or three preserved triggers of 62 or 63 Wait(0) actions each, owned by one player. Each pass starts another of their Waits, so the passes keep coming every 2 frames. A slow pass, 31 frames after the last, comes only when none of them has a Wait to start, and with that many Waits it comes so rarely that it does not matter in practice. The cycle is shared, so one player's hyper triggers speed up every player's triggers. A computer player can carry them. The waits must be one frame long or less: 42 milliseconds at Fastest. Who a trigger runs for # A trigger is owned by one or more of the players and groups : a player, a force, or All Players. A trigger owned by a group runs separately for each player in it, as if each had a copy of their own. Its conditions are checked and its actions carried out once per player, and inside it Current Player means whichever player that copy is running for. The copies are handed out when the game loads the map, and only to players in the game: human and computer players, and rescuable and neutral slots, which run their triggers like anyone else. Only these owners get copies: Players 1 to 8; Force 1 to Force 4; All Players. A trigger owned only by anything else (Players 9 to 12, Current Player, Foes, Allies, Neutral Players, Non-Allied Victory Players, None or the Unused groups) is dropped when the game loads and never runs. Other editors let you tick those owners, but the game ignores them. scmJS's Trigger Editor offers only the owners above; when a map's trigger already has another ticked, it is shown with a note so you can clear it. Only Use Map Settings games read a map's triggers at all. Melee and the other game types run triggers built into the game. (See TRIG in the CHK reference.) Each owner gets its own copies, so a player reached twice, as with both "Player 1" and "Force 1" ticked, has two copies of the trigger and runs it twice in every pass. A player who is defeated, or leaves, stops running triggers. In a single-player game a player who has won keeps running them until the victory screen stops the game. Once, or every time # A trigger runs once for each player it runs for and is then finished, unless it carries Preserve Trigger . Then, once its actions are done, the game asks its conditions again on the next pass. A preserved trigger whose conditions stay true keeps firing: one that adds a mineral adds one each pass. Preserve Trigger works wherever it stands in the list, even after a Wait: the game looks for it when the actions end. While a trigger is part way through its actions, held at a Wait, the game does not ask its conditions again. On each pass it carries on from the action it stopped at. Waits # Each player has one wait slot . A Wait takes it and holds the rest of its trigger until its time has passed. While the slot is taken, another trigger of that player that reaches a Wait stops there without starting its time, and tries again on each pass until it finds the slot free. The player's triggers with no Wait in their way keep running every pass, and every player's slot is their own. A Transmission for a person, and Center View in a single-player game, take the same slot. A Wait's time is in milliseconds of the game's speed, close to real time, not game time. Each frame takes a fixed number of milliseconds at each speed, the Wait lasts its time in frames, rounded up and at least one, and the trigger goes on in the pass on the frame after: Speed Milliseconds a frame Wait(0) goes on after Wait(1000) goes on after Fastest 42 2 frames 25 frames Faster 48 2 frames 22 frames Fast 56 2 frames 19 frames Normal 67 2 frames 16 frames Slow 83 2 frames 14 frames Slower 111 2 frames 11 frames Slowest 167 2 frames 7 frames A Wait of 4,294,967,295 never runs out, and takes that player's wait slot for the rest of the game. On a map with hyper triggers, a Wait in another trigger below them in the list hardly ever gets the slot: it can start only in the one slow pass. A Wait above them takes the slot first, and while it runs no hyper Wait can start, so the passes fall back to every 31 frames until it runs out. Check Map points this out. Timers with a death counter # A death count of a unit type the map never uses makes

Conditions A condition is a test a trigger makes on every pass, unless the trigger is part way through its actions. These are all of them: Condition True when Accumulate a player has a given amount of ore or gas Always always Bring a player has a given number of units in a location Command a player has a given number of units anywhere Command the Least the player has the fewest of a unit type Command the Least At the player has the fewest of a unit type in a location Command the Most the player has the most of a unit type Command the Most At the player has the most of a unit type in a location Countdown Timer the countdown timer shows a given time Deaths a player's death count for a unit type is a given number Elapsed Time a given time has passed since the game started Highest Score the player has the highest score of a kind Kill a player has killed a given number of a unit type Least Kills the player has killed the fewest of a unit type Least Resources the player has the least ore or gas Lowest Score the player has the lowest score of a kind Mission Briefing used by briefings only Most Kills the player has killed the most of a unit type Most Resources the player has the most ore or gas Never never Opponents a player has a given number of opponents left Score a player's score of a kind is a given number Switch a switch is set, or clear Conditions that compare a number take a comparison : At least, At most or Exactly. All of a trigger's conditions must hold for it to run. Accumulate # True when the player has at least, at most or exactly the amount of ore, gas, or ore and gas. Condition 4 · Accumulate(Player, Comparison, Amount, Resource); Argument Takes Stored in the condition Player a player or group bytes 4–7 Comparison At least, At most or Exactly byte 14 Amount a whole number, 0 to 4,294,967,295 bytes 8–11 Resource ore, gas, or ore and gas byte 16 Accumulate ( "Current Player" , At least, 500 , ore); Always # Always true. A trigger that should run as soon as the game starts, or on every cycle with Preserve Trigger , has this as its condition. A trigger with no conditions at all behaves the same. Condition 22 · Always(); It takes no arguments. Always (); Bring # True when the player has at least, at most or exactly the number of units of the type inside the location. A location's elevation settings (which of low, middle and high ground and air it covers) decide which units it counts. A unit counts when its box touches the location. With At least or Exactly, Bring counts finished units and the units aboard a transport in the location; with At most, it counts every unit there, finished or not, but nothing aboard. See Counting units . A location stored inverted, its right edge left of its left edge or its bottom above its top, holds nothing for Bring: the condition finds no units in it, so At least 1 is never true. (Run in 1.16.1 and found playing Remastered.) Create Unit uses only a location's middle, which is the same point for an inverted location. The counts are taken once in each pass, so a unit created later in the pass is not seen until the next one. See Counting units . The example is the standard melee defeat rule, which every melee game runs: a player who commands no buildings loses. Mission briefing actions A mission briefing is the screen before a single-player mission: portraits, text and speech, one briefing per player. It is stored in the map's MBRF section, in the same record as a trigger, with the condition Mission Briefing and its own set of actions, numbered separately from a trigger's. Four portrait slots, 0 to 3, hold the portraits. The editor's Triggers ▸ Mission Briefing Editor… edits them. The game keeps the briefing triggers owned by the person playing, by All Players, or by the person's force, and plays a briefing trigger only when its first condition is Mission Briefing. A briefing written as text without that condition never plays; Check Map points it out. (Read in 1.16.1's code; not checked in a game.) Wait (briefing) # Holds the briefing for the time. Players and groups The sections from here on are reference tables. These are the values a trigger stores for a player. The same 27 values number the owners a trigger can have (one byte each in the record) and are what the Player arguments of conditions and actions store. Players 9 to 12 are not; Player 12 is the neutral player, which owns the resources and critters a map places as Neutral. Current Player is the player the trigger is running for (see Who a trigger runs for ). Foes and Allies are counted from that player's point of view: Allies are the players allied for victory with it, and players who are plain allies count as Neutral Players . A rescuable or neutral slot is in the game like anyone else, so it is counted in All Players, in its force and in every Most and Least comparison. The four Unused groups have no players behind them. All Players as a condition's or action's player means more than the players in the game. In a condition it also takes in Players 9 to 12, always, so Command(All Players, …) counts Player 12's units too. In actions that act on units, such as Kill Unit, Give Units to Player or Modify Unit Hit Points, it reaches Players 9 to 12's units as well. Create Unit, Set Deaths, Set Resources and Set Score do nothing for Players 9 to 12, whether they are named or reached through All Players, except Set Deaths in Remastered's EUD mode . As a trigger's owner, All Players is only the players in the game. None is no player. As a condition's player it reads somewhere unexpected, and a player value past this table reads outside the game's tables; see EUD .

The trigger record Triggers are stored in the map's TRIG section, one 2400-byte record per trigger, in the order of the list. Mission briefings are in MBRF , in the same record with a different set of actions. A trigger # Bytes Holds 0–319 16 conditions, 20 bytes each 320–2367 64 actions, 32 bytes each 2368–2371 the trigger's flags 2372–2398 27 bytes, one per player or group : non-zero where the trigger runs for it 2399 used by the game while the trigger runs; 0 in a saved map The trigger's flags: Bit Meaning 0x04 Preserved: the same as a Preserve Trigger action 0x08 Disabled, or finished: the trigger never runs. Editors set it to disable a trigger, and the game sets it on a trigger that has run and is not preserved 0x02 Each time the trigger's actions run, the player counts as having won without winning: every other player still in the game with no result is defeated, and the player's game goes on. A Defeat or Draw in the same trigger never takes effect. Some editors call it "ignore Defeat and Draw", which is not what it does 0x01 The trigger is part way through its actions; byte 2399 says which is next 0x10 Esc is skipping the trigger's Waits, transmissions and text 0x20 The trigger paused the game, and unpauses it when it finishes 0x40 Esc may not skip the trigger ( Disable Debug Mode ) The game sets 0x01, 0x10, 0x20 and 0x40 itself while the trigger runs, and StarEdit saves them as 0. A file that sets them is still obeyed: with 0x01 set, the first pass skips the conditions and starts at the action byte 2399 names. The list of conditions ends at the first slot whose type is 0, and so does the list of actions. A condition # Bytes Holds 0–3 Location number, counted from 1; 0 for none. 4–7 Player or group. 8–11 Amount compared against. 12–13 Unit type. 14 Comparison, or the switch state for Switch. 15 Which condition this is. 16 Resource type, score type or switch number, depending on the condition. 17 Flags: 0x02 disabled; the others are editor and game bookkeeping. 18–19 Unused by ordinary triggers; some EUD tools store a mask here. All numbers are little-endian. An unused condition slot is all zeros. An action # Bytes Holds 0–3 Location number, counted from 1; 0 for none. The source location where there are two. 4–7 String-table entry of the text. 8–11 String-table entry of the sound file's name. 12–15 A time: milliseconds, or seconds for Set Countdown Timer. 16–19 Player or group; the first player where there are two. 20–23 Second player, destination location, amount, properties slot or AI script, depending on the action. 24–25 Unit type, or the score, resource or alliance type. 26 Which action this is. 27 Unit count, modifier, switch action, order or state, depending on the action. 28 Flags: 0x02 disabled, 0x04 always display; the others are editor and game bookkeeping. 29 Unused. 30–31 Unused by ordinary triggers; some EUD tools store a mask here. All numbers are little-endian. An unused action slot is all zeros.

EUD An EUD trigger uses a player or unit value outside the game's tables to reach other parts of the game's memory. The editor's player pick has an EPD box that turns a memory address into the player value that reaches it. A condition with a player value past the players and groups table reads memory outside its table. Deaths reads the 4 bytes at 0x58A364 + 4 × player + 48 × unit, for any player and unit number. In 1.16.1 this works for reading only. Set Deaths , Set Resources and Set Score write nothing for a player above Player 8, and Set Deaths writes nothing for a unit number above 232, so 1.16.1 has no EUD writes. StarCraft: Remastered has an EUD mode of its own. When it loads a map it looks through the triggers, disabled ones included, for a Deaths condition or a Set Deaths action whose player value is above 26 or is 12 (None), or whose unit number is above 232. One is enough to turn the mode on for the whole map, and a Deaths condition with None as its player counts. (Read in Remastered's code.) In EUD mode, EUD conditions and Set Deaths use the addresses they would in 1.16.1, for the parts of the game's memory Remastered allows, and Set Deaths also writes Players 9 to 12's death counts. This is what EUD maps for Remastered, and the editor's TrigScript and Magenta plugins, are built on. In a map with no EUD trigger, Set Deaths writes nothing for Players 9 to 12, as in 1.16.1. (Found playing Remastered.) None as a condition's player does not check anything: it reads the cell after Player 12's, which is Player 1's count of the next unit type. Deaths(None, unit 7) is Player 1's deaths of unit 8, and Accumulate(None, ore) is Player 1's gas.
