Opening and saving maps What the editor does with a map file: what it preserves, what Save can strip, revisions, protected and built maps. What scmJS does with a StarCraft map file when it opens and saves one. This is for map makers deciding what to keep in a release copy, for people fixing a broken or protected map, and for anyone writing a tool that reads what the editor writes. The user guide covers the Save dialog itself; the format, section by section, is in the CHK format reference . The short version: the editor opens .scm , .scx and bare .chk files, rewrites only the parts of the scenario you changed, and copies everything else through byte for byte, including things it does not understand. A map loses nothing by passing through the editor unless you ask for it in the Save dialog. The exceptions are two sections the game would refuse as they stand, which a save puts right ( below ). The archive A .scm or .scx file is an MPQ archive, the container format Blizzard used for its games' data. The scenario The scenario is a flat sequence of sections, each a four-character name, a length and that many bytes of data: MTXM holds the terrain, UNIT the placed units, TRIG the triggers. Saving The Save dialog's What to keep choice decides what goes into the file. Revisions The revision is the VER value. New maps File ▸ New writes a Brood War map with the sections StarEdit writes for one: the x layouts of the settings tables only, and no IVER, SWNM or CRGB, which StarEdit adds when there is someth… Replays A replay (.rep) is not a map, but it carries the map it was played on. Protected and damaged maps A protected map is one written to be played but not edited: sections repeated, resized or given nonsense names, the archive's file list removed, the scenario member renamed or duplicated,… Looking at the bytes The Section Explorer plugin, installed from Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins…, is a hex editor over the scenario: every section with what the editor knows about it, its bytes coloured by field, e… In the source For developers.

The archive A .scm or .scx file is an MPQ archive, the container format Blizzard used for its games' data. The scenario is one member of that archive, always named staredit\scenario.chk . Everything else in the archive is extra: custom sounds, custom graphics, files another editor or a plugin put there. The editor keeps those members and writes them back on save, so a map with its own sound files keeps them. A bare .chk file, the scenario with no archive around it, opens too; some tools pass scenarios around that way. An archive whose file list was removed, as protectors often do, still opens. The editor asks for the members the scenario refers to (its sounds, its script files) by name, so they are still listed and editable. Any member it cannot name is carried across a save exactly as stored, and the Save dialog says how many there are. A bare .chk cannot hold them. The Save dialog's Archive fold decides how the scenario is stored: Option What it means PKWARE The compression StarEdit uses and every Blizzard map is stored with. Every version of the game reads it. zlib Smaller. Read by Remastered only: 1.16.1 and older builds cannot open the map. None The largest, readable by anything. Encrypt StarEdit's light encryption of the members. It hides nothing from a map editor; some tools expect it. A map is written back the way it was opened: a map that came in as PKWARE goes out as PKWARE. A new map gets StarEdit's layout, PKWARE and encrypted. A member stored with a method the editor can read but not write (bzip2, for one) is written with whichever layout the dialog shows. Built maps # A plugin can put a compiler between the map and the disk; the TrigScript plugin does, for a map with programs. The file then holds two scenarios: staredit\scenario.chk is the compiler's output, which is what the game reads. scmjs\source.chk is the map as the editor shows it. scmjs\build.json records which steps ran, which archive members they added, and the SHA-256 of the built scenario. The two scmjs\ members are always zlib-compressed, since the game never opens them. Opening such a file gives back the map from scmjs\source.chk , so the trigger list shows your triggers and not the generated ones. That only happens while the built scenario still has the recorded hash. If another editor or a protector has changed it since, the editor cannot tell which of the two you mean, so it opens the file as it stands, says so, and leaves both members where they are. A bare .chk is never built.

h: What the editor does with it
Sections a map may not have
b: The scenario The scenario is a flat sequence of sections, each a four-character name, a length and that many bytes of data: MTXM holds the terrain, UNIT the placed units, TRIG the triggers. The CHK format reference has a page for every section, and explains what the game does when a file repeats a section or gives one an odd length . Map protectors rely on those cases: a protected map is written so that the game reads it correctly and a naive editor reads it wrongly. What the editor does with it # The editor keeps every section in the order it found it, repeats included, and reads them the way the game does. Opening a protected map shows what the game would show. On save, only the sections you changed are written from the editor's own model. Edit a trigger and TRIG is re-encoded; every other section, known or not, is written back from the bytes it came in with, in its original order and with its original repeats. A section an edit creates goes in where StarEdit would put it, not at the end. Bytes after the last section are kept too, unless the Save dialog is told to drop them. So: A section this editor does not model survives. Nothing is lost by opening a map here, whatever made it. Repeated sections stay repeated. Flattening a protected map into one copy of each section is a deliberate choice: the Save dialog's Merge repeated sections into one does it by the game's own rules. Every piece of text in the map lives in one string table, STR (or STRx on a Remastered map), and other sections point into it by number. The editor reads STRx where the game does, in a VER 64 or 206 file, and there it wins over STR . A STRx in any other revision is kept in the file as it is, and the editor shows the STR text players see. The editor never renumbers the table on save, since sections it carries as bytes still point at the old numbers; a string that stops being used is blanked, not removed. STR counts its offsets in 16 bits, so its text must fit in 64 KB: Save refuses a map whose strings run past that, and Check Map says which. Shorter text, or a Remastered revision with STRx , fixes it. The table does not say which character encoding its text is in. The editor guesses as the game would read it and shows the guess in Scenario ▸ Map Revision, where you can change it. The text is written back in that encoding; a character it cannot hold becomes ? , which Check Map and the Save dialog report. The STR page says how the guess is made. Known and unknown sections # The CHK format reference lists every section the editor knows. It decodes all of them into its own model and re-encodes them when you change them, except VCOD , IVER and IVE2 , which it only carries as bytes. Any other section is carried through untouched. Tools ▸ Check Map reports a section the game requires and the file lacks as an error. Two sections are rewritten without an edit, because the game would refuse the file as it stands: A VCOD that fails the game's check for the map's players would keep the map from loading at all. Save writes StarEdit's table in its place, which passes for any players, and Check Map says so beforehand. A MRGN of the wrong length for the map's revision is written at the right one on the next save. Earlier versions of scmJS wrote 255 location slots into StarCraft 1.00 files, and a Use Map Settings game refuses to start such a file. Sections a map may not have # ISOM , MASK , WAV , CRGB , SWNM , the CUWP slots and every settings table may be missing from a map, and the editor does not add one to a file that had none: a map without MASK stays without it, rather than gaining an all-clear fog table. The one exception is a change of revision, below. The game is stricter. A melee game never reads MASK , the CUWP slots or the settings tables, but a Use Map Settings game needs them and stops at the start without them (see What a map needs ). The editor shows a map with no MASK fully fogged, which is how a melee game starts. A map with no ISOM cannot use the isometric brush until the record is rebuilt.

h: What the game reads and what it skips
b: Saving What to keep # The Save dialog's What to keep choice decides what goes into the file. None of it changes the map you have open, only the file being written. Choice What the file holds Everything Every section and archive member. The file opens in any editor with nothing lost. Smallest that plays All five ticks below, and StarEdit's PKWARE compression with encryption. The map plays the same; an editor opening it later has less to work with. Custom The ticks you choose. The five ticks under Custom : Leave out terrain editing data: ISOM , TILE and DD2 . Leave out editor bookkeeping: IVER , IVE2 , IOWN , UPUS , SWNM and WAV . Leave out sections the format reference does not know. Merge repeated sections into one, by the game's rules. Drop bytes after the last section. Each extra archive member also has its own tick in the Archive fold. What the game reads and what it skips # The nine sections in the first two ticks are read by editors and skipped by the game. The map plays the same without them. What changes is what an editor can do with the file afterwards: Without ISOM , the isometric brush has nothing to paint with. The Repair plugin can rebuild the record from the tiles, and does well on terrain that was laid isometrically to begin with. Without TILE and DD2 , doodads are no longer objects. Their tiles are still in the terrain and their sprites in THG2 , but an editor cannot pick one up or restore the ground beneath it. Without SWNM and WAV , switches lose their names and the Sound Editor its list; the triggers that use them are unaffected. IOWN , IVER , IVE2 and UPUS are StarEdit's own notes and cost nothing. Stripping these is what map protectors and "map compressors" have always done. It can be undone only as far as the Repair plugin can rebuild the record, so keep an unstripped copy of any map you are still working on. The file you replace # A save that writes over a file keeps what it replaced. The desktop app copies the old file to a .bak beside it ( Lagoon.scx to Lagoon.scx.bak ). A browser cannot write beside the file, so it keeps the last three versions of each file name in its own storage, listed in File ▸ Previous Versions…. A download replaces nothing, so Firefox and Safari have nothing to keep. While a map has unsaved changes, the editor also keeps a recovery copy of it, offered at the next start if the editor closed without saving. The user guide covers both: Saving and Recovery copies .

Revisions The revision is the VER value. It decides which sections the game reads, and so which versions of the game can play the map: Revision VER TYPE Extension Plays in StarCraft 1.00 59 RAWS .scm every version of the game Hybrid 1.04 63 RAWS .scm every version; carries both settings layouts Brood War 1.04 205 RAWB .scx Brood War and Remastered Remastered 1.21+ without Brood War 64 RAWS .scm Remastered only; STRx is read Remastered 1.21+ 206 RAWB .scx Remastered only; STRx is read What the revision changes in the file: Settings tables. Brood War widened the five settings tables and gave the wider versions new names: a 1.00 map carries the original five, a Brood War map the x five, and a hybrid both (the CHK format reference lists the pairs). The editor reads them as the game does, and writes whichever layouts the revision calls for plus any the file already carried, so a hybrid map stays a hybrid. Locations. A 1.00 file has 64 location slots and every later revision 255, the only sizes the game accepts. A 1.00 map is saved with its first 64, and Check Map names any location past them. Scenario ▸ Map Revision changes the revision. It rewrites VER and TYPE , switches the string table between STR and STRx for Remastered (and the text to UTF-8 with it), and sets the encoding the text is written in. Every string keeps its number, so triggers and locations still point at the right text. A VER 64 map, Remastered's revision without Brood War, keeps its revision: Map Revision offers it only for a map that already is one. Sections the new revision needs and the file lacks are added — COLR for Brood War, the settings tables of the new layout from the game's defaults — so the map still starts in the game. Tables the new revision no longer needs are not discarded; the Save dialog lists what will be written. A map moved to StarCraft 1.00 or Hybrid whose players do not have their slots' own colours gains a CRGB , the only place Remastered reads colours in those revisions.

New maps File ▸ New writes a Brood War map with the sections StarEdit writes for one: the x layouts of the settings tables only, and no IVER , SWNM or CRGB , which StarEdit adds when there is something to put in them. The terrain is one flat terrain type at the size and tileset chosen, laid as StarEdit lays it, with a matching isometric record. The location table has 255 slots with Anywhere in place, the fog table starts every player unexplored, and the start locations the dialog places are part of the new map, so there is nothing to undo.

Replays A replay ( .rep ) is not a map, but it carries the map it was played on. With the Aftermath plugin, File ▸ Open Replay… opens that map in a view-only tab, beside the replay viewer. A view-only map is never saved as itself, and the editor never writes a .rep . Save a Copy or Edit a Copy gives you an ordinary map to keep.

Protected and damaged maps A protected map is one written to be played but not edited: sections repeated, resized or given nonsense names, the archive's file list removed, the scenario member renamed or duplicated, or VCOD and ISOM stripped. Nothing about the format is secret, so every trick depends on an editor reading the file differently from the game. The editor reads what the game would play. If the archive is damaged so badly that the scenario cannot be read, the error says so. When the scenario is readable, the Repair plugin, on by default, checks it on every open. It looks for: a missing required section, a repeated section, or one of the wrong size; a stripped isometric record; content problems, such as strings whose colours look different in Remastered, which changed how a line break resets the colour. What happens to a finding depends on what the repair would change: A safe repair , one that only writes what the game already does with the file or puts back what the editor needs, is made as the map opens. The map does not count as changed for it. Anything else waits in the status bar. Each finding says what the game does with the file as it is and what the repair would change, and nothing changes until you say so. The original bytes stay available to restore. Preferences ▸ Plugins ▸ Repair can make the plugin ask before every repair. Tools ▸ Repair Map… runs the same check by hand. The editor does not add protection. The Save dialog can strip the editor-only sections, which is the part of protection that costs an editor something, and that is as far as it goes.

Looking at the bytes The Section Explorer plugin, installed from Plugins ▸ Browse Plugins…, is a hex editor over the scenario: every section with what the editor knows about it, its bytes coloured by field, each value shown with its meaning, and sections added, removed, renamed or reordered. An edit there rewrites the file and reads it back, so a raw change to any section reaches the whole editor, at the cost of the undo history. Plugins reach the same thing through api.document.sections in the plugin API : the file as Save would write it, every occurrence with its offset, and the same replace, rename, insert, remove and move operations.

In the source For developers. The archive and the scenario are under src/formats/mpq/ and src/formats/chk/ , and the file-level policy is in src/editor/ : File Does src/formats/mpq/scm.ts Opens and writes the archive over mopaq : finds the scenario, accepts a bare .chk , reports how the member was stored, keeps the other members. src/formats/chk/reader.ts Reads the run of sections: every occurrence in order, odd lengths, trailing bytes. src/formats/chk/sections/registry.ts One entry per known section: how copies combine, its size, and which Save groups it belongs to. src/formats/chk/scenario.ts The scenario model, reading and writing it, the revisions, and where a new section goes. src/formats/chk/sections/*.ts The codecs for each kind of section. src/formats/chk/create.ts File ▸ New, and the sections Check Map requires. src/formats/text/encoding.ts The text encodings and how one is guessed. src/editor/save.ts The save plan: what to keep, merging repeats, compression, and the dialog's warnings. src/editor/mapBuild.ts , src/services/mapBuild.ts Built maps: packing, restoring the source on open, running the steps. src/editor/sections.ts Section-level reads and writes for the Section Explorer plugin and api.document.sections . src/editor/validate.ts Check Map. development.md covers the tests and the conventions for changing any of this.

h: How the game loads a map
b: CHK format reference Every section of a scenario file: its byte layout, what a repeat does, whether the game needs it, the values its fields take. This reference gives the byte layout of every section of a StarCraft and Brood War scenario file ( scenario.chk ), with what each section is for, what the game does with it when it loads a map, and the values its fields take. This page describes the format, not any one editor. What scmJS does with a file as a whole (the archive around the scenario, protected maps, what Save keeps and what it can strip) is in Opening and saving maps . Sources. The byte layouts and the value tables are generated from the code the editor reads and writes maps with, which re-encodes Blizzard's own maps byte for byte. What the game does with a section (whether it reads it, needs it, which lengths it accepts, what a second copy does) describes StarCraft: Brood War 1.16.1, confirmed by loading test maps in the game. StarCraft: Remastered's loader has been studied too, and reads maps much the same way; the differences are listed under Where Remastered differs . Where this page and the community's older reference, wiki.staredit.net/wiki/Scenario.chk , disagree about the game, this page is the one checked against it. The same layouts are also published as a Kaitai Struct description, chk.ksy , generated from the same tables as this page. The Kaitai compiler turns it into a parser for C++, C#, Go, Java, JavaScript, Python and several other languages, and the Kaitai Web IDE opens a scenario.chk with it and shows every section field by field. It reads a file as it is laid out, one section after another, and leaves the rules for lengths and repeated sections to the program using it. The container A scenario is a flat run of sections, with no header of its own. How the game loads a map StarCraft reads a map up to three times, and each time it reads only the sections it needs then: a short read for the map list, a longer one when a game starts, and one more for the brief… Protected maps StarCraft reads a map differently from how a simple editor does, and a map can be "protected" by building it so that the game reads it correctly while an editor misreads it or gives up. Sections The sections are listed here in the order StarEdit writes them, and each has a page below in the same order. Revisions The VER value is the file's revision, and it decides which sections the game reads. How the sections fit together Most sections stand alone, but many numbers in them point into another section, and a few sections decide the size or the meaning of others. TYPE Which game the file is for. VER The file's revision, which decides which sections the game reads. IVER A version stamp older versions of StarEdit wrote. IVE2 StarEdit's version stamp. VCOD A verification table the game checks the file against when it loads a map, and refuses the map when the check fails. IOWN StarEdit's own copy of OWNR. OWNR Who controls each of the 12 player slots: a human, a computer, a rescuable player, a neutral one, or nobody. ERA The tileset. DIM The map's size in tiles. SIDE Each player's race. MTXM The terrain the game draws: one 16-bit tile number per tile, including the tiles of placed doodads. PUNI Which unit types each player may build. UPGR How far each player may research each upgrade, and the level they start at, for the 46 upgrades of the original game. PTEC Whether each player may research each ability, and whether they start with it, for the 24 abilities of the original game. UNIT The units placed on the map, 36 bytes each. ISOM The isometric record, which an editor's isometric brush paints with: the lattice of terrain diamonds from which it works out the cliffs and edges between terrain types. TILE The terrain with the doodads left out: what is under each doodad. DD2 The doodads placed on the map, as objects an editor can select and remove. THG2 Sprites placed on the map. MASK Fog of war at the start: which players begin with each tile unexplored. STR The string table. STRx The string table of StarCraft: Remastered: the same as STR with 32-bit numbers, so the table has no 64 KB limit. UPRP The 64 unit properties slots used by the Create Unit with Properties action. UPUS Which of the 64 UPRP slots StarEdit considers in use. MRGN The locations. TRIG The triggers, 2400 bytes each, in the order they run. MBRF The mission briefings, in the same 2400-byte record as a trigger, with their own set of actions. SPRP The scenario's name and description, as string numbers. FORC The four forces: which force each of Players 1 to 8 is in, each force's name, and its settings. WAV StarEdit's list of the sounds in the map: the name of each sound file in the archive, as a string number. UNIS Unit settings for the original game. UPGS Upgrade costs and research times for the 46 upgrades of the original game. TECS Ability costs, research times and energy costs for the 24 abilities of the original game. SWNM The names of the 256 switches, as string numbers. COLR The colour of each of Players 1 to 8. PUPx UPGR for Brood War: the same tables, for 61 upgrades. PTEx PTEC for Brood War: the same tables, for 44 abilities. UNIx UNIS for Brood War: the same tables, with 130 weapons. UPGx UPGS for Brood War: the same tables for 61 upgrades, with one unused byte after the first column. TECx TECS for Brood War: the same tables, for 44 abilities. CRGB StarCraft: Remastered's player colours. The isometric record explained This part explains the ISOM record: how its words describe a lattice of terrain diamonds, what the values mean, and how an editor's isometric brush turns the lattice into tiles. In the source

The container A scenario is a flat run of sections, with no header of its own. Each section is a four-character name, a 32-bit length, and that many bytes of data: Offset Type Holds 0 4 characters The name, padded with spaces to four: VER , DIM , STR 4 i32 The length of the data, in bytes 8 the length The data The next section starts straight after the data. The order of the sections in the file does not matter: the game first lists every section, and then handles them in an order of its own. StarEdit's order, the order of this reference, is only a convention. All numbers in every section are little-endian. Unsigned unless a layout says i32 . Positions are in pixels, and a tile is 32 pixels square. Player slots are numbered from 0 for Player 1 to 11 for Player 12. Text is never stored in a section itself: a section holds a string number , the position of the text in the string table , and 0 means no text. Odd lengths # The game finds the sections by reading a header, jumping over the length it gives, and reading the next header there. It does not check the names, and it does not check that a jump goes forward. A name the game does not know is passed over. It need not be text: any four bytes will do. A negative length jumps backwards. The game then reads bytes it has already read as new headers, which lets a file hide a section inside another one's data. A length of −8 lands on the same header again and again, and the game hangs. A length that runs past the end of the file ends the walk. The section is still kept, cut short, and refuses the map if the game reads that section, because every read checks that a section's bytes are really there. On a section the game never reads, such as ISOM , it does no harm. Bytes after the last section : fewer than 8 are ignored. Eight or more are read as one more header. Lengths # Every section the game reads has a length it insists on, and a section of any other length refuses the map. A fixed-size section one byte too long makes the map invalid, and a record section must hold whole records. The game wants Sections A different length Exactly this many bytes VER␠ 2, VCOD 1040, OWNR 12, ERA␠ 2, DIM␠ 4, SIDE 12, PUNI 5700, UPGR 1748, PTEC 912, UPRP 1280, MRGN 1280 ( VER 59) or 5100, SPRP 4, UNIS 4048, UPGS 598, TECS 216, COLR 8, PUPx 2318, PTEx 1672, UNIx 4168, UPGx 794, TECx 396 Refuses the map Whole records of this size UNIT 36, THG2 10, TRIG 2400, MBRF 2400 Refuses the map At most this many bytes MTXM 131072, FORC 20 Longer refuses the map; shorter is taken Any length MASK , STR␠ Taken Three sections may be shorter than the map needs. A short MTXM leaves the rest of the map's tiles as the game found them in memory. A short FORC is filled out with zeros. MASK takes any length, and the tiles it does not reach start unexplored. Each section's page gives its rule in the row The game accepts . Repeated sections # A section can appear more than once. The game hands every copy, in file order, to the part of its code that reads that section, and what happens then depends on the section. Each section's page says which in its More than one copy row; there are four main ways: The last copy replaces the others. Most sections: with two DIM sections the map has the size the second one gives. Every copy is still checked, so a decoy copy of the wrong length refuses the map rather than being passed over. Each copy is written over the start of the same space. The terrain and the fog: the copies go into one space of a fixed size in file order, so a later copy replaces only as many bytes as it carries. A second MTXM half the size of the map rewrites the top half of the terrain and leaves the bottom as the first copy had it. The copies are joined into one list. Units, sprites, triggers and briefings: the records of all the copies, in file order, so two TRIG sections are one longer trigger list. The settings tables are combined entry by entry. A copy of UNIx changes only the unit types it marks as not using the game's own values. A unit type it leaves on the defaults keeps what an earlier copy gave it. A few sections have rules of their own: VCOD : every copy is checked, and one bad copy refuses the map. STR : in 1.16.1 the last copy wins whatever its length, even 1 byte. Remastered passes over a copy shorter than 2 bytes. MRGN : every copy must be the full size. COLR : each copy rearranges the colours the copy before left. UNIT : the start locations come from the last copy alone, and an add-on or nydus canal is linked only to a unit in its own copy.

t: How the game loads a map
h: When a map will not load
b: How the game loads a map StarCraft reads a map up to three times, and each time it reads only the sections it needs then: a short read for the map list, a longer one when a game starts, and one more for the briefing. Before each read it checks VER , which must be 59, 63 or 205. Remastered also takes 64 and 206; see Revisions . Read When Sections, in the order the game handles them Fails with Map list When the map list shows the map, when a game is created, and again when it starts VER␠ , DIM␠ , ERA␠ , OWNR , SIDE , STR␠ , SPRP , FORC , VCOD Invalid Scenario Melee start When a game of any type but Use Map Settings starts VER 59 and 63: STR␠ , MTXM , THG2 , UNIT VER 205: STR␠ , MTXM , THG2 , UNIT , COLR Error loading scenario file. Use Map Settings start When a Use Map Settings game starts VER 59 and 63: STR␠ , MTXM , THG2 , MASK , UNIS , UPGS , TECS , PUNI , UPGR , PTEC , UNIx (if present), UPGx (if present), TECx (if present), PUPx (if present), PTEx (if present), UNIT , UPRP , MRGN , TRIG VER 205: STR␠ , MTXM , THG2 , MASK , UNIx , UPGx , TECx , PUNI , PUPx , PTEx , UNIT , UPRP , MRGN , TRIG , COLR Error loading scenario file. Briefing When the briefing room of a Use Map Settings game opens STR␠ , MBRF Nothing: the game carries on with no briefing A read fails at the first section it needs that is missing, or at the first copy of a section that it does not accept. What is read before the failure stays read, but the map goes no further. The map list read runs every time the list shows the map, again when a game is made with it, and again at the start. So the nine sections it needs are needed by every map, and a map that lacks one is shown in the list but cannot be chosen. Melee and Use Map Settings # The game type decides what the second read takes. Melee, and every type except Use Map Settings (Free for All, One on One, Capture the Flag, Greed, Slaughter, Sudden Death, Top vs Bottom and the team types), reads four sections: the strings, the terrain, the sprites and the units, plus the colours in a Brood War file. It never reads the map's triggers, locations, fog, unit settings, upgrades, technologies or availability. Of the placed units, a melee game keeps only the start locations and the mineral fields, geysers and critters of Player 12. Of the unit sprites in THG2 , it keeps only Player 12's. Every other unit is left out. Use Map Settings reads everything else that matters to play. What a map needs # The smallest file each kind of game will load: A map for Needs Melee and the other game types VER , DIM , ERA , OWNR , SIDE , STR , SPRP , FORC , VCOD , MTXM , THG2 and UNIT , and COLR in a Brood War file ( VER 205). Remastered also needs TRIG , and takes STRx in place of STR in a VER 64 or 206 file. Use Map Settings All of those, and MASK , PUNI , UPRP , MRGN , TRIG and five settings tables: UNIx , UPGx , TECx , PUPx and PTEx in a Brood War file ( VER 205 or 206); UNIS , UPGS , TECS , UPGR and PTEC in a VER 59, 63 or 64 file THG2 can be empty when the map has no sprites. Everything else is optional or for editors. MBRF , the briefing, is not needed: without it there is no briefing and nothing else changes. TYPE is looked for but never read. When a map will not load # What a player sees, and what causes it: The player sees When Why Invalid Scenario , with "This scenario is unreadable because it is invalid or corrupted." In the map list The map list read failed, and the file's VER is 59 or lower, or could not be read at all. Any fault gives this message in a StarCraft 1.00 file. Invalid Scenario , with "This scenario is intended for use with a StarCraft Expansion Set." In the map list The map list read failed, and the file's VER is above 59. That covers a Brood War map in the original StarCraft, but also every other fault : a missing DIM , a SIDE of the wrong length, a failed VCOD check, a VER the game does not know such as Remastered's 64 and 206, and in Remastered a missing TRIG , a CRGB of the wrong length or a DIM above 256. The game names the expansion set whatever the real fault. Remastered gives the same message. "This map can only be played with the 'Use Map Settings' game type." Making a game The tileset is Installation and the game type is not Use Map Settings. Installation maps can only be played as Use Map Settings. "Error loading scenario file." Starting a game A section this game type needs is missing, the wrong length, or runs past the end of the file. Melee needs MTXM , THG2 , UNIT and, in a Brood War file, COLR ; Use Map Settings also needs MASK , PUNI , UPRP , MRGN , TRIG and the settings tables. The same map may still start as melee. "WARNING: Unit unplaceable! (name) (x,y)" The first moments of a game A placed unit had no room where it stands, and was removed. Remastered gives the same warning. No briefing The briefing room MBRF is missing or not a whole number of records. The file name in place of the map's name In the map list The name in SPRP is string 0, or an empty string. Where Remastered differs # What this page says about the game describes StarCraft: Brood War 1.16.1, the last version before Remastered. Remastered's own loader has been studied the same way, and twelve of the test maps played in it. It reads a map almost exactly as 1.16.1 does: the same walk through the sections, the same reads in the same order, the same lengths and the same rules for repeated sections. These are the differences. Two more revisions. Remastered also knows VER 64 and 206, the two revisions that can carry the STRx string table. A 206 file is read like a Brood War 205 file and needs Brood War. A 64 file is read like a hybrid 63 file and does not. See Revisions . The map list reads two more sections , in a file of any revision: TRIG , which every map now needs. The game looks through the triggers for EUD triggers, Deaths conditions and Set Deaths actions that reach outside the table of death counts, and marks the map as using them. A map with no TRIG , or a TRIG that is not whole tr

Protected maps StarCraft reads a map differently from how a simple editor does, and a map can be "protected" by building it so that the game reads it correctly while an editor misreads it or gives up. None of it is encryption. Each trick relies on a rule on this page that the game follows and a simple reader does not, so a reader that follows the rules reads the map as the game does. The archive around the scenario has tricks of its own, such as a missing file list or a renamed scenario; those are in Opening and saving maps . The table says what 1.16.1 does. Protectors write for Remastered, which differs on short STR copies and checks string offsets, so a trick that works there may refuse the map in 1.16.1 or lose its text. In the container # What the file does What the game does What a reader has to do Repeats a section Combines the copies by the section's rule ( Repeated sections ) Keep every copy in file order and combine them by the same rule. A reader that takes the first copy, or the last, sees a decoy wherever the rule is a different one. Gives the terrain or the fog a copy shorter than the section's size Writes it over the start of the space, leaving the rest as it was Start from a space of the full size and write every copy over it in turn. Gives a section more bytes than it needs Refuses the map, except for MTXM (up to 131,072 bytes), MASK , STR , and sections it never reads Nothing: such a map does not load. Ends a record section in part of a record Refuses the map Nothing: such a map does not load. Declares a length that runs past the end of the file Stops walking there. It refuses the map if it reads that section, and does not mind if it never does Keep what is there, and stop. Declares a negative length Moves backwards by that much and reads on from there, so bytes are read a second time as different sections. Remastered stops if the jump lands before the start of the file Follow the jump. A reader that stops there misses the sections found after it. Includes sections whose names mean nothing, or are not text at all Passes over them Pass over them rather than rejecting the file. Leaves bytes after the last section Ignores fewer than 8; reads 8 or more as another header Keep them or drop them; they are not part of the map. Puts the sections in an unusual order Reads them in its own order whatever the file's Do not depend on StarEdit's order. In the sections # Section What the file does What it means ISOM , TILE , DD2 Leaves them out, or fills them with zeros The game never reads them, so the map plays the same. An editor loses the isometric brush, the ground under each doodad, and the doodads as objects it can select. ISOM can be rebuilt from the tiles (exactly where the terrain was painted isometrically), and a new TILE copied from MTXM , which gives back the ground but keeps the doodads' tiles in it. IVER , IVE2 , IOWN , UPUS , SWNM , WAV Leaves them out Only editors read these either. The switch names and the list of sounds are gone; the sounds themselves stay in the archive, and the trigger actions that play them still name them. STRx Adds a STRx with different text to a VER 205 file No game reads it there, so players see the STR text. A reader that prefers STRx wherever it finds one shows the decoy. STR Adds a 1-byte copy after the real string table Remastered passes over a copy too short to hold its string count and reads the real table. 1.16.1 takes it, and the map loses its text. A reader that takes the last copy finds no text, and a file saved with only that copy no longer loads: Remastered says the scenario is intended for an expansion set. MTXM , MASK Splits them into several copies, some of them short or full of junk Only the combined result counts: each copy written over the one before, in file order. A copy of junk followed by a full copy of the real terrain draws the real terrain. UNIT , THG2 , TRIG , MBRF Splits the records across several copies The copies are joined into one list, in file order. A reader that keeps only one copy loses units or triggers. Start locations come from the last UNIT copy only. STR Makes strings overlap, share bytes, or start inside the offset table A string is whatever lies between its offset and the next 0 byte. Read each one from its own offset and assume nothing about where it sits. An editor that writes the table back has to lay the strings out afresh. ERA Sets bits above the low three Brood War uses the low three bits. The original StarCraft refuses a value above 4. Any section the game never reads Fills it with junk, makes it any length, or ends the file inside it No effect on the game. Reading a protected map # A reader that does these things reads a protected map as the game does: Read the headers one after another, and keep every section with its place in the file, repeats included. At a negative length, follow the jump, as the game does. Guard against a jump that returns to a header already read with the same bytes after it, which would loop for ever. At a length past the end of the file, take the bytes that are there and stop. Pass over any name you do not know. Combine the copies of each section by its rule, the More than one copy row of its page. For the terrain and the fog, start from the size the page gives. Read each string from its own offset. A map the game accepts has no partial records and no sections of the wrong length, so a reader that meets one is reading a map the game would refuse, or one the game never reads that part of. Writing the result back as one copy of each section, in StarEdit's order, gives an ordinary file that holds the same map.

Revisions The VER value is the file's revision, and it decides which sections the game reads. TYPE goes with it. Revision VER TYPE Extension StarCraft 1.00 59 RAWS .scm Hybrid 1.04 63 RAWS .scm Brood War 1.04 205 RAWB .scx Remastered 1.21+ without Brood War 64 RAWS .scm Remastered 1.21+ 206 RAWB .scx 1.16.1 knows the first three values and refuses any other: Remastered's 64 and 206 always, and 205 too when Brood War is not on. Remastered knows all five. It reads a 64 file as it reads a hybrid 63 file, and a 206 file as a Brood War 205 file, with one difference: either may carry its strings in STRx instead of STR . Like 205, a 206 file needs Brood War. Brood War added units, upgrades and technologies, so it has wider versions of the five settings tables, under new names: UNIS and UNIx , UPGS and UPGx , UPGR and PUPx , TECS and TECx , PTEC and PTEx . Only Use Map Settings reads any of them, and the revision decides which: VER 205 , a Brood War file, and Remastered's 206: the x five, and the map needs them. The original five are never read. Blizzard's own Brood War maps carry only the x tables. VER 59 and 63 , and Remastered's 64: the original five, which the map needs, and then the x five on top when the file has them. Each x table changes only what it sets, as a second copy of the table would. This happens whether or not Brood War is on. So a hybrid file (63) does not need the x tables, though StarEdit writes them, and the one thing that sets 63 apart from 59 in the game is the number of locations: 64 in a VER 59 file, 255 from 63 up ( MRGN ). A file can hold both of a pair whatever its VER says, and the two need not agree: some editors write the x tables into an original StarCraft map and later change only the original ones, so the x tables keep what they held before. In a VER 59 or 63 file the game applies those stale x values over the new ones, and the editor reads the file the same way, so it shows the settings the game will use. When it saves a change it writes both tables, the other one in step, and keeps the columns only the x tables have (the Brood War upgrades, technologies and weapons) from the file.

How the sections fit together Most sections stand alone, but many numbers in them point into another section, and a few sections decide the size or the meaning of others. A number in Points at SPRP , FORC , MRGN , UNIS and UNIx , SWNM , WAV , and the actions of TRIG and MBRF A string in STR , or in STRx when a VER 64 or 206 file has one. String numbers count from 1, and 0 means none. A condition or action of TRIG A location of MRGN , counted from 1: location 1 is the first record, and Anywhere, the 64th record, is location 64. The Create Unit with Properties action A slot of UPRP , counted from 1. UPUS The slots of UPRP , in the same order. A UNIT record's linked unit Another UNIT record, by its serial number: an add-on and the building it belongs to, or two nydus canals. IOWN The same twelve player slots as OWNR ; editors show one and the game reads the other. MTXM and TILE Tile groups of the tileset ERA names. ISOM The values of the tileset ERA names. A DD2 record A doodad of the tileset ERA names. The doodad's tiles are in MTXM and its sprite, if it has one, in THG2 . DIM sets the size of four sections: MTXM and TILE hold two bytes per tile, MASK one, and ISOM (width ÷ 2 + 1) × (height + 1) × 8 bytes. VER decides which of the settings tables the game reads; see Revisions .

More than one copy The game never reads what it holds, so copies make no difference. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Layout: Offset Type Holds 0 4 characters RAWS for a StarCraft file, RAWB for Brood War

Read by The game, first, before every read of the map: the revision decides which sections it reads next. Required Yes. Without it the map list shows the map as Invalid Scenario , and it cannot be played. The game accepts Exactly 2 bytes. Any other length refuses the map. Name IVER (49 56 45 52) Size 2 bytes. Read by Editors only. The game never reads it. Required No. In scmJS Kept as it is and written back unchanged. Layout: Offset Type Holds 0 u16 StarEdit's version number, an older form

IVE2 StarEdit's version stamp. The game does not read it. Name IVE2 (49 56 45 32) Size 2 bytes. Read by Editors only. The game never reads it. Required No. In scmJS Kept as it is and written back unchanged. Layout: Offset Type Holds 0 u16 StarEdit's version number; 11 in a map StarEdit saves for Brood War

VCOD A verification table the game checks the file against when it loads a map, and refuses the map when the check fails. What it checks is narrow: the players' types and races, and nothing else. Every map StarEdit writes carries the same 1040 bytes, the table built into the game, and a new map made in the editor gets them too. Name VCOD (56 43 4F 44) Size 1040 bytes. Read by The game, for the map list. It reads it again when a game is created and when it starts. Required Yes. Without it the map list shows the map as Invalid Scenario , and it cannot be played. The game accepts Exactly 1040 bytes. Any other length refuses the map. More than one copy Every copy is checked, and one copy that fails refuses the map. A good copy after a bad one does not help. In scmJS Kept as it is, unless it fails the game's check for the map's players: then Save writes StarEdit's table in its place. Layout: Offset Type Holds 0 u32 × 256 Seeds 1024 u8 × 16 Operations The check # When the game reads a map for the map list, it builds 432 bytes from the player slots: twelve records of 36 bytes, one per slot. Each record is zero except byte 8, the player's type from OWNR , and byte 9, the race from SIDE , for all twelve players as the file has them. It hashes those bytes twice, once with the map's VCOD and once with the table built into the game, and refuses the map as Invalid Scenario when the two answers differ. Remastered carries the same table and does the same check. Nothing else in the map goes in: not the terrain, the units, the strings or the triggers. VCOD is not a checksum of the map, and a change to anything but OWNR and SIDE never upsets it. The hash, for a table of 256 seeds followed by its 16 operation bytes: hash = 0 for each 4 bytes of the 432, read as a little-endian 32-bit number w: b0, b1, b2, b3 = the four bytes of w, low byte first for each operation byte, in order: 0: hash = hash XOR w 1: hash = hash + w (all arithmetic wraps at 32 bits) 2: hash = hash - w 3, 4, 5: hash = hash XOR seed[b0] XOR seed[b1] XOR seed[b2] XOR seed[b3] 6: rotate hash left by b0 mod 32, then by b1, b2 and b3 the same way 7: rotate hash right the same way 8 to 255: nothing The map passes when the two hashes are equal. So the table the game carries passes whatever OWNR and SIDE hold, and a different table passes when it happens to give the same answer for this map's players: a change to a seed that none of the 432 bytes picks makes no difference, and operations 3, 4 and 5 can stand in for each other. The table StarEdit writes, which is the one built into the game, for a program that wants to check whether a map carries it: Fact Value Length 1040 bytes SHA-256 c13ca25290b5d075eae9705d68a7b8c30af498c36c10e138627f8b49b795392f The 16 operation bytes 01 04 05 06 02 01 05 02 00 03 07 07 05 04 06 03 An editor making a new map should copy this table: it is the only one that passes for every combination of players.

IOWN StarEdit's own copy of OWNR . The game reads OWNR ; StarEdit shows this one. The editor writes both the same, and Check Map warns when a file's two disagree. Name IOWN (49 4F 57 4E) Size 12 bytes. Read by Editors only. The game never reads it. Required No. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Layout: Offset Type Holds 0 u8 × 12 StarEdit's copy of each player's type , one byte per player slot, Player 1 first

OWNR Who controls each of the 12 player slots: a human, a computer, a rescuable player, a neutral one, or nobody. Players 9 to 12 are normally Neutral or Inactive. The game does not check the values. It reads all twelve for the VCOD check, and then clears the type, race and force of Players 9 to 12 in the lobby, so for those four OWNR matters only to that check. When a game starts, the units the map places for Players 1 to 8 are made only for a slot that is in the game: a human or computer who joined, or a rescuable or neutral player. An open slot nobody took, or an Inactive one, loses its units (see UNIT ). Name OWNR (4F 57 4E 52) Size 12 bytes. Read by The game, for the map list. It reads it again when a game is created and when it starts. Required Yes. Without it the map list shows the map as Invalid Scenario , and it cannot be played. The game accepts Exactly 12 bytes. Any other length refuses the map. More than one copy The last copy replaces the others. Every copy must still be the right size, or the map is refused. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Layout: Offset Type Holds 0 u8 × 12 Each player's type, one byte per player slot, Player 1 first Value Type 0 Inactive — the slot does not exist 1 Computer (game) — set by the game once it starts; rarely stored 2 Occupied — set by the game for a joined human; rarely stored 3 Rescuable — units join whoever reaches them 4 Computer (unused) 5 Computer — AI-controlled 6 Human — open slot in the lobby 7 Neutral — owned by no one; players 9–12 are usually this 8 Closed — lobby slot closed 9 Observer

An Installation map can only be played as Use Map Settings: the game will not make a game of any other type with it, and says so. Name ERA␠ (45 52 41 20) Size 2 bytes. Read by The game, for the map list. It reads it again when a game is created and when it starts. Required Yes. Without it the map list shows the map as Invalid Scenario , and it cannot be played. The game accepts Exactly 2 bytes. Any other length refuses the map. More than one copy The last copy replaces the others. Every copy must still be the right size, or the map is refused. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Layout: Offset Type Holds 0 u16 The tileset. The game uses the low three bits Value Tileset 0 Badlands 1 Space Platform 2 Installation 3 Ashworld 4 Jungle World 5 Desert 6 Ice 7 Twilight

Remastered also shows a map wider or taller than 256 tiles as Invalid Scenario . Name DIM␠ (44 49 4D 20) Size 4 bytes. Read by The game, for the map list. It reads it again when a game is created and when it starts. Required Yes. Without it the map list shows the map as Invalid Scenario , and it cannot be played. The game accepts Exactly 4 bytes. SIDE Each player's race. In a Use Map Settings game, a player whose race is User Selectable gets the melee starting units of the race they pick, and the units the map places for them are left out, all but the neutral kinds: mineral fields, geysers, critters, power-ups, doors and traps, Map Revealers, Dark Swarm and Disruption Web. A map that places units for a player should give that player a race. 1.16.1 and Remastered both do this. The game does not check the values. In the lobby it turns User Selectable into Random. SIDE is one of the two sections the VCOD check covers. Name SIDE (53 49 44 45) Size 12 bytes. Read by The game, for the map list. It reads it again when a game is created and when it starts. Required Yes. Without it the map list shows the map as Invalid Scenario , and it cannot be played. The game accepts Exactly 12 bytes. Any other length refuses the map. More than one copy The last copy replaces the others. Every copy must still be the right size, or the map is refused. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Layout: Offset Type Holds 0 u8 × 12 Each player's race, one byte per player slot, Player 1 first Value Race 0 Zerg 1 Terran 2 Protoss 3 Independent 4 Neutral 5 User Selectable 6 Random 7 Inactive

h: What a tile number points at
b: MTXM The terrain the game draws: one 16-bit tile number per tile, including the tiles of placed doodads. A tile number is a tile group of the tileset times 16 plus the tile's place in the group, 0 to 15. The top bit, 0x8000, is not part of the number. Name MTXM (4D 54 58 4D) Size 2 bytes per tile: width × height × 2. Read by The game, at the start of every game, whatever its type. Required Yes. Without it the map is listed, but every game on it stops at the start with Error loading scenario file. The game accepts Up to 131072 bytes, the most a 256 × 256 map needs. A longer section refuses the map; a shorter one is taken. More than one copy Each copy is written over the start of the same space, in file order, so a later copy replaces only as many tiles as it carries. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Tile (x, y), counting from 0 at the top left, is at byte (y × width + x) × 2. Whatever the tiles say, the game makes the whole bottom row of the map, and a block five tiles wide and two high in each bottom corner, ground that nothing can walk on or be built on: that is where the console covers the screen. A ground unit placed there is removed when the game starts. Checked against 1.16.1; Remastered's code does the same. The game copies the section into a space the size of a 256 × 256 map, which it does not clear first, and uses the first width × height tiles of it. A section shorter than the map leaves the rest of the tiles as they were in memory, which is nothing to rely on. Melee and Use Map Settings both read it. What a tile number points at # A tile number is a tile group and a variation : the group is the number divided by 16, and the variation the remainder. Tile 0x0132 is group 19, variation 2. The top bit takes no part in this: the game reads the group from the next eleven bits, so tile 0x8084 draws as tile 0x0084. The game files the bit as a creep flag, but in play it does nothing you can see: Remastered shows no creep there, and a Zerg building that needs creep cannot be placed on it. A group past the end of the tileset's table is drawn as plain ground (tile 0x0020) by Remastered, while StarCraft 1.16.1 reads past the end of the table. The groups are the records of the tileset's CV5 file, 52 bytes each: Offset Type Holds 0 u16 The terrain type the group belongs to; 1 for a doodad's group 2 u16 Flags: buildability and walkability in the low byte, ground height in the high byte. The game drops the walkability, height and view bits and keeps the others, buildability and creep among them 4 u16 × 4 Links for the left, top, right and bottom sides, which the isometric brush matches ( ISOM ) 12 u16 × 4 Stack links for the same sides, which say how pieces of a cliff face continue above and below 20 u16 × 16 The megatile of each of the 16 variations A megatile is a 32 × 32 picture made of sixteen 8 × 8 minitiles, and leads to its pixels as Game data describes. Walkability and height are kept per minitile, in the VF4 file, and that is where the game takes them from: it ignores the walkability and height bits of the group's flags and works out a tile's height from its sixteen minitiles. On a cliff or edge piece the two often disagree, so an editor that shows height from the CV5 flags will be wrong for some of those tiles. A doodad's group keeps other things where terrain groups keep their links: the sprite or unit drawn over it at offset 4, its name in stat_txt.tbl at 8, its number in the tileset's doodad list (the number a DD2 record stores) at 12, and its width and height in tiles at 14 and 16. A doodad spans one group per row of tiles: row r of a doodad whose first group is g is group g + r, and column c is variation c.

PUNI Which unit types each player may build. For every player and unit type there is an answer of its own and a flag saying whether to use the default answer instead, and one default answer per unit type. Only Use Map Settings reads it; melee lets everyone build everything. Name PUNI (50 55 4E 49) Size 5700 bytes. Read by The game, at the start of a Use Map Settings game. Melee and the other game types never read it. Required For Use Map Settings. Without it a Use Map Settings game stops at the start with Error loading scenario file. Melee and the other game types play without it. The game accepts Exactly 5700 bytes. Any other length refuses the map. More than one copy The last copy replaces the others. Every copy must still be the right size, or the map is refused. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Layout: Offset Type Holds 0 u8 × 2736 Per player, per unit type: 1 if the player can build it. Player 1's 228 bytes first 2736 u8 × 228 Per unit type: 1 if it can be built, for every player that uses the default 2964 u8 × 2736 Per player, per unit type: 0 to use this player's own byte above; anything else for the default Example # The answer for a player and a unit type is the player's own byte, unless the player's uses the default byte is anything but 0, in which case it is the unit type's default. The byte for Player p and unit type u is at p × 228 + u in each of the two per-player tables. The same three tables, in the same order, make up UPGR , PTEC , PUPx and PTEx . Here Carriers (unit type 72) are allowed by default, every player takes the default except Player 3, and Player 3's own byte says no: 72 00 Player 1, Carrier: may not build it, but see below 528 00 Player 3, Carrier: may not build it 2808 01 the default for Carriers: may build them 3036 01 Player 1 uses the default, so may build them 3492 00 Player 3 does not, so may not Player 1's own byte also says no, but it is never read, because Player 1 takes the default.

UPGR How far each player may research each upgrade, and the level they start at, for the 46 upgrades of the original game. Laid out as PUNI is: each player's own values, the defaults, and whether each player uses the defaults. A Brood War file has PUPx in its place; in an older file the game reads this table and then PUPx on top, if the file has one. Only Use Map Settings reads either. Name UPGR (55 50 47 52) Size 1748 bytes. Read by The game, at the start of a Use Map Settings game, in a VER 59 or 63 file, or Remastered's 64. A Brood War file's copy is never read. Required For Use Map Settings in a StarCraft 1.00 or hybrid file ( VER 59 or 63), and in Remastered's VER 64. The game accepts Exactly 1748 bytes. Any other length refuses the map. More than one copy The last copy replaces the others. Every copy must still be the right size, or the map is refused. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Layout: Offset Type Holds 0 u8 × 552 Per player, per upgrade: the highest level they may research. Player 1's 46 bytes first 552 u8 × 552 Per player, per upgrade: the level they start at 1104 u8 × 46 Per upgrade: the default highest level 1150 u8 × 46 Per upgrade: the default starting level 1196 u8 × 552 Per player, per upgrade: 0 to use this player's own values above; anything else for the defaults

A Brood War file has PTEx in its place; in an older file the game reads this table and then PTEx on top, if the file has one. Only Use Map Settings reads either. Name PTEC (50 54 45 43) Size 912 bytes. Read by The game, at the start of a Use Map Settings game, in a VER 59 or 63 file, or Remastered's 64. A Brood War file's copy is never read. Required For Use Map Settings in a StarCraft 1.00 or hybrid file ( VER 59 or 63), and in Remastered's VER 64. The game accepts Exactly 912 bytes. Any other length refuses the map.
