Player 1's 24 bytes first 288 u8 × 288 Per player, per ability: 1 if they start with it 576 u8 × 24 Per ability: the default for may research 600 u8 × 24 Per ability: the default for start with 624 u8 × 288 Per player, per ability: 0 to use this player's own values above; anything else for the defaults

UNIT The units placed on the map, 36 bytes each. Start locations are units too, of type 214. A unit record can set the unit's hit points, shields, energy, resources and hangar as percentages or amounts, and states such as cloaked or burrowed. Each of these is used only when its bit is set in the record's fields-set or special-states word, so a record can set the hit points alone. When a game starts, each record goes through these checks, in this order, before a unit is made: A start location (type 214) makes no unit. Its place becomes the owner's start location. An owner among Players 1 to 8 whose slot is empty in this game : the unit is dropped. Neutral units stay. 1.16.1 and Remastered both do this. Melee, or any game type but Use Map Settings : the unit is kept only if it is a Player 12 mineral field, geyser or critter. Use Map Settings, and the owner's race is User Selectable (see SIDE ): the unit is kept only if it is a neutral kind: a mineral field, geyser, critter, power-up, door or trap, or a Map Revealer, Dark Swarm or Disruption Web. A Brood War unit in a game of the original StarCraft is not made. No room to place it : a ground unit standing on another is moved aside to the nearest free spot, but one whose footprint touches ground it cannot walk on, such as water or a cliff, is removed, with WARNING: Unit unplaceable! on screen. Buildings are made where the record puts them, on any ground and over other units. Checked against 1.16.1; Remastered removed a Marine placed on water the same way. Then the unit is made, and the record's fields are applied, each only when its bit is set. Some of what the game does with the fields is not what the layout suggests: The link flags at offset 10 are never read. An add-on is attached to its building, and a nydus canal paired with its exit, only when each of the two records names the other's serial number, as StarEdit writes them, and only with a unit in the same UNIT section. A link written on one side alone leaves the add-on detached and the canal without an exit. An add-on also attaches only to the building it is made for: a Comsat Station to a Command Center, a Machine Shop to a Factory. The owner bit of the fields-set word, and bit 0x40, are never read: the owner byte always counts. Hit points, shields and energy are per cent of the unit's maximum, and capped at it. Hit points of 0% leave the unit with 1/256 of a hit point, the least the game can store. Resources are kept in 16 bits, so 70,000 minerals become 4,464. The hangar count is used only for Carriers, Reavers and their heroes, only its low byte, and no more than the unit can hold: 300 is read as 44, and a Carrier gets 4. A state is applied only when its bit is set in both the special-states-set word and the states word. A Ghost placed cloaked starts cloaked only if its owner has Personal Cloaking, and a Zerg unit placed burrowed starts burrowed only if its owner has Burrowing (a Lurker burrows without it). The screen starts at the local player's start location. Start locations come from the last UNIT section alone. A map that splits its units over two sections and puts the start locations in the first loses all of them: in a melee game the starting buildings and workers have nowhere to go, and every player is defeated at once. When a player has two start locations, the later record counts. Only Players 1 to 8 can have a start location. Remastered ignores one for Players 9 to 12; 1.16.1 writes it past the end of its table of eight, over whatever the game keeps there. Name UNIT (55 4E 49 54) Size 36 bytes per unit. Read by The game, at the start of every game, whatever its type. Required Yes. Without it the map is listed, but every game on it stops at the start with Error loading scenario file. The game accepts Whole units only. A length that is not a multiple of 36 refuses the map. More than one copy The copies are joined into one list, with two exceptions: start locations come from the last copy alone, and an add-on or nydus canal is linked only to a unit in the same copy. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Each unit: Offset Type Holds 0 u32 The unit's serial number, unique in the map; add-ons and nydus canals are linked by it 4 u16 X position in pixels 6 u16 Y position in pixels 8 u16 Unit type 10 u16 Link flags editors write; the game ignores them (below) 12 u16 Which special states the record sets (below) 14 u16 Which of the following fields the record sets (fields set, below) 16 u8 Owner, 0 for Player 1 17 u8 Hit points, per cent of the maximum 18 u8 Shields, per cent 19 u8 Energy, per cent 20 u32 Resources, for a mineral field or geyser 24 u16 Units in the hangar: interceptors or scarabs 26 u16 The special states themselves 28 u32 Unused 32 u32 Serial number of the linked unit Link flags: Bit Meaning 0x0200 StarEdit writes it on both units of every linked pair, an add-on and its building or two nydus canals. The game ignores it 0x0400 Called the add-on link in older references. The game ignores it Special states: Bit Meaning 0x01 Cloaked 0x02 Burrowed 0x04 In transit: a Terran building that can fly starts lifted off 0x08 Hallucinated 0x10 Invincible Fields set: Bit Meaning 0x01 Owner 0x02 Hit points 0x04 Shields 0x08 Energy 0x10 Resources 0x20 Hangar 0x40 State Example # A Protoss Carrier for Player 2 with half its hit points, full shields and four interceptors. The record's fields-set word names the owner, hit points, shields and hangar, so the game uses the hit points, shields and hangar and ignores energy and resources. The owner bit is set as StarEdit sets it, though the game reads the owner byte either way: 0 11 00 00 00 serial number 17 4 50 06 x 1616 px (tile 50) 6 50 03 y 848 px (tile 26) 8 48 00 unit type 72, Protoss Carrier 10 00 00 no link flags (the game ignores them) 12 00 00 sets no special states 14 27 00 sets: owner, hit points, shields, hangar 16 01 owner: Player 2 17 32 hit points 50% 18 64 shields 100% 19 00 energy 0% (not set,

ISOM The isometric record, which an editor's isometric brush paints with: the lattice of terrain diamonds from which it works out the cliffs and edges between terrain types. Only editors read it. Without it the map plays the same, but an editor cannot paint it isometrically until the record is rebuilt, which the Repair plugin can do from the tiles. How the record works, from the lattice of diamonds to the tiles a stroke writes, is explained in The isometric record explained at the end of this page. Name ISOM (49 53 4F 4D) Size (width ÷ 2 + 1) × (height + 1) × 8 bytes. Read by Editors only. The game never reads it. Required No. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Each rect: Offset Type Holds 0 u16 The word on the rect's left side 2 u16 Its top side 4 u16 Its right side 6 u16 Its bottom side

TILE The terrain with the doodads left out: what is under each doodad. Only editors read it, to put the ground back when a doodad is removed. Name TILE (54 49 4C 45) Size 2 bytes per tile: width × height × 2. Read by Editors only. The game never reads it. Required No. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds.

DD2 The doodads placed on the map, as objects an editor can select and remove. Only editors read it: the game sees a doodad as its tiles in MTXM and its sprite in THG2 . Name DD2␠ (44 44 32 20) Size 8 bytes per doodad. Read by Editors only. The game never reads it. Required No. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Each doodad: Offset Type Holds 0 u16 Doodad number in the tileset's list of doodads 2 u16 X of the middle of the doodad, in pixels 4 u16 Y of the middle of the doodad, in pixels 6 u8 Owner 7 u8 1 if disabled, else 0 Example # 0 2B 00 doodad 43 of the tileset's list 2 10 04 x 1040 px, the middle of the doodad 4 F0 02 y 752 px 6 0B owner: Player 12 7 00 enabled This record is all an editor has to say a doodad is there. What the game shows comes from elsewhere: the doodad's tiles are written into MTXM , where the game draws them, while TILE keeps the ground they cover so an editor can put it back when the doodad is removed. A doodad with a sprite, such as a tree top, also has a THG2 record, and so does one that is a unit, such as a door. The tileset's CV5 says how big the doodad is and which tiles it uses (see what a tile number points at ). Deleting the DD2 record alone leaves the doodad on the map for the game, just no longer selectable in an editor.

THG2 Sprites placed on the map. A pure sprite (flag 0x1000) is a picture drawn where it stands: a tree top, a glow, a doodad's overlay. Without that flag the record is a unit sprite, and the game creates a unit of that type when the map loads; that is how StarEdit places the Installation's doors and traps. Flag 0x8000 starts such a unit disabled. Pure sprites are drawn in every game type. A unit sprite is made only in a Use Map Settings game or when Player 12 owns it, and the game always gives the four Installation doors (unit types 205 to 208) to Player 12, whatever the record says. Unlike a placed unit, a unit sprite is made even for a player who is not in the game. The game reads no flag but 0x1000 and 0x8000: 0x4000, which editors call flipped, has no effect in play, and the sprite faces the way the game's own animation turns it. StarEdit still writes 0x4000 on the overlays of some doodads, such as the right-hand doors and traps of Installation. Checked against 1.16.1; Remastered's code reads the same two flags. Name THG2 (54 48 47 32) Size 10 bytes per sprite. Read by The game, at the start of every game, whatever its type. Required Yes. Without it the map is listed, but every game on it stops at the start with Error loading scenario file. The game accepts Whole sprites only. A length that is not a multiple of 10 refuses the map. More than one copy The copies are joined into one list: the records of all of them, in file order. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Each sprite: Offset Type Holds 0 u16 Sprite number, or the unit type for a unit sprite (see the flags) 2 u16 X in pixels 4 u16 Y in pixels 6 u8 Owner 7 u8 Unused 8 u16 Flags (below) Flags: Bit Meaning 0x1000 Pure sprite 0x4000 Flipped 0x8000 Disabled Example # Two records: a pure sprite, drawn and nothing more, and an Installation door, which the game makes into a unit of that type when the map loads. Its disabled flag makes it start closed. 0 82 00 sprite 130 2 80 02 x 640 px 4 90 01 y 400 px 6 0B owner: Player 12 7 00 unused 8 00 10 flags: pure sprite 10 CD 00 unit type 205, Left Upper Level Door 12 C0 04 x 1216 px 14 50 02 y 592 px 16 0B owner: Player 12 17 00 unused 18 00 80 flags: disabled

MASK Fog of war at the start: which players begin with each tile unexplored. A new map made in StarEdit or the editor starts every tile unexplored for every player. Only Use Map Settings reads it, and it needs it: a Use Map Settings game of a map without MASK stops with Error loading scenario file. Melee never reads it, and starts every tile unexplored. Name MASK (4D 41 53 4B) Size 1 byte per tile: width × height. Read by The game, at the start of a Use Map Settings game. Melee and the other game types never read it. Required For Use Map Settings. Without it a Use Map Settings game stops at the start with Error loading scenario file. Melee and the other game types play without it. The game accepts Any length. More than one copy Each copy is written over the start of the same space, in file order. The space starts with every tile unexplored, so tiles no copy reaches stay unexplored. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Only Players 1 to 8 have a bit. A byte of 0x05, bits 0 and 2, means Players 1 and 3 start with that tile unexplored and the other six start with it explored. The game starts every tile unexplored and writes the section over that, one byte per tile, so tiles past the end of a short MASK stay unexplored. Remastered uses at most the first 65,536 bytes, one for each tile of a 256 × 256 map. Blizzard's melee maps have 0xFF in every byte; some of the campaign and scenario maps, where the maker set the fog, do not.

STR The string table. Every piece of text in the map is here, and other sections refer to it by number: the scenario name and description, force names, location names, custom unit names, switch names, sound file names, and the text and sounds of trigger actions. The section starts with the number of strings, then one offset per string, counted from the start of the section, and then the text. Each string ends with a 0 byte. String numbers count from 1: the first offset is string 1. Several strings may share the same offset. Because the offsets are 16-bit, every string has to start within the first 64 KB of the section; only the last one may run on past it. A table too big for that needs fewer or shorter strings, or STRx in a Remastered file. scmJS puts the longest string last when that makes the table fit, and will not save a table that still does not. Every read of the map reads STR again, and a map without one is shown in the map list as Invalid Scenario , not under its file name. StarCraft 1.16.1 shows the first 31 bytes of the scenario's name and the first 255 of its description. Remastered's map list shows the whole description, and as much of the name as fits on two lines, with an ellipsis after it. Its lobby and game keep only the first 31 bytes of the name, counted after the name is turned into UTF-8 whatever the file holds: ten Korean syllables, where a CP949 file holds them in 20 bytes. A long name in Latin letters is cut shorter still, to the room the lobby has. Both games show the first 29 bytes of a force's name. (Remastered's limits found playing it.) The table does not say how its bytes spell characters. StarEdit wrote the code page of the Windows it ran on: EUC-KR (CP949) for Korean, Shift_JIS for Japanese, GBK or Big5 for Chinese, Windows-1251 for Russian, Windows-1252 for the rest. 1.16.1 reads a file in the code page of the machine it runs on. Remastered decides string by string: UTF-8 when the bytes are valid UTF-8, Korean (CP949) when they pass its Korean test, and Windows-1252 for anything else. So a Japanese, Chinese or Russian map that is not UTF-8 shows garbled text in Remastered whatever the player's Windows. The Korean test only asks that every byte above 127 be followed by a byte from 0x41 to 0xFE. Western text in Windows-1252 can pass it: a capital À to Æ, or a curly quote or dash, followed by a letter, or two accented letters in a row. Remastered then turns each part of the string between colour codes into Korean where every such pair is a Korean character, and leaves the other parts as Windows-1252. On an English copy of Remastered, a map whose text was stored in Windows-1252 showed "Ärger Don’t" as "훣ger Don뭪" and "Größe" as "Gr秤e", in the map list, the lobby and the game, while "Défense España" and "café" stayed as written: an accented small letter followed by a plain letter is not a Korean character, and one followed by a space or the end of the text fails the test. (Read in Remastered's code and found playing it.) Writing the table as UTF-8 avoids it. scmJS reads the table as UTF-8 when it is valid UTF-8. Otherwise it tries each legacy code page above, keeps those that decode the bytes without error, and scores each by how much of the non-ASCII text falls in that code page's own script. Korean and Chinese bytes are often valid in each other's code page, so a tie goes to Korean; when nothing scores, the guess is Windows-1252, which decodes anything. The guess is shown in Scenario ▸ Map Revision, where it can be corrected, and the table is written back in the encoding chosen, with ? for a character it cannot hold. Name STR␠ (53 54 52 20) Size Whatever the text needs. Read by The game, every time it reads the map: for the map list, at the start of every game, and for the briefing. Required Yes. Without it the map list shows the map as Invalid Scenario , and it cannot be played. The game accepts Any length. More than one copy The last copy replaces the others, whatever its length: a copy of 1 byte replaces the real table, and the map loses its text. Remastered passes over a copy shorter than 2 bytes, and in a VER 64 or 206 file a STRx of 4 bytes or more replaces it. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Layout: Offset Type Holds 0 u16 How many strings there are 2 u16 × that many Where each string starts, counted from the start of the section after the offsets text The strings, each ending in a 0 byte A string runs from its offset to the next 0 byte, and nothing else marks where it ends. So two strings can share their bytes, one string can be the end of another, and an offset can point anywhere in the section, the offset table included. 1.16.1 checks neither the count nor the offsets against the section's length: an offset at or past the end reads whatever lies after the table in memory, so an editor has to read it as no string. A string number past the count is an empty string. Remastered checks both, and shows <MISSING> for a string that falls outside the table: a map whose last STR copy holds no strings is listed with <MISSING> as its name and description (found playing Remastered). StarEdit writes a table of 1024 strings, and points every unused one at a single 0 byte straight after the offsets: an empty string. Blizzard's maps are laid out this way. Example # A table of three strings, the first and the third the same text. The third shares the first one's bytes, and the lone 0 after the offsets is where an unused string would point: 0 03 00 3 strings 2 09 00 string 1 starts at 9 4 0F 00 string 2 starts at 15 6 09 00 string 3 starts at 9 8 00 a lone 0: an empty string 9 48 69 6C 6C 73 00 "Hills" and its 0 15 46 6F 72 63 65 20 31 00 "Force 1" and its 0 Control codes # Bytes 0x01 to 0x1F in a string are not characters. Most set the colour of the text after them, and a few align it, hide it or cut it short. Editors write them as <XX> , the byte in hexadecimal, and the game draws the text from the byte where the code stands. In 1.16

STRx The string table of StarCraft: Remastered: the same as STR with 32-bit numbers, so the table has no 64 KB limit. Only Remastered reads it, and only in a VER 64 or 206 file. There it reads every STR copy first and every STRx copy after, so a STRx wins whatever the order in the file, and a map may have either table or both but not neither. Its text is read string by string the way STR 's is: UTF-8 when it is valid UTF-8, then Korean, then Windows-1252. Editors write it as UTF-8. Name STRx (53 54 52 78) Size Whatever the text needs. Read by StarCraft: Remastered only, every time it reads a VER 64 or 206 file. Older revisions' copies are never read, and 1.16.1 does not know it. Required In a VER 64 or 206 file, STR or STRx : without either the map list shows the map as Invalid Scenario . The game accepts Any length. A copy shorter than 4 bytes is passed over. More than one copy The last copy of 4 bytes or more replaces the others, and replaces STR whatever the file order. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Layout: Offset Type Holds 0 u32 How many strings there are 4 u32 × that many Where each string starts, counted from the start of the section after the offsets text The strings, each ending in a 0 byte

UPRP The 64 unit properties slots used by the Create Unit with Properties action. A slot is laid out as a UNIT record's properties are, and each field or state is only applied when its bit is set, so a slot can set the hit points alone. The game copies the section as it is and checks nothing until a unit is made from a slot. Then it keeps only the low 16 bits of the resources and the low byte of the hangar count, and makes a unit cloaked or burrowed only if its owner has the ability that allows it. A plain Create Unit uses a slot too, when its action holds a slot number from 1 to 64 where Create Unit with Properties keeps it. Any other number, in either action, means no slot. (Checked against 1.16.1.) Name UPRP (55 50 52 50) Size 1280 bytes: 64 slots of 20. Read by The game, at the start of a Use Map Settings game. Melee and the other game types never read it. Required For Use Map Settings. Without it a Use Map Settings game stops at the start with Error loading scenario file. Melee and the other game types play without it. The game accepts Exactly 1280 bytes. Any other length refuses the map. More than one copy The last copy replaces the others. Every copy must still be the right size, or the map is refused. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Each slot: Offset Type Holds 0 u16 Which special states the slot sets (below) 2 u16 Which fields the slot sets (below) 4 u8 Owner; unused 5 u8 Hit points, per cent 6 u8 Shields, per cent 7 u8 Energy, per cent 8 u32 Resources 12 u16 Units in the hangar 14 u16 The special states themselves 16 u32 Unused Special states: Bit Meaning 0x01 Cloaked 0x02 Burrowed 0x04 In transit 0x08 Hallucinated 0x10 Invincible Fields set: Bit Meaning 0x01 Owner 0x02 Hit points 0x04 Shields 0x08 Energy 0x10 Resources 0x20 Hangar

UPUS Which of the 64 UPRP slots StarEdit considers in use. The game does not read it. Name UPUS (55 50 55 53) Size 64 bytes. Read by Editors only. The game never reads it. Required No. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Layout: Offset Type Holds 0 u8 × 64 Per slot: 1 if StarEdit considers it in use

MRGN The locations. A StarCraft 1.00 file ( VER 59) has exactly 64 slots, and any later file exactly 255: a Use Map Settings game of a map whose MRGN is any other size stops with Error loading scenario file. Slot 64 is Anywhere . Editors keep it as the whole map, but the game uses the box it holds, as for any other location. StarEdit treats a slot with no name and no size as unused. Melee never reads the locations. The game takes each box as it is stored, and does not straighten one whose right edge is left of its left edge, or whose bottom is above its top. Conditions that look for units in such a location, such as Bring, never find any. Actions that work from its middle, such as Create Unit, use the point halfway between its edges, as for any other location. (Checked against 1.16.1, with boxes inverted across, and across and down; found playing Remastered for Bring.) scmJS writes exactly as many slots as the revision takes. When it opens a map whose MRGN is another length, the next save writes it at the right length, and changing the revision adds or removes slots. The elevation word works the other way round from how StarEdit shows it: a set bit leaves out that elevation, so 0 means the location covers every elevation. Conditions such as Bring only count units on the elevations the location covers. Name MRGN (4D 52 47 4E) Size 20 bytes per location. Read by The game, at the start of a Use Map Settings game. Melee and the other game types never read it. Required For Use Map Settings. Without it a Use Map Settings game stops at the start with Error loading scenario file. Melee and the other game types play without it. The game accepts Exactly 1280 bytes (64 locations) in a VER 59 file, and 5100 (255 locations) in VER 63 and 205, and Remastered's 64 and 206. Any other length refuses the map. More than one copy The last copy replaces the others. Every copy must be the full size, so a short copy refuses the map rather than overwriting part of the first. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Each location: Offset Type Holds 0 i32 Left edge, in pixels 4 i32 Top edge 8 i32 Right edge 12 i32 Bottom edge 16 u16 Name, a string number 18 u16 Elevations the location leaves out (below) Elevations: Bit Meaning 0x01 Low ground 0x02 Medium ground 0x04 High ground 0x08 Low air 0x10 Medium air 0x20 High air Example # A location covering five tiles across and four down, for ground units only. The right and bottom edges are the pixel just past the last tile, and the elevation word lists what the location leaves out: 0 40 01 00 00 left 320 px (tile 10) 4 80 01 00 00 top 384 px (tile 12) 8 E0 01 00 00 right 480 px: tiles up to 14 12 00 02 00 00 bottom 512 px: tiles up to 15 16 05 00 name: string 5 18 38 00 leaves out low air, medium air, high air

TRIG The triggers, 2400 bytes each, in the order they run. The record is laid out in the trigger reference , which also has a page for every condition and action. Only Use Map Settings reads the map's triggers. Melee and the other game types run triggers of their own, built into the game, and never read this section. Remastered's map list reads it for every map, to see whether the map uses EUD triggers, so there a map with no TRIG section is refused, even for melee. When the game loads the triggers, it hands each player in the game a copy of every trigger that runs for them, and drops the rest. Which owners that covers is in the trigger reference, under Who a trigger runs for . Name TRIG (54 52 49 47) Size 2400 bytes per trigger. Read by The game, at the start of a Use Map Settings game. Melee and the other game types never read it. Required For Use Map Settings. Without it a Use Map Settings game stops at the start with Error loading scenario file. Melee and the other game types play without it. In StarCraft: Remastered every map needs it, whatever the game type: its map list reads the triggers, and shows a map without them, or with a length that is not whole triggers, as Invalid Scenario . The game accepts Whole triggers only. A length that is not a multiple of 2400 refuses the map. More than one copy The copies are joined into one list: the records of all of them, in file order. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Each trigger: Offset Type Holds 0 u8 × 2400 One trigger; see the trigger record

MBRF The mission briefings, in the same 2400-byte record as a trigger, with their own set of actions . Only the briefing reads it, and the game does not need it: without it, or with one that is not a whole number of records, the briefing room shows nothing and the game starts as usual. Each player keeps only the briefings meant for them: their own, All Players', or their force's. Name MBRF (4D 42 52 46) Size 2400 bytes per briefing. Read by The game, for the briefing of a Use Map Settings game. Required No. Without it there is no briefing, and nothing else changes. The game accepts Whole briefings only. With any other length the map plays without a briefing. More than one copy The copies are joined into one list: the records of all of them, in file order. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Each briefing: Offset Type Holds 0 u8 × 2400 One briefing, in the same record as a trigger

SPRP The scenario's name and description, as string numbers. When the name is string 0, a number past the end of the string table, or an empty string, the map list shows the file name in its place. How much of the name and description each game shows is under STR . Name SPRP (53 50 52 50) Size 4 bytes. Read by The game, for the map list. It reads it again when a game is created and when it starts. Required Yes. Without it the map list shows the map as Invalid Scenario , and it cannot be played. The game accepts Exactly 4 bytes. Any other length refuses the map. More than one copy The last copy replaces the others. Every copy must still be the right size, or the map is refused. In scmJS Read, and written again when you change what it holds. Layout: Offset Type Holds 0 u16 The scenario's name, a string number 2 u16 Its description, a string number

FORC The four forces: which force each of Players 1 to 8 is in, each force's name, and its settings. Players 9 to 12 are in no force. A FORC shorter than 20 bytes is filled out with zeros, and a longer one refuses the map. A force whose name is string 0 is called Force 1 to Force 4, and one whose name is a number past the end of the string table has no name. StarCraft 1.16.1 shows only the first 29 bytes of a force's name, and so does Remastered (found playing it). Only a human, computer, rescuable or neutral slot is put in a force; an Inactive or closed one is in none. Name FORC (46 4F 52 43) Size 20 bytes. Read by The game, for the map list. It reads it again when a game is created and when it starts. Required Yes. Without it the map list shows the map as Invalid Scenario , and it cannot be played. The game accepts Up to 20 bytes. A shorter section is filled out with zeros; a longer one refuses the map. More than one copy The last copy replaces the others. A copy shorter than 20 bytes is filled out with zeros. CRGB StarCraft: Remastered's player colours. For each of Players 1 to 8, how its colour is chosen, and three bytes that go with it. Remastered reads it for the map list, in a file of any revision: Random gives the player a random colour. Player choice leaves the colour to the player in the lobby. Custom uses the three bytes as red, green and blue. Palette gives the player a colour from the palette. Any mode above 3 counts as Palette. Which palette colour depends on the revision. The third byte of a Palette entry is a colour number from the table under COLR , 0 to 21, and the lobby shows it; it shows a Custom entry as Map specified . In a Brood War file ( VER 205 or 206) the game then applies COLR over it: a VER 206 test map whose Palette entries said Blue, Orange and Pink played with every player in its COLR colour. A VER 59, 63 or 64 file has no COLR to read, so there the third byte is the player's colour: a Hybrid test map's Palette entry saying Orange played orange. scmJS writes the COLR colour into the third byte, so the two agree in every revision, and in a VER 59, 63 or 64 file it writes CRGB whenever a colour is not the slot's own, since that is the only way those colours reach the game. StarCraft 1.16.1 reads neither section in those files. Custom was checked in a game, in VER 206, 205 and 63 files: the player's units took the stored colour. So Custom is the way to give a player one of Remastered's colours past the first twelve, or any other colour. Random and Player choice were played in a VER 63 file: the lobby showed both as Random, Player choice as a list the player can change, and each game gave those players a different colour, once black, one of the colours past the first twelve. All of these were single-player games against computers (found playing Remastered). What a game with several people does with Random, Player choice and Palette entries has not been played. h: The four words of a rect
b: The isometric record explained This part explains the ISOM record: how its words describe a lattice of terrain diamonds, what the values mean, and how an editor's isometric brush turns the lattice into tiles. It describes StarEdit's brush as worked out for Chkdraft , and the facts about real files hold for Blizzard's own maps. Diamonds and rects # The isometric brush does not paint tiles. It paints diamonds , 128 pixels wide and 64 tall: four tiles across and two down. Their centres sit on a lattice of points 64 pixels apart across and 32 apart down, at every other point of it, the ones whose coordinates add up to an even number. Diamond (x, y) is centred on pixel (64 × x, 32 × y), so the diamonds along the top and left edges of the map are half off it. The section does not store diamonds one by one. It stores rects : 64 by 32 pixels, two tiles side by side, with rect (x, y) having its top-left corner on lattice point (x, y). Two corners of every rect are diamond centres, and the line between its other two corners cuts the rect into two triangles, each one quarter of one of those diamonds: When x + y is even, the diamonds are centred on the top-left and bottom-right corners, and the cut runs from the top-right corner to the bottom-left. When x + y is odd, the diamonds are centred on the top-right and bottom-left corners, and the cut runs the other way. The rects are stored row by row from the top left, width ÷ 2 + 1 of them across and height + 1 down. That is one column and one row more than the map covers, so that the diamonds centred on the right and bottom edges have all four quarters stored. Rect (x, y) starts at byte (y × (width ÷ 2 + 1) + x) × 8. The four words of a rect # A rect is four 16-bit words, one for each of its sides, in the order left, top, right, bottom. Each word belongs to the quarter of a diamond that lies along that side, and holds the diamond's value and which quarter it is: word = value × 16 + flags value = word >> 4 flags = word & 0xF So every diamond's value is stored eight times, twice in each of the four rects it covers. In Blizzard's maps all eight copies agree. The flag bits give the quarter (bits 2 and 3) and which of its two sides of the rect the word is on (bit 1): Low four bits Quarter of its diamond The diamond's centre is the rect's Side of the rect 0x0 top-left bottom-right corner right 0x2 top-left bottom-right corner bottom 0x4 top-right bottom-left corner left 0x6 top-right bottom-left corner bottom 0x8 bottom-right top-left corner left 0xA bottom-right top-left corner top 0xC bottom-left top-right corner top 0xE bottom-left top-right corner right Bits 0 and 15 are scratch space for StarEdit's brush while it paints. They are 0 in a saved file. StarEdit writes the flag bits when its brush sets a diamond. The ground a map was started with, where nobody has painted since, can hold the right value with the flag bits left at 0. In Blizzard's maps every word with wrong flags is of this kind: the one flat terrain the map was started with. So a program reading the lattice should work out which diamond a word belongs to from where the word is in its rect, and treat the flags as a check at most. The words in the extra column and row that belong to diamonds past the edge of the lattice still hold values on Blizzard's maps. Nothing on the map depends on them. What a value means # A value is one of two things: A flat terrain. The diamond is that terrain all over. Every terrain StarEdit's palette offers has one value; on Jungle World, 1 is Dirt, 2 High Dirt and 3 Water. One shape of an edge set. An edge set is the border between two terrains that can touch: a cliff between low and high ground, a shore, the edge of jungle on dirt. A set takes fourteen values in a row, one for each shape the border can take through a diamond, and a diamond's value is the set's first value plus its shape, 0 to 13. Of the two terrains a set joins, one is laid as a patch on the other: high dirt on dirt, dirt on water, jungle on dirt. Here the terrain underneath is called the outside terrain and the patch the inside one, since the border runs around the inside. North is up the map. Shape The diamond is +0 Edge; the outside terrain to the north-west +1 Edge; the outside terrain to the north-east +2 Edge; the outside terrain to the south-east +3 Edge; the outside terrain to the south-west +4 Corner of the inside terrain, pointing north +5 Corner of the inside terrain, pointing east +6 Corner of the inside terrain, pointing south +7 Corner of the inside terrain, pointing west +8 Corner of the outside terrain, pointing east +9 Corner of the outside terrain, pointing west +10 Corner of the outside terrain, pointing south +11 Corner of the outside terrain, pointing north +12 Crossing: the inside terrain at the north and south corners, the outside at the east and west +13 Crossing: the outside terrain at the north and south corners, the inside at the east and west Each quarter of a diamond is the outside terrain, the inside terrain, or crossed by the border. The border runs through the centre of the diamond and meets the middle of a side, where the diamond beside it carries it on, so a run of edge diamonds draws one unbroken line. The values are not in any game file: StarEdit has them built in, for each tileset. Values by tileset lists them all. A worked example # A Jungle World map covered in Dirt, value 1, with one diamond of High Dirt painted on it with StarEdit's smallest brush: The painted diamond takes High Dirt's value, 2. The brush then joins it to the Dirt around it with the cliff between the two, values 17 to 30. The four diamonds that share a side with the centre become the four straight edges, 17 to 20, and the four beyond them, which only touch it at a point, become the corners where the high ground ends, 21 to 24. On the map this is a small raised plateau with a cliff all the way round, and no flat High Dirt tile at all: the centre diamond's four quarters all lie in rects that

h: Testing a map in the game
b: Game data Where the graphics come from, what is kept, Remastered, mods as data sets, and how the pictures are drawn. A map file holds numbers: a tile id per cell, a unit type per placed unit. The pictures those numbers refer to are in StarCraft's own files. That is Blizzard's data, not covered by this project's MIT license and not redistributable, so none of it ships with the editor. The editor reads it from a StarCraft installation you own, classic (1.16) or Remastered, copies what it needs once, and keeps the copy. This document is for map makers who want to know where the graphics come from and what is kept where, and for mod makers who want the editor to use a mod's files in place of the game's. It ends with how the pictures are drawn. The steps of the first-run dialog are in the installing guide ; building the editor from source is in Extracting for a source build . Attribution is not permission. Before publishing a fork or hosting a build, read ATTRIBUTION.md . Getting the files The recommended source is your own StarCraft installation. What is kept From either kind of installation, or the download, the editor copies about 930 files it draws with, about 30 MB from the classic archives: StarCraft: Remastered A Remastered installation keeps the game in its Data folder as a few large files with an index over them, and the editor reads the files it needs out of that with kascade. Data sets The editor draws from one set of game files at a time, and a *data set* names one. Testing a map in the game Tools ▸ Test Map needs the installed game rather than a copy of its data. Extracting for a source build A clone has no game data until it is extracted. How terrain is drawn Each tileset is five files. How units are drawn A unit type leads to its picture through four tables: In the source For developers.

Getting the files The recommended source is your own StarCraft installation. Blizzard's free map editor download is the fallback for anyone without one. Both are offered by the Game Data dialog on first use and by Help ▸ Game Data… afterwards; the installing guide walks through it. Source What you can do with it A StarCraft: Remastered installation Edit, with classic or Remastered graphics; test and play maps; watch replays A classic StarCraft (1.16) installation Edit, with classic graphics; test and play maps; watch replays Blizzard's map editor download Edit, with classic graphics; watch replays The map editor download carries the whole game's files, but it is a map editor's download, not the game. A copy made from it is enough to edit maps and watch replays. Testing a map or playing one, in the game or on the site's play page, needs StarCraft installed. A classic installation has two archives, StarDat.mpq and BrooDat.mpq , with a patch_rt.mpq beside them that is applied over both, as the game applies it. Brood War's archive is required: its unit table is the layout the editor reads, and the Ice, Desert and Twilight tilesets exist only there. A Remastered installation has no .mpq archives. The editor reads the same files out of its Data folder instead, along with Remastered's own pictures; see StarCraft: Remastered . Blizzard's map editor download is a 101 MB zip carrying both archives and a patch_rt.mpq . With that applied, they give the same files a 1.16.1 installation does. The editor fetches only those three members, 83 MB, through a small forwarder at gamedata.scmjs.dev , because a web page cannot read Blizzard's download server directly. The forwarder stores nothing. Either way the copy is made on your machine, in a background thread in the browser and in the app's own process on the desktop, so it happens once. Open maps pick the graphics up as they arrive. Where it looks # The editor settles on one source of game data when it starts, in this order: A data set you chose. When a data set other than the game's own is selected, its stored copy is asked for first. If that copy is gone, the editor says so and continues with the game's own files. Bundled with the build. A source build that ran npm run extract serves the files from its own folder. The desktop app serves its own copy the same way. A copy kept in the browser. An earlier install left the files in the browser's private storage for the site. The copy survives reloads and browser restarts. A browser with no such storage holds the files for the session only. The desktop app's search. The desktop app looks next to the app itself (so the two archives dropped beside it are found), in its own data folder, in SCM_DATA_DIR or STARCRAFT_DIR from the environment, in the usual install locations ( C:\Program Files (x86)\StarCraft , /Applications/StarCraft , a Wine prefix on Linux), and in ~/StarCraft and ~/Games/StarCraft . The first folder with the archives or a Remastered installation is copied into the app's data folder, which is then step 2. Someone whose game is where the installer put it never sees a dialog. Nothing. The editor runs without graphics and opens the Game Data dialog. Nothing is ever fetched from an address you did not name. scmjs.dev/editor , the nightly at scmjs.dev/nightly and the play page at scmjs.dev/play share one copy, so the game is installed once for all three. The page scmjs.dev/editor/data lists every copy the browser holds: what it is, where it came from, how many files and how large, and when it was made. Removing a copy # Remove copy in Help ▸ Game Data… deletes the stored copy. The editor then goes back to whatever step of the search above it would have reached without it, which in the browser is the dialog's first page again.

What is kept From either kind of installation, or the download, the editor copies about 930 files it draws with, about 30 MB from the classic archives: Files For tileset/<name>.cv5 , .vx4 , .vr4 , .vf4 , .wpe each tileset's terrain: tile groups, megatiles, pixels, walkability and height, palette tileset/<name>.ofire.pcx and three more remaps fire and explosion colours tileset/<name>.dddata.bin , stat_txt.tbl the doodad placement table; doodad and unit names arr/units.dat , flingy.dat , sprites.dat , images.dat , images.tbl the chain from a unit type to its picture arr/weapons.dat , upgrades.dat , techdata.dat the defaults in the Unit, Upgrade and Technology Settings dialogs arr/sfxdata.dat , sfxdata.tbl the list of the game's sounds, for the trigger sound picker game/tunit.pcx team colours scripts/iscript.bin animation scripts unit/**/*.grp , unit/**/*.lo? about 750 sprite sheets and their overlay positions unit/cmdbtns/cmdicons.grp , ticon.pcx command card icons, which plugins show The eight tilesets, in the order the map file numbers them, are Badlands, Space Platform, Installation, Ashworld, Jungle, Desert, Ice and Twilight. Files for playing # A copy kept in the browser also holds the files the game itself runs on: its sounds, its computer players' scripts, the rules of each game type, its cursors and interface pictures, and the pictures of things only a game in play draws (buildings going up, spell effects, selection circles). The editor opens none of them. They are for the play page at scmjs.dev/play, which runs maps and replays in the browser from the same copy. The desktop app's own copy leaves them out. From a Remastered installation, the copy can also keep what the game's real-time lighting reads: tick Keep the files for real-time lighting on the play page when you choose the folder. Choosing the folder again with the box ticked adds them to an existing copy. Copy In the browser In the desktop app From a classic installation or the download about 140 MB about 30 MB From a Remastered installation about 650 MB about 365 MB From Remastered, with the lighting files about 850 MB — Most of the difference is sounds, which Remastered stores uncompressed, and Remastered's own pictures. The files are written one at a time as they are read, so the size is on disk, not in memory. The play page can make the copy itself: choose a Remastered folder there and it is installed by the same code, into the same place. The editor then opens with Remastered graphics on, as it does after installing from its own dialog. Without game data # Without any of this the editor still runs. Terrain is drawn in flat colours, one per tileset, units and sprites as coloured markers, and everything else works: every layer, every dialog, opening and saving. The palettes that would need the graphics say so.

StarCraft: Remastered A Remastered installation keeps the game in its Data folder as a few large files with an index over them, and the editor reads the files it needs out of that with kascade . Choose the folder the game is installed in, the one that holds .build.info . Nothing in the folder is changed. The browser asks whether to upload the folder's files; nothing is uploaded, and the editor reads only the parts it needs. Out of an installation of several gigabytes the editor keeps about 1,700 files, 365 MB. Most of that is Remastered's own terrain and sprite pictures, and what its water and lava need to move; see Remastered graphics . A Remastered copy turns View ▸ Remastered Graphics on when it is made. Remastered also added tiles, and so doodads, to seven of the eight tilesets (Installation is unchanged). Everything the 1.16 tile tables hold is in its tables unchanged, so a map made for 1.16 draws the same from either copy. A map that uses the added tiles needs the Remastered files: from a 1.16 copy those tiles have no picture. There are two ways in: With no graphics yet , choose the Remastered folder in the Game Data dialog. The result is the editor's copy of the game's files. The desktop app's search finds a Remastered installation in the usual places the same way. With a classic copy or the download already in place , choose Add StarCraft: Remastered… under Data sets in Help ▸ Game Data…. It is installed beside that copy as a data set of its own, and the list switches between the two. Of Remastered's high-definition art, the terrain and sprites are read at twice the classic size. The four-times versions in the same installation are not used.

Data sets The editor draws from one set of game files at a time, and a data set names one. The default is the game's own. Any other is a mod's: the game's files in the same formats with some of them replaced, such as its own units.dat , graphics, sounds or stat_txt.tbl . A Remastered installation added beside a classic copy is a data set too. To add one, open Help ▸ Game Data…, choose Add a data set… , give it a name and pick a folder. The folder holds the game's two archives, because a mod replaces files rather than bringing all of them, together with the mod's own files: MyMod/ StarDat.mpq the game's archives, required BrooDat.mpq patch_rt.mpq applied over the two, if present mymod.mpq a mod's own archive arr/units.dat loose files, by the game's paths unit/terran/marine.grp rez/… Where several sources have the same file, the later one wins, as in the game: StarDat.mpq , then BrooDat.mpq , then the other archives in name order, and loose files under arr , unit , tileset , game , scripts or rez over all of them. Anything else in the folder is ignored. The data set is stored under its own name beside the game's copy, so removing one leaves the others alone. The Data sets list appears in Help ▸ Game Data… once there is a second one, and the choice is remembered. Switching drops everything decoded from the previous files, since the same ids now mean different pictures, and loads again; an open map stays open and picks the new graphics up as they arrive. What a data set cannot be: A mod that extends the game's tables. The table sizes (228 unit types, 130 weapons, 61 upgrades, 44 technologies), the tileset formats and the map file's fixed-width sections are the game's. A mod with more unit types, a longer .dat layout or extended tilesets is not supported. A mod made for Remastered's storage. A data set is read from .mpq archives and loose files; a mod packaged in Remastered's own storage format is not supported. Names # The game names things in stat_txt.tbl : entries 0 to 227 are the unit types, and the weapon, upgrade and technology tables each point into the same file. The editor's own name tables are StarEdit's, which read better in about fifty places ("Cargo Ship (Unused)" where the game says "Unused") and are the names the text trigger format and other editors share. The rule is per entry: where the loaded data's name differs from what the game's own data says for that id, the loaded name shows; everywhere else, StarEdit's stands. With Blizzard's files nothing changes. With a mod's, whatever it renamed shows the new name in every palette, list and dialog, and the text trigger parser accepts both names, so a trigger printed under a mod reads back.

t: Testing a map in the game
b: Testing a map in the game Tools ▸ Test Map needs the installed game rather than a copy of its data. Neither version of StarCraft opens a map handed to it from outside, so the editor writes the map into a scmJS folder under the game's Maps folder, where Single Player ▸ Custom Game lists it. The desktop app finds the installation in the same places its search looks, or takes a folder you pick and remembers it, and starts the game. Chrome and Edge write into a folder you pick once and remember. Other browsers download the file. At scmjs.dev, Tools ▸ Test Map in Browser plays the map on the play page instead, from the copy described above. It needs a copy made from your own installation, not from the map editor download.

Extracting for a source build A clone has no game data until it is extracted. The script finds the archives on its own or takes them as arguments: npm run extract # look for an installation npm run extract -- --from "/mnt/c/Program Files (x86)/StarCraft" # a folder npm run extract -- path/to/StarDat.mpq path/to/BrooDat.mpq # the archives themselves SCM_DATA_DIR=~/games/sc npm run extract # from the environment With no arguments it looks in SCM_DATA_DIR or STARCRAFT_DIR , then in the repository's own fixtures/data/ , then in the usual install locations for the platform, including the Windows drives a WSL session sees under /mnt . A patch_rt.mpq found with the two is applied over them. The script reads .mpq archives only, from a classic installation or the map editor download; it cannot read a Remastered installation. With only Remastered, run the dev server and install from Help ▸ Game Data… as in the browser. Command Does npm run extract everything npm run extract:tilesets the tileset graphics only npm run extract:units the unit tables, sprites and scripts only npm run check:assets report what is on disk without opening any archive Everything lands in public/ (its README is the inventory), which is gitignored along with fixtures/ . The run takes a few seconds and can be repeated at any time; repeat it after a game patch or after changing what the scripts take. npm run dev and npm run build warn when the files are missing and carry on, because the editor runs without them. A green test run and a working dev server therefore prove nothing about the extraction; run it. The container image # The container image at ghcr.io/scm-js/scm-js carries no game data and refuses to serve the paths the files would be at, so a container starts at step 5 of the search and asks, like the hosted editor. To serve your own extraction to your own browser instead, mount an extracted tree over those paths: docker run --rm -p 8080:80 \ -v "$PWD/public/tileset:/usr/share/nginx/html/tileset:ro" \ -v "$PWD/public/arr:/usr/share/nginx/html/arr:ro" \ -v "$PWD/public/unit:/usr/share/nginx/html/unit:ro" \ -v "$PWD/public/game:/usr/share/nginx/html/game:ro" \ -v "$PWD/public/scripts:/usr/share/nginx/html/scripts:ro" \ ghcr.io/scm-js/scm-js:latest That is a copy on your own machine served to your own browser. Publishing an image with the files inside, or serving one from a public address, is redistributing Blizzard's data; see ATTRIBUTION.md .

How terrain is drawn Each tileset is five files. A tile id in the map file leads through them to pixels: MTXM tile id ──(bits 4–14)──▶ CV5 group ──(bits 0–3)──▶ VX4 megatile VX4 megatile ──▶ 16 minitile refs (bit 0 = flipped) ──▶ VR4 8×8 bitmaps ──▶ WPE palette Bit 15 of a tile id is not part of the tile. The game files it as a creep flag, but a tile with it set plays as the plain tile: no creep shows and no Zerg building can go there. The editor draws such a tile as the tile the other bits name. A tile is a 32×32 megatile made of sixteen 8×8 minitiles, each an index into the tileset's 256-colour palette. The CV5 groups megatiles into terrain types with their variations and edge pieces, which is where the terrain palette's list of terrains comes from. The VF4 holds each minitile's walkability and height, which the elevation and buildability overlays, the placement checks and the Walkability plugin all read. The editor draws each tileset once into one large image, the atlas , and draws the map by copying tiles out of it. Only the tileset the open map uses is decoded; the others are fetched into the browser's cache in the background so a later map opens faster. Water and lava # The graphics are indexed colour, and StarCraft animates water and lava by rotating a few short bands of the palette every eight game frames, about a third of a second at the Fastest speed. The band tables per tileset are the game's own; Space Platform and Installation have none. View ▸ Animate Water turns the animation on, and Preferences ▸ View sets the speed from a quarter to four times the game's. The minimap and the far zoom levels, which draw average tile colours, do not animate. Remastered graphics # View ▸ Remastered Graphics draws the terrain, units and sprites from StarCraft: Remastered's own pictures in place of the classic ones, and switches back at any time. It needs game data from a Remastered installation ; with a 1.16 copy the option says so and the classic graphics stay. Installing from Remastered turns the option on; from then on it is yours, and Preferences ▸ View holds whether the editor starts with it. Terrain. Remastered keeps one picture per megatile, 64 pixels square where the classic one is 32, numbered as the same installation's tile tables are. So the map is untouched, and so is everything the editor works out from the tiles (walkability, height, buildability, the terrain brushes): only where a megatile's pixels come from changes. Each picture is decoded the first time it is drawn. Turning the option on loads the tileset's Remastered file once (3 to 21 MB); the classic terrain keeps drawing until it has arrived. Units and sprites. Where the classic game has a GRP per image, Remastered has a sprite sheet whose frame N is the GRP's frame N. So the animation scripts, facings and positions are the same, and only the pixels differ. A second picture marks what takes the player's colour. About 780 of the 885 images the editor uses have a Remastered sprite; the rest, and any whose file has not arrived yet, are drawn from their GRP, so the two can appear side by side. At 100% zoom both are drawn at half their size, at 200% pixel for pixel, where the classic graphics are each pixel doubled. The tile palette, doodad and unit thumbnails, the paste preview and an exported map image follow the same option. A plugin that asks for a unit's or a sprite's picture is always given the classic one. Water and lava. Remastered does not rotate the palette. It draws the ground and then bends the picture: water is the ground seen through two layers of ripples drifting across the map, and lava the ground seen through heat, which shows on whatever glows red and leaves dark rock alone. A table per tileset says which megatiles take the effect, and a mask for each says where on it, so a shoreline tile moves on its water side only. The editor does the same with View ▸ Animate Water on. Ashworld's is the lava; the other tilesets' is water; Space Platform and Installation have neither. Desert's tar is left still, as in the game. How far the picture bends and how the ripples drift are the game's own figures. How large the ripples are and how fast they change are not in its files, so they can be adjusted: Preferences ▸ View ▸ Graphics ▸ Water and lava has the bend, the glint, the two ripple sizes, their rate and the lava's heat, and the water speed on the same page applies to both. This needs WebGL, which every current browser has; without it the water and lava are drawn still. An exported map image is always still. Three things differ from the game: The water's glint comes from the ripples alone; the game places a highlight by the middle of the screen, which in an editor would follow the window about. The sprites are drawn flat, without the game's lighting. The minimap and the far zoom levels keep the classic average colours.

How units are drawn A unit type leads to its picture through four tables: units.dat[id].flingy ─▶ flingy.dat.sprite ─▶ sprites.dat.image ─▶ images.dat.grp ─▶ images.tbl ─▶ unit\…\*.grp A GRP is a sprite sheet: a set of frames in the tileset's palette, with one frame per facing for anything that turns. The copy follows this chain from all 228 unit types and from all 517 entries of the sprite table, so pure sprites and doodad overlays have graphics as well. Sprite sheets are loaded the first time something needs them, so a melee map loads minerals, geysers and start locations and nothing else. Team colour is palette indices 8 to 15 of a GRP, remapped through the row of tunit.pcx for the owning player's colour and painted through the tileset's palette. Sprites therefore need the tileset loaded as well. Pink and the custom RGB colours a Remastered map can set have no row to remap to, so the editor makes a ramp for them. Animation # Placed units run their idle animations when View ▸ Animate Units is on. Every unit's script is stepped once per game frame, 42 ms at Fastest, on the same clock as the water, and Preferences ▸ View scales the rate on its own. Each unit is a stack of images (shadow, body and overlays), each with its own script. Buildings play their Built animation; tanks and Goliaths play StarEditInit , StarEdit's own hook, which adds the turret. That is what gives turning turrets, pulsing Hatcheries, marines looking around, the Nexus glow, Starport lights and refinery smoke. Damage overlays follow hit points: a building below two thirds burns (Terran), sparks (Protoss) or bleeds (Zerg) at the positions its .lo file gives, with more of them the lower the hit points and the large effect below one third. Fire draws through the tileset's own remap tables. Cloaked units draw half transparent. Anything that needs the running game (attacks, sounds, projectiles and condition jumps) is skipped.

In the source For developers. The extraction is one module shared by every route, and the drawing is under src/formats/ . Development Running from source, the repository layout and conventions, tests, the desktop app, releases and the docs site. How to run scmJS from source, how it is tested, built and released, and what to know before changing it. This is for contributors, and for anyone building the desktop app or the container image themselves. Each topic is written down in one place: Topic Where What the editor does, for map makers guide.md ; the README is the short version Installing the editor installing.md What happens to a map file on open and save file-formats.md The scenario format, section by section chk-format.md Triggers, conditions and actions triggers.md TrigScript, the trigger scripting language trigscript.md , trigscript-language.md for the language of programs, and trigscript-library.md for its standard library; the compiler is in the TrigScript plugin 's repository Where the graphics come from, data sets, how they are drawn game-data.md Using and writing plugins, the plugin API plugins.md , and the reference at docs.scmjs.dev/api Each plugin's internals its own repository's README Running, building, releasing, contributing this file Per-area design notes for working on the code .claude/internals/*.md , indexed by CLAUDE.md Provenance of adapted code and data ATTRIBUTION.md Release notes docs/releases/ The design notes under .claude/internals/ are one file per area of the code (terrain, saving, the plugin host, sync, …). They record why the code is the way it is, and the traps that are not visible from the code. Read the note for an area before changing it. Getting started You need Node.js 22.18 or newer (the extraction scripts import TypeScript directly through Node's type stripping) and git. Commands npm run build is the type-check: tsc -b covers the app, the scripts and the desktop main process (tsconfig.app.json, tsconfig.node.json, tsconfig.desktop.json). Repository layout Conventions These are the rules everything else follows. The plugin host plugins.md is written for someone who has the npm package and none of this repository. h: With the game engine beside it
b: Getting started You need Node.js 22.18 or newer (the extraction scripts import TypeScript directly through Node's type stripping) and git. git clone https://github.com/scm-js/scm-js cd scm-js npm install npm run dev # http://localhost:5173 The first npm run dev or npm run build needs a network connection: a predev / prebuild hook fetches the default plugins at their pinned versions into the gitignored plugins/ folder, where the build compiles them in (see Defaults and vendoring ). After that it works offline. The same hook reports what game data is on disk, and warns rather than fails when there is none. Game data. The editor draws with StarCraft's own graphics, which are never committed. Without them terrain is flat colours and units are markers, and everything else works. There are two ways to get them into a source build: Help ▸ Game Data… in the running dev editor. Point it at your StarCraft folder, the classic game (1.16) or StarCraft: Remastered. This is the recommended way, and the only one for Remastered: the copy goes into the browser's storage, as it does for any user. npm run extract reads StarDat.mpq and BrooDat.mpq from a classic installation (it finds them on its own, or takes --from <folder> ) and writes the files into public/ . It does not read Remastered's files. game-data.md has the details. No build, container image or hosted site carries the data or an address to fetch it from; ATTRIBUTION.md has the terms. Dev deep links # Query parameters jump straight to a UI state, which is the fastest way to work on a screen or take a screenshot: /?nosplash skip the splash /?nosplash&layer=units select a layer: terrain, doodads, units, sprites, locations, fog, clipboard /?nosplash&dialog=playerSettings open a dialog by id; repeatable /?nosplash&dialog=preferences&page=editing open a dialog at one of its pages /?nosplash&zoom=0.5&tileset=ice zoom level and tileset /?nosplash&mode=tile terrain palette mode: isom, rect, tile /?nosplash&layer=fog&fogPlayer=3 view and paint one player's fog An unknown layer or dialog id is reported in the console with the list of valid ones. React's "Components" performance track is off in development because it slows mounting badly; set VITE_REACT_TRACKS=1 to turn it on when profiling renders. With the game engine beside it # Tools ▸ Test Map in Browser, and the replay analysis other plugins use, come from the scm-sim plugin . The plugin holds no engine: it opens the play page, which has to be on the editor's own origin at /play/ , as it is on scmjs.dev. The play page is built from the scm-sim engine repository, which is not public, so without it these features do not work in a local build. With a checkout of it, run both dev servers and put one origin in front of them: SCMJS_BASE=/editor/ npm run dev -- --port 5173 # this repository npm run dev:web # in scm-sim, port 5174 npm run dev:site # this repository: http://localhost:5180/editor/ Both dev servers keep their own hot reload. DEV_SITE_PORT , DEV_SITE_EDITOR and DEV_SITE_SIM change the three ports.

Commands npm run dev # Vite dev server npm run dev:site # one origin over the editor and scm-sim (above) npm run build # tsc -b (the type-check) + vite build → dist/ npm run preview # serve dist/ locally npm run lint # oxlint, with the React hook rules; does not type-check npm test # vitest, a few seconds, no browser npm run test:watch npm run test:maps # write tests/maps again from the code that makes them npm run test:e2e # the browser tests, against dist/ (build first) npx vitest run tests/chk.test.ts # one file npx vitest run -t "flood fill" # tests matching a name npm run extract # game data from a classic installation → public/ npm run check:assets # what game data is on disk npm run i18n # check the translations against the source (-- --write updates them) npm run docs:reference # rewrite the generated tables of the trigger and CHK references npm run build:docs # the documentation site → docs-site/ npm run vendor:plugins # bring plugins/ up to date (predev and prebuild run it) npm run bundle:runtimes # copy the default plugins' runtimes into dist/ (desktop and image builds) npm run build:plugin-types # the plugin typings → plugin-api/ npm run desktop # run the desktop app against dist/ npm run build:desktop # installers for this OS → release/ npm run build:image # the container image, tagged scmjs npm run build is the type-check: tsc -b covers the app, the scripts and the desktop main process ( tsconfig.app.json , tsconfig.node.json , tsconfig.desktop.json ). The app config is strict: noUnusedLocals , noUnusedParameters , verbatimModuleSyntax (so import type for types) and erasableSyntaxOnly (so no enums and no constructor parameter properties). Lint, the tests and the build run on every pull request and every push to main .
